|L(j\omega )|&=A_{v}^{3}\left[1+(\omega b)^{2}\right]^{-1/2}
\left[1+(\omega a)^{2}\right]^{-1}\cr
{\rm arg}L&=\pi -\tan ^{-1}\omega b-2\tan ^{-1}\omega a\cr}\tag{9}$$

Oscillation in the Barkhausen sense needs
${\rm arg}L=2k\pi $,

$$\tan ^{-1}\omega_{0}b+2\tan ^{-1}\omega_{0}a=\pi \tag{10}$$

$0<{\rm arg}<{3\pi /2}$, so (10) has a
solution for every $b$, nominally

$$\omega_{0}\approx {1\over a}\tag{11}$$

for $b\gg a$, because $\tan ^{-1}\omega_{0}b
\to \pi /2$ and $2\tan ^{-1}\omega_{0}a\to
\pi /2$.  At that $\omega_{0}$

$$|L(j\omega_{0})|\approx {A_{v}^{3}\over
\sqrt{1+(b/a)^{2}}\;2}\approx A_{v}^{3}{a\over 2b}
\tag{12}$$

so that

$$|L(j\omega_{0})|>1\iff A_{v}^{3}>2{b\over a}
\tag{13}$$

which is (7) for $b\gg a$.  In other words the
dominant pole compensation kills the loop gain
at the $0\,{\rm deg}$ crossover.  There is an

$$b_{c}\approx {1\over 2}A_{v}^{3}a\tag{14}$$

$$C_{Lc}\approx \left({1\over 2}A_{v}^{3}-1\right)C_{0}\tag{15}$$

${\cal O}(10^{2}-10^{3})C_{0}$ for a normal
$A_{v}\sim 10-20$, beyond which the small
signal pole pair is in the ${\rm Re}\,s<0$
half plane.  The meta stable $V_{A}=V_{B}=
V_{C}=V_{T}$ point becomes small signal stable.
For $b\to \infty $,

$$L(s)\to -{A_{v}^{3}\over sb(1+sa)^{2}}\tag{16}$$

a two pole amplifier dominant pole compensated,
which is stable; $C_{L}\to\infty $ shorts the
loop for $a.\,c.$  The normal $360^{0}$ linear
sinusoidal ring mode is extinguished and the
circuit will not start up from thermal noise.

That is the {\it linear\/} story.

Put the inverters back as large signal relays,
$I_{o}=I$ when on, $V_{T}=V_{DD}/2$,
$T_{d}=t_{p2}+t_{p3}$ the delay of the two
unloaded inverters.  With

$$C_{L}{{dV_{A}}\over {dt}}=I_{1}(V_{C})\tag{17}$$

$$V_{C}(t)= {\rm sgn}\left[V_{A}(t-T_{d})-V_{T}\right]\tag{18}$$

in the ideal relay approximation the circuit is
a first order plus delay relay.  Let $V_{A}$
cross $V_{T}$ upward at $t=0$.  $V_{C}=1$ for
$T_{d}$ more, so

$$V_{A}=V_{T}+I\,T_{d}/C_{L}\equiv V_{T}+\Delta
\tag{19}$$

at $t=T_{d}$ when $V_{C}$ flips to $0$ and
$V_{A}$ ramps down with $dV_{A}/dt=-I/C_{L}$,
recrosses $V_{T}$ at $t=2T_{d}$, continues to
$V_{T}-\Delta $ at $t=3T_{d}$ etc.  The system
has a limit cycle

$$\eqalign{
\Delta &= I\,T_{d}/C_{L}\cr
T_{0}&\approx 4T_{d}\cr}\tag{20}$$

for {\it any\/} finite $C_{L}$.  For $C_{L}$
small $\Delta \gg V_{DD}$ the relay saturates
and you get the ordinary rail to rail
$T_{0}\approx 2N\,t_{p}+k\,R_{o}C_{L}$ ring
oscillator.  For $C_{L}$ large

$$\Delta \propto 1/C_{L}\to 0\tag{21}$$

so the large signal swing collapses to an
infinitesimal triangle about $V_{T}$ of period
$\approx 4T_{d}$ and (20) ceases to be valid
as soon as $\Delta $ becomes of the order of the
linear transition width of the inverter,
${\cal O}(V_{DD}/A_{v})$.  Inside the transition
width the relay model has to be replaced by the
linear model (1) which, as we have seen, is
damped.  The infinitesimal limit cycle is then
damped to the stable $V_{T}$ DC point.

In text book digital language that is normally
phrased as {\it the circuit continues to oscillate
for any $C_{L}$, only more and more slowly\/}.
If oscillation is meant as a robust, self starting
rail to rail clock that grows out of noise, the
statement is: beyond (15) the conventional ring
mode disappears, the amplitude $\Delta \to 0$,
and for all engineering purposes the ring has
stalled at $V_{A}\approx V_{B}\approx V_{C}
\approx V_{DD}/2$.

With $C_{L}\to\infty $ {\it qua\/} $a.\,c.$
short the familiar $RC$ astable consisting of
one inverter loaded by $C_{L}$ buffered by the
other two is recovered as the $a.\,c.$
degenerate form of (20).  It is normally drawn
as the one inverter $RC$ relaxation oscillator
and, with ideal comparators, it does oscillate
for any $R\,C$.  With normal CMOS inverters the
oscillation is vanishingly small once (15) is
exceeded.

> {\it Remark:\/}  In most introductory treatments
> the ${\cal O}(1/C_{L})$ collapse of the swing
> is neglected and the circuit is said {\it not\/}
> to fail to oscillate: $f_{0}\approx
> \left[2Nt_{p}+0.7R_{o}C_{L}\right]^{-1}\to 0$ but
> $\ne 0$.  The linear, Barkhausen, start up
> failure described above is the correct analog
> description.

With the usual ${\rm ideal~self~loaded}$ language
the circuit is the textbook Hajimiri Lee inverter ring.

Put $W_{p}/W_{n}$ so that the rise and the fall are
symmetric and change it with $W_{p}/W_{n}={\rm const}$

$${C_{L}\approx C_{g}+C_{d}\propto W\qquad 
R_{o}\approx 1/g_{m}\propto 1/W\qquad 
I_{av}\propto W}$$

so that to first order

$$t_{d}\approx 0.69R_{o}C_{L}\approx 
{{C_{L}V_{DD}}\over {I_{av}}}={\rm const.}$$

$$\omega _{0}\approx {1\over {2Nt_{d}}}={\rm const.}\tag{*}$$

for the $W$ dependent, intrinsic, load.
With a fixed wiring load $C_{\rm ext}$

$$C_{L}=C_{\rm ext}+Wc_{0}\qquad 
\omega _{0}\propto {W\over {C_{\rm ext}+Wc_{0}}}\tag{**}$$

and ($*$) is the $C_{\rm ext}\ll Wc_{0}$ limit.
The normal, saturated, short channel, current
is still $\propto W$ so that

$$P_{DC}=NC_{L}V_{DD}^{2}f_{0}\propto Wf_{0}\tag{***}$$

i. e. in the self loaded limit $f_{0}={\rm const.}$
and you burn twice the power.

For the Hajimiri-Lee ISF

$${\cal L}\{\Delta \omega \}=10\log \left[
{1\over {8\pi ^{2}\Delta f^{2}}}\,
{{{\overline{i_{n}^{2}}}\over {\Delta f}}\,
{\Gamma _{rms}^{2}\over {q_{max}^{2}}}}\right] \tag{1}$$

$$q_{max}=C_{L}V_{DD}\propto W\tag{2}$$

$${{{\overline{i_{n}^{2}}}\over {\Delta f}}=
4kT\gamma g_{d0}+K_{f}{{g_{m}^{2}}\over {WLC_{ox}} }{1\over f}
\propto W\tag{3}}$$

in white and in the normal $S_{v}=K_{f}/WLC_{ox}f$,
$S_{i}=g_{m}^{2}S_{v}$, flicker model.
$g_{d0}\propto g_{m}\propto W$ in the square law
or in the velocity saturated limit.
$\Gamma _{rms}$ and $c_{0}$, the rms and the
d.c. value of the impulse sensitivity function, depend
only on the normalized wave form and stay {\it pro
forma} constant if the symmetry $W_{p}/W_{n}$ is kept,
i. e. if the wave form stays symmetric the ${\rm 1/f}$
up conversion $c_{0}\approx 0$ stays suppressed.

Hence from (1)-(3)

$${\cal L}\propto {{{\overline{i_{n}^{2}}}}\over
{q_{max}^{2}}}\propto {W\over {W^{2}}}={1\over W}\tag{4}$$

in power.  In the familiar Leeson form, for the
$N$ stage ring, Razavi,

$${\cal L}\{\Delta \omega \}\approx
{8\over {3\eta }}{{kT}\over {P_{DC}}}{{V_{DD}}\over
{V_{{\rm char}}}}\left({{\omega _{0}}\over {\Delta
\omega }}\right)^{2}\tag{5}$$

$$P_{DC}= {\rm (***)} $$

the same $1/P_{DC}\propto 1/W$ law.

I. e. in ($*$) $f_{0}$ does not move, $P_{DC}$ doubles
and the white, ${1\over {f^{2}}}$, side band power is
halved,

$${\cal L}_{w}\rightarrow {1\over 2}{\cal L}_{w}\;\;
-3\,{\rm dB~in~}{\cal L},-6\,{\rm dB~in~}{\cal L}^{1/2}
\tag{6}$$

$$\sigma _{J}^{2}= {{\kappa ^{2}}t}\qquad 
\kappa ^{2}\propto {{kT}\over {C_{L}V_{DD}^{2}}}\propto
{1\over W}\tag{7}$$

$$\kappa \propto {1\over {\sqrt{W}}}\qquad 
\sigma _{T}= \kappa \sqrt{T_{0}}\propto {1\over {\sqrt{W}}}$$

for the period jitter.  Colloquially you have put two
identical rings in parallel.

For the ${\rm 1/f}$ induced ${1\over {f^{3}}}$ skirt
(1) is normally written with the $c_{0}$ term,

$${\cal L}_{1/f^{3}}\propto c_{0}^{2}
{{{\overline{i_{n,1/f}^{2}}}}\over {q_{max}^{2}}}
{1\over {\Delta f^{3}}}\propto {1\over W}\tag{8}$$

in the $S_{i}\propto W$ model, i. e. another $3\,{\rm
dB}$ per octave of $W$.  Writing the flicker explicitly
as $K_{f}/WL$,

$${\cal L}_{1/f^{3}}\propto {{K_{f}}\over {WLC_{ox}}}
{{g_{m}^{2}}\over {q_{max}^{2}}}\propto
{1\over {W}}\,{{W^{2}}\over {W^{2}}}={1\over W}\tag{9}$$

and, if you count the $WL$ in the denominator as an
independent area factor, often quoted as

$${\cal L}_{1/f^{3}}\propto {1\over {W^{2}L}}\approx
{6\,{\rm dB~per~octave~of}~W}\tag{10}$$

and with $q_{max}^{2}\propto W^{2}$ as ${1\over {W^{3}}}$,
$9\,{\rm dB}$ per octave, in the current
$S_{i}=K_{f}I_{D}^{2}/WLC_{ox}f$ notation.  Any of (8)-(10)
is quoted as {\it the close in noise goes down
$6-9\,{\rm dB}$ per doubling of area.}

In Leeson FoM language

$${\rm FoM}={\cal L}\{\Delta f\}
-20\log \left({{f_{0}}\over {\Delta f}}\right)
+10\log \left({{P_{DC}}\over {1\,{\rm mW}}}\right)
\approx {\rm const.}\tag{11}$$

so that the ${\rm FoM}$ is to first order $W$
independent.  You buy the $3\,{\rm dB}$, $6\,{\rm dB}$
close in, at the price of twice the dissipation and,
in the ideal ($*$) limit, at the same $f_{0}$.
Normalised to $f_{0}$, i. e. at the same fractional
offset $\Delta f/f_{0}$ or the same jitter FoM,
there is no net improvement.

With ($**$) the absolute side band at a fixed absolute
$\Delta f$ is

$${\cal L}\{\Delta f\}\propto 
20\log f_{0}-10\log P_{DC}\tag{12}$$

so that with an extrinsic, $W$ independent, load the
$f_{0}$ increase $\propto 20\log f_{0}$ eventually
wins and the absolute ${\cal L}\{\Delta f\}$ gets
{\it worse} by $\approx +3\,{\rm dB}$ per octave of $W$
while ${\cal L}\{\Delta f/f_{0}\}$ and the jitter FoM
remain $\approx $ flat.  In deep sub $\mu$ the $g_{m}
\propto W^{\alpha }$, $\alpha <1$, wiring $C$ and
gate leakage make the $3\,{\rm dB}$ an upper bound.
Loosely phrased as {\it doubling the device has, to
first order, no effect on the oscillator FoM.}

> {\it Remark:} For a current starved, fixed $I_{SS}$,
> ring $P_{DC}={\rm const.}$, $f_{0}\propto 1/C_{L}\propto
> 1/W$ in ($*$) and (5) gives ${\cal L}\{\Delta f\}
> \propto f_{0}^{2}\propto 1/W^{2}$, $-6\,{\rm dB}$
> at fixed $\Delta f$, $-3\,{\rm dB}$ at fixed
> $\Delta f/f_{0}$, i. e. the same $1/W$ law for the
> fractional side band.

With the (text book) ${\cal C}_{L}\propto W$
normalisation the ring is a constant ${\cal F}{\cal O}{\cal M}$
oscillator.  In Leeson's form

$$ {\cal L}(\Delta \omega )\propto 
{\overline {i_{n}^{2}}\over q_{{\rm max}}^{2}}
{1\over {\Delta \omega }^{2}}\propto 
{FkT\over P_{{\rm diss}}}{\omega _{0}^{2}\over {\Delta \omega }^{2}}\tag
{*}$$

$P_{{\rm diss}}$ is the D.C. plus the dynamic power

$$P_{{\rm diss}}\approx NP_{av}\approx Nf_{0}{\cal C}_{L}V_{DD}^{2}
+N I_{av}V_{DD}\propto {\cal C}_{L}\propto W \tag{1}$$

$$f_{0}\approx {1\over {2Nt_{d}}}\qquad 
t_{d}\approx {{\cal C}_{L}V_{DD}\over I_{av}}\approx 
{{\cal C}_{L}\over g_{m}}\tag{2}$$

$${\cal C}_{L}=N_{S}W{\cal C}_{{\rm ox}}+{\cal C}_{w}\propto W\qquad 
I_{av}\propto W\qquad g_{m}\propto W\tag{3}$$

$$\overline {i_{n}^{2}}=4kT\gamma g_{m}\propto W\tag{4}$$

$$q_{{\rm max}}={\cal C}_{L}V_{DD}\propto W\tag{5}$$

for the white noise and, for the conventional
${\overline {v_{n,1/f}^{2}}}=K_{F}/WLC_{{\rm ox}}f$,

$$\overline {i_{n,1/f}^{2}}=g_{m}^{2}{\overline {v_{n,1/f}^{2}}}
\propto W^{\alpha }\tag{6}$$

So that in the normal time domain language the
r.m.s. threshold jitter in one transition

$${\sigma _{t}^{2}}={{\overline {v_{n}^{2}}}\over S^{2}}
={{kT/{\cal C}_{L}}\over {\left(I_{av}/{\cal C}_{L}\right)^{2}}}
={{kT{\cal C}_{L}}\over {I_{av}^{2}}}\propto {1\over W}\tag{7}$$

$S=I_{av}/{\cal C}_{L}$ is the slew rate at the
threshold, and for the $N$ stage ring

$${\sigma _{T}^{2}}\approx N{\sigma _{t}^{2}}\tag{8}$$

$${\cal L}(\Delta \omega )\approx
{{\omega _{0}^{2}{\sigma _{T}^{2}}}\over {2T_{0}{\Delta \omega }^{2}}}
\approx {{\Gamma _{{\rm rms}}^{2}}\over {8\pi ^{2}{\Delta \omega }^{2}}}
{{\overline {i_{n}^{2}}}\over {q_{{\rm max}}^{2}}}\propto 
{{\overline {i_{n}^{2}}}\over {q_{{\rm max}}^{2}}}\tag{9}$$

cf. Hajimiri-Lee, {\it JSSC} {\bf 33}, 179 (1998)

$${\cal L}(\Delta \omega )={8\over 3\eta }N{{kT}\over P}
{{V_{DD}}\over {V_{{\rm char}}}}{{\omega _{0}^{2}}\over {\Delta \omega
^{2}}}\tag{10}$$

$$V_{{\rm char}}=E_{c}L/\gamma \tag{11}$$

for the $1/f^{2}$ region and with (6) for the
$1/f^{3}$ region.  I. e. to first order on a $W/L=$
const, $V_{DD}=$ const. basis

$$f_{0}\propto {g_{m}\over {\cal C}_{L}}={\rm const.}\tag{12}$$

$$ {\cal L}_{{\rm white}}\propto {1\over P}\propto {1\over W}
\qquad {\cal L}_{1/f^{3}}\propto {1\over {W^{1\to 2}}}\tag{13}$$

The often quoted form is ($*$): the oscillator
figure of merit

$${\cal F}{\cal O}{\cal M}= {\cal L}(\Delta \omega )
+10\log {{P_{{\rm diss}}}\over {1{\rm mW}}}
-20\log {{\omega _{0}}\over {\Delta \omega }} ={\rm const.}\tag{14}$$

is (to first order) independent of $W$.  If you are
willing to burn the $\times 2$ power the absolute
(single side band) phase noise power ${\cal L}$,
${\rm dBcHz^{-1}}$, goes down by

$${{{\cal L}(2W)}\over {{\cal L}(W)}}\approx {1\over 2}\;\;
{\rm in\;power}\approx {1\over {\sqrt{2}}}\;\;{\rm in\;
voltage\;or\;jitter}\tag{15}$$

$10\log 2\approx 3\,{\rm dB}$ in power,
$20\log \sqrt{2}\approx 3\,{\rm dB}$ in amplitude, for
the normal $1/f^{2}$ thermal region, $\approx 3-6\,{\rm dB}$
for the $1/f^{3}$ region according as $A_{F}\approx
2\to 1$ in ${\overline {i_{n,1/f}^{2}}}\propto
I_{D}^{A_{F}}/WL$, at the expense of a $\times 2$ in
$I_{DD}$ and in $P_{{\rm diss}}$.  Normally quoted,
loosely, as {\it no (first order) change in (normalised)
phase noise} or {\it no change in ${\cal F}{\cal O}{\cal M}$}.

In particular for the textbook $3\times C_{g}$
loaded loop (12) $f_{0}$ stays put and you get the full
$3\,{\rm dB}$ ($1/f^{2}$) $3-6\,{\rm dB}$ ($1/f^{3}$)
improvement for $P\to 2P$.

If the comparison is made at {\it fixed external}
(white) load, ${\cal C}_{L}\approx {\cal C}_{w}={\rm
const.}$,

$$f_{0}\propto g_{m}\propto W\tag{16}$$

so that with (10)

$${\cal L}\propto {{f_{0}^{2}}\over P}\propto W\tag{17}$$

the $20\log f_{0}$ increase eats the $10\log P$
decrease and

$${\cal L}(2W)\approx {\cal L}(W)\;\;{\rm to\;}{\cal O}(1)
\tag{18}$$

formally ${\cal L}(2W)\approx 2{\cal L}(W)$, $+3\,{\rm dB}$,
in the ${\cal C}_{w}$ dominated limit, i. e. to within
$\pm 3\,{\rm dB}$ the un--normalised ${\cal L}$ is flat
with $W$.  With the usual renormalisation to constant
$f_{0}$, e. g. by adding ${\cal C}_{{\rm ext}}\propto
W$ to keep (12) satisfied, (15) is recovered.  This is
normally abbreviated to {\it doubling $W$ does
(essentially) nothing to the phase noise.}  The $3\,{\rm dB}$
in (15) is the textbook {\it nothing.}

> {\it Remark:}  With ${\cal L}$ in ${\rm dBcHz^{-1}}$
> (noise power) the improvement is $10\log 2=3\,{\rm dB}$;
> often quoted as $6\,{\rm dB}$ in voltage (field)
> units.  Any $F\propto \gamma $ increase with short
> channel excess noise will erode $1-2\,{\rm dB}$ from the
> numbers above.

With the normal {\it rail to rail, ${\cal
E}\ne {\cal E}_{sat}$} idealisation the ring
is a

$${\cal L}\propto {{S_{i,n}}\over {q_{max}^{2}}}
\propto {{S_{v,n}}\over {S^{2}}}$$

oscillator.  In the familiar notation e. {\it g.}
Hajimiri-Lee

$${\cal L}\left(\Delta \omega \right)=
{1\over {8\pi ^{2}}}{{{\bar I_{n}^{2}}\over {\Delta f}}
\Gamma_{rms}^{2}\over {q_{max}^{2}\Delta \omega ^{2}}}\tag{*}$$

for the $1/f^{2}$ region and

$${\cal L}_{1/f^{3}}\propto {{c_{0}^{2}}\over {8\pi ^{2}}}
{{{\bar I_{n,1/f}^{2}}\over {\Delta f}}\over
{q_{max}^{2}\Delta \omega ^{3}}}$$

for the $1/f^{3}$ region.  For the
conventional inverter

$$q_{max}=CV_{DD}\qquad C=C_{G}+C_{D}\propto W_{n}+W_{p}$$
$$S_{i,n}^{2}/\Delta f =4kT\gamma g_{m}\qquad 
g_{m}\propto W\tag{{\rm sat.}}$$
$$S_{v,1/f}^{2}/\Delta f ={{K}\over {WLC_{ox}}}{{1}\over {f}}
\qquad S_{i,1/f}^{2}=g_{m}^{2}S_{v,1/f}^{2}$$

and

$$f_{0}={1\over {2NT_{d}}}\qquad 
T_{d}\approx {{CV_{DD}}\over {I_{D}}}\propto {W\over W}\approx
{\rm const.}$$

The form factor $\Gamma _{rms}$ , $c_{0}$, depends only
on the wave shape and to first order does not scale.
Hence to first order $f_{0}$ and $\Gamma _{rms}$ do not
scale.

$$\eqalign{
S_{v,n}^{2}&=kT/C\cr
\sigma _{t}^{2}&=S_{v,n}^{2}/S^{2}\propto {{kT/C}\over {(I/C)^{2}}}
={{kTC}\over {I^{2}}}}$$

so that apart from the change of $q_{max}$

$${\cal L}_{1/f^{2}}\propto {{S_{i,n}^{2}}\over {q_{max}^{2}}}
\propto {{W}\over {W^{2}}}\propto {1\over W}\tag{1}$$
$${\cal L}_{1/f^{3}}\propto {{S_{i,1/f}^{2}}\over {q_{max}^{2}}}
\propto {{g_{m}^{2}K/WL}\over {W^{2}}}\propto {{W^{2}/W}\over {W^{2}}}
\propto {1\over W}\tag{2}$$

on a power spectral density basis.  Putting $S_{i,n}^{2}
\propto g_{m}\propto \sqrt{W}$ in the long channel square
law language $g_{m}\propto \sqrt{WI_{D}}$, (1) becomes
${\cal L}\propto W^{-3/2}$.  The often quoted
Hajimiri form

$${\cal L}\left(\Delta \omega \right)\approx
{8\over {3\eta }}N{{kT}\over P}{{V_{DD}}\over {V_{char}}}^{2}
\left({{\omega_{0}}\over {\Delta \omega}}\right)^{2}\tag{3}$$

$P=NCI_{D}V_{DD}/C\propto W$ is the dc power,
makes the power trade explicit: $P{\cal L}\propto N$ is
$W$ independent.

In round numbers for the usual $I_{D}\propto W$,
$g_{m}\propto W$, velocity saturated, argument, {\it at
constant $V_{DD}$, i. e. at twice the dc power},

* {\it White FM, $1/f^{2}$, region:}  from (*) $q_{max}
\to 2q_{max}$, $S_{i,n}^{2}\to 2S_{i,n}^{2}$ so that

$${\cal L}_{1/f^{2}}\to {1\over 2}{\cal L}_{1/f^{2}}$$

$-10\log 2\approx -3\,{\rm dB}$ single side band,
$-20\log 2\approx -6\,{\rm dB}$ in $S_{\varphi}=2{\cal L}$
or in rms period jitter.  In power variance

$$\sigma_{T}^{2}\propto {{kTC}\over {I^{2}}}\to {1\over 2}
\sigma_{T}^{2}\qquad \sigma _{T}\to \sigma_{T}/\sqrt{2}$$

i. e. $6\,{\rm dB}$ in $S_{\varphi }$.

If you count ${\cal L}\propto 1/q_{max}^{2}\propto 1/C^{2}$
and keep $S_{i,n}^{2}$ fixed the text book $6\,{\rm dB}$
SSB, $12\,{\rm dB}$ DSB, number is often quoted.
Normalised to dc power ${\cal F}={\cal L}+10\log P_{\rm
mW}-20\log \left(f_{0}/\Delta f\right)$ is invariant.
That is the usual loose statement {\it the {\rm FoM}
phase noise does not change}.

With the $C_{w},C_{int}$ fringe and interconnect
capacitance that does not scale and with the slight drop
in $f_{0}$ because $C_{w}$ is now a smaller fraction of
$C_{tot}$ the net absolute improvement is

$${\cal L}_{new}\approx {\cal L}_{old}-2{\rm \;to\;}3\,{\rm dB}
\;\;{\rm SSB}\approx {\cal L}_{old}-4{\rm \;to\;}6\,{\rm dB}
\;\;{\rm DSB}\;\;{\rm at}\;\;2\times P_{DC}$$

and ${\cal F}\approx {\rm const.}$ to within a dB.
Neglecting $C_{w}$ and the $f_{0}^{2}$ factor this is
normally abbreviated to {\it no {\rm FoM} improvement}.
For constant $P_{DC}$, i. e. constant
$WI_{D}$, $g_{m}\propto \sqrt{W}$ and ${\cal L}{\cal F}$
is $\propto \sqrt{W}$ - it gets worse.

* {\it $1/f$ induced $1/f^{3}$ region:}  From (2)

$${\cal L}_{1/f^{3}}\to {1\over 2}{\cal L}_{1/f^{3}}$$

$-3\,{\rm dB}$ SSB, $-6\,{\rm dB}$ DSB, per octave of
$W$, i. e. $S_{\varphi ,1/f^{3}}\propto K/WLC^{2}$, at
constant $K$.  With $K\propto 1/WL$ sometimes absorbed in
the $K$ the $1/f^{3}$ ${\cal L}$ is quoted as $\propto
1/(WL)^{2}\propto 1/W^{2}$ or $-6\,{\rm dB}$ SSB,
$-12\,{\rm dB}$  DSB, per $W$ octave.  The $1/f^{3}$
corner $\omega _{1/f^{3}}\propto c_{0}^{2}K/WL$ moves down
$\propto 1/W$.

In particular to first order the oscillation frequency,
the small signal loop gain $g_{m}R$, $R\propto 1/g_{m}$,
and the loaded $Q\approx 1$ do not scale, so that
Leeson's

$${\cal L}\propto {{FkT}\over {2P_{s}}}{{f_{0}}\over
{2Q\Delta f}}^{2}$$

gives ${\cal L}\propto 1/P_{s}\propto 1/W$ at constant
$V_{DD}$, ${\cal L}P_{s}\approx {\rm const.}$

> {\it Remark:}  What is normally meant by {\it the phase
> noise does not improve} is ${\cal L}P_{DC}\approx {\rm
> const.}$  The absolute, un-normalised, SSB ${\cal L}$
> at the same $V_{DD}$ and the same $\Delta f$ does go
> down $\propto 1/W$, $3\,{\rm dB}$ per $W$ octave,
> $6\,{\rm dB}$ in $S_{\varphi }$, at the expense of
> $3\,{\rm dB}$ more $P_{DC}$.  Including the normally
> non scaling $C_{int}$ the absolute improvement is
> normally $<3\,{\rm dB}$ and is quite often neglected
> altogether in hand waving discussions.

With the customary ${\cal G}_{m}=g_{m}+g_{mb}$
put a $V_{x}$ on the $V_{DD}$ rail, Fig. 1, and
let $V_{1},V_{2},V_{3}$ be the small signal
outputs.

$${\rm Fig.\;1:}\;\;V_{i+1}= -A_{v}V_{i}+A_{DD}V_{x}\tag{1}$$

For the $k$-th ${\rm CMOS}$ inverter

$${\eqalign{
i_{dn}&=g_{mn}v_{g}+g_{dsn}v_{d}\cr
i_{dp}&=g_{mp}v_{sg}+g_{dsp}v_{sd}\cr
v_{sg}&=V_{x}-v_{g}\quad v_{sd}=V_{x}-v_{d}\cr}} \tag{2}$$

so that with

$$\eqalign{
g&=g_{dsn}+g_{dsp}=r_{on}^{-1}+r_{op}^{-1}\cr
g_{m}&=g_{mn}+g_{mp}\cr
{\cal G}_{p}&=g_{mp}+g_{dsp}\approx g_{mp}\cr
{\cal G}_{n}&=g_{mn}+g_{dsn}\approx g_{mn}\cr} \tag{3}$$

$${\cal G}_{p}V_{x}-g_{mp}V_{gk}-g_{dsp}V_{dk}
      =g_{mn}V_{gk}+g_{dsn}V_{dk}\tag{4}$$

and, with $v_{dk}=V_{k}$ and $v_{gk}=V_{k-1}$,
$V_{0}\equiv V_{3}$,

$$gV_{k}+g_{m}V_{k-1}={\cal G}_{p}V_{x}
      -sC_{k}V_{k}-sC_{2k}\left(V_{k}-V_{x}\right)\tag{5}$$

$C_{1k}$ is the $\,V_{k}-0\,$ capacitance,
$C_{2k}$ the $V_{k}-V_{x}$ capacitance,
$C_{k}=C_{1k}+C_{2k}$.
For $s=0$

$$gV_{k}+g_{m}V_{k-1}={\cal G}_{p}V_{x}\qquad k=1\ldots N
\tag{6}$$

Adding the $N$ equations, $S=\sum V_{k}$,

$$\left(g+g_{m}\right)S=N{\cal G}_{p}V_{x}\tag{7}$$

so that, for $s=0$, all the $V_{k}$ are equal,
$V_{k}= {\cal G}_{p}V_{x}/(g+g_{m})$.
With $C_{k}\ne 0$

$$S=N\left({\cal G}_{p}+sC_{2}\right)V_{x}/\left(g+g_{m}+sC\right)
\tag{8}$$

The current that $V_{x}$ has to furnish is the sum
of the $p$ source currents and, at $s\ne 0$, of the
$C_{2k}$ currents,

$$\eqalign{
I_{x}&=\sum_{k}\left[g_{mp}\left(V_{x}-V_{k-1}\right)
      +g_{dsp}\left(V_{x}-V_{k}\right)
      +sC_{2}\left(V_{x}-V_{k}\right)\right]\cr
     &=\left({\cal G}_{p}+sC_{2}\right)\left(NV_{x}-S\right)} \tag{9}$$

so that, with (8),

$$I_{x}=N\left({\cal G}_{p}+sC_{2}\right)
      \left({\cal G}_{n}+sC_{1}\right)V_{x}/
      \left(g+g_{m}+sC\right) \tag{10}$$

and

$$Z_{x}(s)={V_{x}\over I_{x}}
      ={g+g_{m}+sC\over N\left({\cal G}_{p}+sC_{2}\right)
                          \left({\cal G}_{n}+sC_{1}\right)} \tag{11}$$

$${\cal G}_{n}=g_{mn}+g_{dsn}\qquad 
  {\cal G}_{p}=g_{mp}+g_{dsp}\qquad 
  g+g_{m}={\cal G}_{n}+{\cal G}_{p}\tag{12}$$

In the conventional $r_{o}\to \infty ,\;C\to 0$
low frequency incremental form, $s\to 0$,

$$R_{X0}={{\cal G}_{n}+{\cal G}_{p}\over N{\cal G}_{n}{\cal G}_{p}}
      ={1\over N}\left({1\over {\cal G}_{n}}+{1\over {\cal G}_{p}}\right)
\tag{13}$$

i. e. the $N$ $p$-sources $\approx 1/{\cal G}_{p}$ in
parallel in parallel with the $N$ $n$-sources
$\approx 1/{\cal G}_{n}$ in parallel.
With $g_{mb}$ put in ${\cal G}$,

$$R_{X0}={1\over N}\left[
{1\over g_{mn}+g_{mbn}+g_{dsn}}+
{1\over g_{mp}+g_{mbp}+g_{dsp}}\right] \tag{14}$$

$$R_{X0}={1\over 3}\left[{r_{on}\over 1+(g_{mn}+g_{mbn})r_{on}}
                +{r_{op}\over 1+(g_{mp}+g_{mbp})r_{op}}\right] \tag{15}$$

if the current is taken as leaving the $V_{DD}$
node the sign is reversed.
Neglecting $r_{o}^{-1}$ against $g_{m}$,

$$R_{X0}\approx {1\over N}\left({1\over g_{mn}}+{1\over g_{mp}}\right)
      ={g_{mn}+g_{mp}\over Ng_{mn}g_{mp}} \tag{16}$$

For the usual symmetric design $g_{mn}\approx g_{mp}=g_{m0}$

$$R_{X0}\approx {2\over Ng_{m0}}\approx {1\over Ng_{m}} \tag{17}$$

where in the last form $g_{m}=g_{mn}+g_{mp}$ is
counted as {\it the} inverter $g_{m}$.

E. {\rm g.} for $N=3$, $r_{o}\to \infty$,

$$R_{X}(0)\approx {g_{mP}+g_{mN}\over 3g_{mP}g_{mN}}
          \approx {2\over 3g_{m0}}\approx {1\over 3g_{m}} >0\tag{18}$$

as seen with the current {\it entering} the
$V_{DD}$ terminal.  With the passive sign
convention $I_{x}$ leaving the terminal

$$R_{X}\approx -{1\over N}\left({1\over g_{mN}}+{1\over g_{mP}}\right)
      \approx -{2\over 3g_{m0}}\approx -{1\over 3g_{m}}\tag{19}$$

is normally quoted.  E. {\rm g.} $g_{m0}=2-5\,{\rm mA/V}$,
$|R_{X}|\approx 130-330\,{\rm \Omega}$,
$|R_{X}|\approx 65-170\,{\rm \Omega}$ with the
$g_{m}=2g_{m0}$ definition.  In compact form

$$|R_{X}|\sim {1\over g_{m1}+g_{m2}+g_{m3}}\sim {1\over 3g_{m}}$$

and, in general,

$$|Z_{x}(s)|\approx {1\over N}{1+sC/g_{m}\over g_{m}+sC}$$

capacitive for $s=j\omega$,

$${\rm Re}Z_{x}(j\omega)=
{ {\cal G}_{n}{\cal G}_{p}({\cal G}_{n}+{\cal G}_{p})
  +\omega^{2}\left({\cal G}_{p}C_{1}^{2}+{\cal G}_{n}C_{2}^{2}\right)
 \over N|{\cal G}_{p}+j\omega C_{2}|^{2}
        |{\cal G}_{n}+j\omega C_{1}|^{2}}({\cal G}_{n}+{\cal G}_{p})>0\tag{20}$$

for the ideal ${\rm LTI}$ bias at the meta stable
$V_{DD}/2$ point.  The large signal periodic steady
state conversion resistance around $\pm \omega _{osc}$
is the negative of (13)-(19) and will cancel the
loss of a series $V_{DD}$ inductor, the familiar
inductive peaking of the ring.  Any factor $2$ is
just whether $g_{mN}$ or $g_{mN}+g_{mP}$ is called
$g_{m}$.  Including ${\cal G}_{n},{\cal G}_{p}$ the
usual textbook form is $R_{X}\approx 1/3g_{mP}\approx
1/3g_{m}$.  With $g_{mb}$ included replace $g_{m}$
by $g_{m}+g_{mb}$.

With the usual ``analogue'' schematic, Fig.1, put

$${\rm PM}:~i_{p}=g_{mp}v_{sg}+g_{op}v_{sd}\qquad 
{\rm NM}:~i_{n}=g_{mn}v_{gs}+g_{on}v_{ds}\tag{1}$$

$C_{L}$ the total capacitance on one inverter
output to earth, $N=3$.
For the $k$ th. inverter

$$\eqalign{
v_{sgk}&=v_{x}-v_{ik}\cr
v_{sdk}&=v_{x}-v_{ok}\cr
v_{gsk}&=v_{ik}\cr
v_{dsk}&=v_{ok}} \tag{2}$$

and, at the $k$th. output

$$i_{pk}=i_{nk}+sC_{L}v_{ok}\tag{3}$$

$${g_{mp}}(v_{x}-v_{ik})+{g_{op}}(v_{x}-v_{ok})
 =g_{mn}v_{ik}+g_{on}v_{ok}+sC_{L}v_{ok}\tag{4}$$

Put

$$\eqalign{
G_{m}&=g_{mn}+g_{mp}\cr
G_{o}&=g_{on}+g_{op}\cr
G_{p}&=g_{mp}+g_{op}} \tag{5}$$

so that from (4)

$$G_{p}v_{x}=G_{m}v_{ik}+(G_{o}+sC_{L})v_{ok}
\qquad k=1\dots N\tag{6}$$

i. e., with $A_{v}=G_{m}/(G_{o}+sC_{L})$ the normal
inverter gain and $A_{s}=G_{p}/(G_{o}+sC_{L})$ the
{\it supply} gain,

$$v_{ok}=-A_{v}v_{ik}+A_{s}v_{x}\tag{7}$$

For the closed ring

$$v_{i1}=v_{oN}\;, \qquad v_{ik}=v_{ok-1}\tag{8}$$

so that, e. g. for $N=3$,

$$\eqalign{
G_{m}v_{o3}+(G_{o}+sC_{L})v_{o1}&=G_{p}v_{x}\cr
G_{m}v_{o1}+(G_{o}+sC_{L})v_{o2}&=G_{p}v_{x}\cr
G_{m}v_{o2}+(G_{o}+sC_{L})v_{o3}&=G_{p}v_{x}} \tag{9}$$

The $N$ equations (9) are circulant.  The excitation
${\bf G_{p}}v_{x}[1\,1\dots 1]^{T}$ is the ${\bf k}=0$
Fourier vector.  Only the common mode

$$v_{o1}=v_{o2}=\dots =v_{oN}=v_{c}\tag{10}$$

is excited.  Putting $S=\sum v_{ok}=Nv_{c}$ and adding
(9),

$$S\,(G_{m}+G_{o}+sC_{L})=NG_{p}v_{x}\tag{11}$$

$$S=N\,{\dfrac{G_{p}}{G_{m}+G_{o}+sC_{L}}}\,v_{x}\tag{12}$$

and, from (6), for any $k$

$$v_{c}={\dfrac{G_{p}}{G_{m}+G_{o}+sC_{L}}}\,v_{x}\tag{13}$$

The total current furnished by the test generator
$v_{x}$ is the sum of the $N$ $p$ currents.  From (1)
(2)

$$\eqalign{
I_{x}&=\sum_{k}^{N}i_{pk}
      =\sum_{k}^{N}\left[ G_{p}v_{x}-g_{mp}v_{ik}-g_{op}v_{ok}\right]\cr
     &=NG_{p}v_{x}-G_{p}S\tag{14}}$$

because $\sum v_{ik}=\sum v_{ok}=S$.  With (12)

$$I_{x}=NG_{p}v_{x}\left[1-{\dfrac{G_{p}}
{G_{m}+G_{o}+sC_{L}}}\right] \tag{15}$$

so that the closed loop admittance seen at the common
$V_{DD}$ rail is, for $N$ stages,

$$Y_{x}(s)={{I_{x}}\over {v_{x}}}
      =N\,G_{p}\,{{G_{m}+G_{o}-G_{p}+sC_{L}}\over 
            {G_{m}+G_{o}+sC_{L}}}\tag{16}$$

and, since $G_{m}+G_{o}-G_{p}=g_{mn}+g_{on}$,

$$Y_{x}(s)=N\,(g_{mp}+g_{op})\,
     {{g_{mn}+g_{on}+sC_{L}}\over 
      {g_{mn}+g_{mp}+g_{on}+g_{op}+sC_{L}}}\tag{17}$$

$$Z_{x}(s)=Y_{x}^{-1}(s)\tag{18}$$

is a conventional $R\parallel C$ impedance with a
pole

$$\omega _{p}={{G_{m}+G_{o}}\over {C_{L}}}\tag{19}$$

and a zero

$$\omega _{z}={{g_{mn}+g_{on}}\over {C_{L}}}\tag{20}$$

$\omega _{p}$ is, to within $G_{o}$, the ``oscillation''
pole

$$s_{1,2}={{-\,G_{o}+G_{m}/2\pm j{{\sqrt{3}}\over {2}}G_{m}}
      \over {C_{L}}}\tag{21}$$

of the linearised metastable point, i. e. 
${\rm Im}\,s_{1,2}= \omega _{osc}\approx {{\sqrt{3}}G_{m}/
2C_{L}}$.

In particular, for $|s|C_{L}\ll G_{m}$, the normal low
frequency, $d-c$, resistance is

$$R_{x0}=Y_{x}^{-1}(0)={{G_{m}+G_{o}}\over 
            {NG_{p}(g_{mn}+g_{on})}}\tag{22}$$

$$R_{x0}={1\over N}
      {{g_{mn}+g_{mp}+g_{on}+g_{op}}\over 
       {(g_{mp}+g_{op})(g_{mn}+g_{on})}}\tag{23}$$

With the passive sign convention, $I_{x}$ into the
circuit, $R_{x0}>0$.  With the generator sign convention
normally used in oscillator theory, $I_{x}$ out of the
circuit, $R_{x0}<0$.  Neglecting channel length
modulation, $g_{o}\to 0$,

$$R_{x0}={1\over N}\left({1\over {g_{mn}}}+{1\over {g_{mp}}}
      \right) \tag{24}$$

For the conventional symmetric design $g_{mn}=g_{mp}=g_{m}$

$$|R_{x0}|\approx {2\over {Ng_{m}}}\tag{25}$$

so that for the three stage ring in the figure

$$|R_{x0}|\approx {2\over {3g_{m}}}\approx {1\over {g_{m}}}
\;\;{\rm to\;within\;a\;factor\;2}\tag{26}$$

in the generator convention

$$R_{x0}\approx -{2\over {3g_{m}}}\tag{27}$$

often quoted simply as $R_{x}\approx -1/g_{m}$ or
$|R_{x}|\approx 1/g_{m}$.  Keeping $g_{o}=1/r_{o}$,

$$R_{x0}={2\over {3g_{m}}}{1\over {1+g_{o}/g_{m}}}
      \approx {2\over {3g_{m}}}\left(1-{1\over {g_{m}r_{o}}}
      \right)\tag{28}$$

and in general $|R_{x}|\sim 50-500\,{\rm \Omega}$ for a
normal $g_{m}\sim 1-10\,{\rm mS}$ per device.

Well above the common mode pole, $|s|C_{L}\gg G_{m}$,

$$Y_{x}(\infty )=NG_{p}\approx Ng_{mp}\tag{29}$$

$$|R_{x\infty }|\approx {1\over {Ng_{mp}}}\to {1\over 
      {3g_{m}}}\;\;{\rm sym.}\tag{30}$$

so that, up to the $2\times $ factor,

$$|Z_{x}(s)|\approx |R_{x0}|{{1+s/\omega _{z}}\over 
       {1+s/\omega _{p}}}\tag{31}$$

goes from $\approx 2/3g_{m}$ at $d-c$ to $\approx
1/3g_{m}$ for $\omega \gg \omega _{p}$ with
${\rm Re}\,Z_{x}>0$ for the passive reference arrow.
The magnitude at the (small signal) oscillation
frequency $s=j\omega _{osc}$ is the same order of
magnitude,

$$Y_{x}(j\omega _{osc})\approx Ng_{mp}
      {{1+j\omega _{osc}/\omega _{z}}\over 
       {1+j\omega _{osc}/\omega _{p}}}\tag{32}$$

with ${\rm Re}\,Y_{x}>0$.

Any expression of the form $R_{x}\sim 1/Ng_{m}$ to
$2/Ng_{m}$ i. e. $R_{x}\sim 1/g_{m}$ in order of
magnitude is accepted as correct.  With the bulk effect
included $g_{mp}\to g_{mp}+g_{mbp}$.

Time averaged over the large signal limit cycle the
circuit draws on the average

$$I_{DD,av}\approx N\,C_{L}V_{DD}f_{osc}\approx 
      {{N\,I_{Dsat}}\over 2}\tag{33}$$

so that the large signal, $V_{DD}$ to $I_{DD,av}$,
resistance is

$$R_{x,LS}={{V_{DD}}\over {I_{DD,av}}}\approx 
      {{2V_{DD}}\over {NI_{Dsat}}}\approx {{R_{on,p}}\over N}
      \approx {1\over {N\mu _{p}C_{ox}(W/L)_{p}
      (V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}|)}}\tag{34}$$

again a few $10\,{\rm \Omega}$ to a few $100\,{\rm \Omega}$
per stage, positive in the passive convention, negative
in the generator convention.  E. g. $g_{m}=2\,{\rm mS}$,
$|R_{x0}|\approx 330\,{\rm \Omega}$, 
$|R_{x\infty }|\approx 170\,{\rm \Omega}$;
$g_{m}=5\,{\rm mS}$, $|R_{x0}|\approx 130\,{\rm \Omega}$,
etc.  In round numbers the supply sees a low impedance
$\sim 1/g_{m}$ to ground which, as an active impedance,
is normally written with a minus sign, $Z_{x}\approx
-1/g_{m}$.  Closing $Z_{x}$ on an inductor
$L_{x}=1/\omega _{osc}^{2}C_{x}$ gives the familiar
supply tuned $LC$ VCO.

With the usual ``metastable'' linearisation the
${\rm V}_{DD}$ node is a common mode node.
Put ${\rm V}_{DD}={\rm V}_{x}+v_{x}$ , $v_{o_{i}}$
the small signal output of the $i$th. inverter, Fig.1,
${\rm C}$ the total capacitance on the node, ${\rm W}$ the
$p$ device ${\rm S}$, ${\rm G}$, ${\rm D}$ $={\rm V}_{x}$,
$v_{i}$, $v_{o}$ and the $n$ device ${\rm G}$, ${\rm D}$,
${\rm S}$ $=v_{i},v_{o},0$.

$${\eqalign{
i_{Dp}&=g_{mp}(v_{x}-v_{i})+g_{op}(v_{x}-v_{o})\cr
i_{Dn}&=g_{mn}v_{i}+g_{on}v_{o}\cr}} \tag{1}$$

$${\rm KCL}_{o}:\;i_{Dp}=i_{Dn}+sCv_{o}\tag{2}$$

so that with

$$\eqalign{
A&=g_{mp}+g_{op}\cr
B&=g_{mp}+g_{mn}\cr
C_{0}&=g_{op}+g_{on}\cr
C(s)&=C_{0}+sC\cr}\tag{3}$$

$$\,A\,v_{x}=Bv_{i}+C(s)v_{o}\,\tag{4}$$

and, for the closed loop,

$$\eqalign{
C(s)v_{o1}+Bv_{o3}&=Av_{x}\cr
Bv_{o1}+C(s)v_{o2}&=Av_{x}\cr
Bv_{o2}+C(s)v_{o3}&=Av_{x}\cr}\tag{5}$$

whose determinant is $C^{3}+B^{3}\ne 0$.
For the common mode excitation $v_{x}{\bf 1}$ the
symmetric solution

$$v_{o1}=v_{o2}=v_{o3}=v_{o}={A\over {B+C(s)}}v_{x}\tag{6}$$

satisfies (5).

$${v_{o}\over {v_{x}}}\approx {{g_{mp}}\over
{g_{mp}+g_{mn}}}\approx {1\over 2}\qquad g_{o}\ll g_{m} \tag{7}$$

the conventional small signal inverter supply to output
{\it positive} gain.  The small signal current taken from
the $v_{x}$ source is the sum of the three $p$ source
currents

$$\eqalign{
i_{x}&=\sum_{1}^{3}i_{Dpi}
      =\sum_{1}^{3}\left[ A\,v_{x}-g_{mp}v_{i}-g_{op}v_{o}\right] 
       =3Av_{x}-3Av_{o}\cr
     &=3A\left[1-{A\over {B+C(s)}}\right]v_{x}
      =3A{{B+C(s)-A}\over {B+C(s)}}v_{x} \cr
     &=3A{{g_{mn}+g_{on}+sC}\over {B+C(s)}}v_{x} \tag{8}}$$

so that, in the low frequency metastable bias, the small
signal impedance seen looking into the common ${\rm V}_{DD}$
rail is

$$\eqalign{
Z_{x}(s)&={v_{x}\over {i_{x}}}
        ={1\over {3A}}{{B+C(s)}\over {g_{mn}+g_{on}+sC}}\cr
        &={{g_{mn}+g_{mp}+g_{on}+g_{op}+sC}\over
                {3(g_{mp}+g_{op})(g_{mn}+g_{on}+sC)}} \tag{9}}$$

I. e. the ${\rm V}_{DD}$ node sees three diode connected
inverters in parallel.  At $s=0$

$$R_{x0}=Z_{x}(0)={{B+C_{0}}\over {3A(g_{mn}+g_{on})}}
      ={{g_{mn}+g_{mp}+g_{on}+g_{op}}\over
             {3(g_{mp}+g_{op})(g_{mn}+g_{on})}} \tag{10}$$

$${R_{x0}={1\over 3}\left[{1\over {g_{mn}+g_{on}}}+
                 {1\over {g_{mp}+g_{op}}}\right] } \tag{11}$$

in parallel with $r_{on}\Vert r_{op}$.
For $g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1$

$$\;R_{x0}\approx {1\over 3}\left({1\over {g_{mn}}}+{1\over
{g_{mp}}}\right)={{g_{mn}+g_{mp}}\over {3g_{mn}g_{mp}}}\; \tag{12}$$

If the inverter transconductance is put $G_{m}=g_{mn}+
g_{mp}$, (12) is $R_{x0}\approx 1/3G_{m}$ per stage.
For the conventional symmetric bias
$g_{mn}=g_{mp}=g_{m}$, $g_{o}\to 0$,

$$R_{x0}\approx {2\over {3g_{m}}}={4\over {3G_{m}}}\approx
{1\over {3g_{m}}}{\rm \;\;per\;side}\tag{13}$$

positive with the passive sign convention, i.{\rm e.}
$|R_{x}|\sim g_{m}^{-1}$, normally a few $10^{2}{\rm \Omega}$,
e. {\rm g.} $g_{m}=1\,{\rm mA/V}$, $R_{x0}\approx 0.66\,{\rm k\Omega}
\approx 0.33\,{\rm k\Omega}$ per $g_{m}$.

With the oscillator large signal active sign convention the
same magnitude is normally quoted as a negative resistance,

$$|R_{x}|\approx {1\over {N\,g_{m}}}\approx {1\over {3g_{m}}}
\;\;{\rm per\;device,}\;\;|R_{x}|\approx {2\over {3g_{m}}}
\approx {1\over {G_{m}}}{\rm \;for\;the\;CMOS\;inverter,} \tag{14}$$

so that, e. {\rm g.}

$$R_{x}\approx -\,{1\over {3g_{m}}}\;\;{\rm to}\;\;-{2\over {3g_{m}}}
\approx -\,{1\over {G_{m}}}\tag{15}$$

in the $g_{o}\to 0$ square law form, and, retaining
$r_{o}=1/g_{o}$,

$$R_{x}\approx -\,{{(g_{m}r_{o})^{2}}\over {3g_{m}}}\approx
-\,{r_{o}\over 3}\tag{16}$$

at the oscillation frequency, ${\rm Re}\,Z_{x}(j\omega _{{\rm
osc}})<0$, $|\,{\rm Re}\,Z_{x}(j\omega _{{\rm osc}})\,|
\approx r_{o}/3\sim g_{m}^{-1}$.

In round numbers the ${\rm V}_{DD}$ node looks like
$N=3$ diode connected inverters in parallel, i. {\rm e.}
like a resistance $\sim 1/G_{m}$ to ground, normally quoted
simply as $|R_{x}|\sim 1/g_{m}$, more precisely (11)--(13).
With the passive reference direction $R_{x}>0$; with the
usual negative resistance oscillator convention
$R_{x}\approx -|R_{x}|$.  Any of the equivalent forms
(9)--(15) is acceptable; e. {\rm g.} for $r_{o}\to \infty $

$$Z_{x}(s)\approx {1\over 3}{1\over {g_{mp}}}
{{g_{mp}+g_{mn}+sC}\over {g_{mn}+sC}}\approx
{2/3g_{m}}\,{1\over {1+sC/g_{m}}}$$

for $g_{mn}=g_{mp}=g_{m}$, so that $Z_{x}(0)\approx
2/3g_{m}\approx 1/3G_{m}$ and $|Z_{x}(j\omega _{{\rm osc}})|
\approx 1/g_{m}$ negative in the active convention.  For
hand calculation $|R_{x}|\approx 1/3g_{m}\approx 1/G_{m}$
is often quoted, i. {\rm e.} $R_{x}\approx -1/g_{m}$ in
magnitude, $\approx -1/3g_{m}$ per stage.  The $+$
sign is the conventional passive small signal resistance.

With the usual abuse of language the ``$R_{X}$'' is
ill defined for an autonomous circuit.  What is
normally called $R_{X}$ is

$${{dV_{DD}}\over {dI_{DD}}}\Bigl|_{0}\eqno{*}$$

at the {\it metastable} d.c. {\it equilibrium}
$V_{o1}=V_{o2}=V_{o3}=V_{T}\approx V_{DD}/2$.
Put

$$i_{p}=g_{mp}(v_{i}-v_{x})+g_{op}(v_{o}-v_{x})\tag{1}$$
$$i_{n}=g_{mn}v_{i}+g_{on}v_{o}\tag{2}$$

$$i_{p}+i_{n}+sCv_{o}=0\tag{3}$$

$$v_{i\,k}=v_{o\,k-1}\tag{4}$$

and, for the $v_{x}$
perturbation, $v_{ok}=v_{o}\;\forall k$,
$v_{ik}=v_{o}$, the ``common mode'' mode of the
circulant $3\times 3$ system.  From (1)-(3)

$$(g_{m}+g_{o})v_{o}-(g_{mp}+g_{op})v_{x}
+sCv_{o}=0\tag{5}$$

$$g_{m}=g_{mp}+g_{mn}\qquad g_{o}=g_{op}+g_{on}$$

so that for $s\to 0$

$$v_{o}={g_{mp}+g_{op}\over g_{m}+g_{o}}v_{x}
\approx {g_{mp}\over g_{m}}v_{x} \tag{6}$$

$$i_{x\,k}= (g_{mp}+g_{op})v_{x}-g_{mp}v_{i\,k}
-g_{op}v_{o\,k}=(g_{mp}+g_{op})(v_{x}-v_{o}) \tag{7}$$

$${{v_{x}}\over {i_{x\,k}}}=
{g_{m}+g_{o}\over (g_{mp}+g_{op})(g_{mn}+g_{on})}
\approx {g_{m}\over g_{mp}g_{mn}}
={1\over {g_{mp}}}+{1\over {g_{mn}}}\tag{8}$$

i. e. the PMOS, common gate, loaded with the
NMOS common gate, i. e. the two ``diode connected''
devices in series, and for $N=3$ in parallel

$$R_{X0}\approx {1\over N}\left({1\over {g_{mp}}}+
{1\over {g_{mn}}}\right)\;\;N=3\tag{9}$$

with $g_{m}=g_{m}(V_{T})$, the small signal $g_{m}$
at the trip point.

That $R_{X0}$ is the resistance seen at the
{\it unstable} equilibrium.  It is the resistance
that has to be used for the linear, time invariant,
{\it start up} stability analysis, the $s\to 0$
pole of the $3\times 3$ system.  It is what you
get out of a conventional $.AC$ analysis linearized
about the d.c. solution $V_{o}=V_{T}$.

It is not what you measure on a free running
oscillator.  On the stable periodic orbit the
circuit is a large signal, periodically time
varying, nonlinear circuit.  Linearised about the
orbit it is a linear periodically time variant,
cyclostationary, circuit in the sense of Floquet.
E.g. with obvious notation

$$g_{m}(t)=g_{m}\bigl(V_{I}(t)\bigr)\tag{10}$$

$$g_{m}(t+T_{0})=g_{m}(t),\qquad 
T_{0}=2N\bar\tau _{d}=1/f_{0}\tag{11}$$

is periodic at the oscillation frequency.
Formally

$$\delta i_{x}(t)=Y_{x}(t)\,\delta v_{x}(t)\tag{12}$$

$$Y_{x}(t)=\sum_{k}g_{x\,k}(t),\qquad 
Y_{x}(t+T_{0})=Y_{x}(t)\tag{13}$$

so that a tone at $\omega _{x}$

$$\delta v_{x}= {\rm Re}\,V_{x}e^{j\omega _{x}t}\tag{14}$$

produces

$$\delta i_{x}= {\rm Re}\sum_{n}Y_{n}(j\omega _{x})
V_{x}e^{j(\omega _{x}+n\omega _{0})t}\tag{15}$$

i. e. a conversion matrix $Y_{n,m}=Y_{n-m}(j\omega
+m\omega _{0})$.  The ``$R_{X}$'' is not a number
but the $(0,0)$ element $Z_{0,0}=Y_{0,0}^{-1}$ plus
an infinite set of conversion impedances $Z_{n,0}$.

In the time domain the instantaneous small signal
impedance is

$$r_{x}(t)=1/Y_{x}(t)\approx 
\left[\sum_{k=1}^{N}{1\over {r_{pk}(t)+r_{nk}(t)}}\right]^{-1}
\tag{16}$$

$$r_{pk}(t)\approx 1/g_{mp\,k}(t)\;{\rm sat.},\;
\approx 1/g_{op\,k}(t)\;{\rm triode},\;
\to \infty \;{\rm off}$$

and similarly for $r_{nk}$.  In normal rail to
rail oscillation a gate spends most of its time with
one device OFF, $r_{x}=\infty$ d.c., and only during
the transition, of duration $t_{r}$, are both
devices on in saturation and (16) $\approx
1/g_{mp}+1/g_{mn}\equiv r_{0}$.  For the ideal
$3$ stage ring at any $t$ at most one gate is
commutating, so

$$r_{x}(t)=\cases{
r_{0} & during commutation\cr
\infty & otherwise\cr}\tag{17}$$

In particular

$$\langle Y_{x}\rangle ={1\over {T_{0}}}\int_{T_{0}}
Y_{x}(t)dt = D\,Y_{0},\qquad 
\langle r_{x}\rangle \approx r_{0}/D\tag{18}$$

where $D$ is the fractional conduction duty
cycle of the crow bar current,
$Y_{0}=1/r_{0}$.
If $t_{r}$ is the $0-100\%$ rise time and the
transitions do not overlap

$$D = {2Nt_{r}\over T_{0}}{1\over N}
      ={2t_{r}\over T_{0}}\quad {\rm per\;stage}\tag{19}$$

for the total

$$D_{tot}= {{N_{tr}t_{r}}\over {T_{0}}}\approx
{{6t_{r}}\over {T_{0}}}\tag{20}$$

so that, on the average,

$$\langle G_{x}\rangle = D_{tot}G_{0},\qquad
\langle R_{x}\rangle = R_{X0}{N\over {D_{tot}}}
      =R_{X0}{T_{0}\over {2t_{r}}}\tag{21}$$

For the often quoted $t_{r}\approx \bar\tau_{d}
\approx T_{0}/2N$,

$$\langle R_{x}\rangle \approx N\,R_{X0}
      = {1\over {g_{mp}}}+{1\over {g_{mn}}}\tag{22}$$

i. e. the factor $1/N$ in (9) disappears.  In
general $\langle R_{x}\rangle =R_{X0}(T_{0}/6t_{r})$
for $N=3$.  For abrupt, square wave, switching
$t_{r}\to 0$, $D\to 0$,

$$\langle R_{x}\rangle \to \infty \tag{23}$$

except for the train of short current spikes
$I_{x}(t)$.  The d.c., large signal, incremental
resistance that you get by changing $V_{DD}$ and
measuring the change of the {\it averaged}
supply current,

$$R_{X,DC}={{dV_{DD}}\over {d\langle I_{x}\rangle}}
      \approx {V_{DD}\over {\langle I_{x}\rangle}}
      \propto {1\over {N C V_{DD}f_{0}}}\tag{24}$$

$$\langle I_{x}\rangle \approx N C V_{DD}f_{0}
      +I_{sc},\qquad f_{0}\approx 1/2N\bar\tau_{d}$$

$$\bar\tau_{d}\approx {{C V_{DD}}\over {I_{D}}}$$

is $\propto 1/\langle g_{m}\rangle$, the
{\it large signal}, describing function, averaged
$g_{m}$,

$$\langle g_{m}\rangle ={1\over {T_{0}}}\int g_{m}(t)dt
      < g_{m}(V_{T})\tag{25}$$

typically $0.3-0.7\,g_{m}(V_{T})$, not the small
signal $g_{m}$ in (9).

In a $PSS/PAC$ simulation the $(0,0)$ common mode
small signal $R_{X}$ at $\omega_{x}\ll\omega_{0}$ is
still ${\cal O}(1/g_{m})$ but numerically
(21)-(25), a factor $\approx 3$ large for the
$3$ stage ring and formally infinite for ideal
switching, and, for $\omega_{x}\approx
n\omega_{0}\pm\Delta\omega$, $Z_{x}(\omega_{x})$
has a large conversion component.  To first order
the common mode $Z_{0,0}$ and the differential
oscillation mode are orthogonal, so the magnitude
$|Z_{0,0}(0)|$ stays ${\cal O}(1/g_{m})$, but the
full $N\times N$ harmonic transfer matrix has
poles at $\pm j\omega_{0}$ where
${\rm Re}\,Z_{n,0}<0$.  Physically a $\Delta\omega$
perturbation of the supply at $\omega_{0}\pm
\Delta\omega$ FM modulates the oscillator,
$\Delta\omega =K_{VDD}\Delta V_{DD}$, and appears
as a negative resistance $-K_{VDD}/\Delta\omega$
in the conversion impedance.  That is the supply
pushing induced phase noise / injection pulling
mechanism.  This is normally quoted as ``the supply
impedance becomes negative near the carrier''.

In short: (9) is the correct small signal $R_{X}$
linearised about the metastable d.c. point and is
the one to use for start up/loop gain.  The impedance
you actually measure on the running, hard switching,
oscillator is cyclostationary, $r_{x}=r_{x}(t)$,
(17).  Averaged over many periods at low frequency it
is larger than (9) by $1/D\approx T_{0}/2t_{r}$,
$\approx 3\times$ for a normal $3$ stage ring,
$\to\infty$ for ideal square wave switching, and with
large signal $g_{m}\to\langle g_{m}\rangle$.  At
r.f. it is a frequency converting impedance with
$Z(\omega_{x})\to Z(\omega_{x}+n\omega_{0})$ and,
around $f_{0}$, with a negative real part.  A
conventional $.AC$ $R_{X0}=(1/3)(1/g_{mn}+1/g_{mp})$
is unobservable on the free running oscillator.

In the time invariant sense it is not defined.
Put $V_{x}=V_{DD}+v_{x}$, $V_{i}=V_{I}+v_{i}$
$G_{m}=g_{m{\rm n}}+g_{m{\rm p}}$, $G_{p}=g_{m{\rm p}}$
for the $i$ th inverter, with parasitic $C$

$${\rm KCL}\;\;{\rm at}\;\;v_{i}: G_{p}(v_{x}-v_{i-1})
= g_{mn}v_{i-1}+g_{ds}v_{i}+sCv_{i} \tag{*}$$

in the conventional manner.  Neglect $g_{ds}$ for
the argument.  $i={\rm mod}\;3$.

$$sCv_{1}=G_{p}v_{x}-G_{m}v_{3}$$
$$sCv_{2}=G_{p}v_{x}-G_{m}v_{1}$$
$$sCv_{3}=G_{p}v_{x}-G_{m}v_{2}$$

Put $S=v_{1}+v_{2}+v_{3}$:

$$sCS =3G_{p}v_{x}-G_{m}S$$

$$S={3G_{p}\over{sC+G_{m}}}v_{x}\tag{1}$$

The current supplied to the $i$th inverter is the $p$
channel current

$$i_{xi}=G_{p}(v_{x}-v_{i-1})$$

$$I_{x}=\sum i_{xi}=3G_{p}v_{x}-G_{p}S\tag{2}$$

$$Y_{x}={I_{x}\over v_{x}}=3G_{p}{sC+g_{mn}\over sC+G_{m}} \tag{3}$$

$${1\over{Y_{x}}}=R_{x}(s)={1\over 3}{sC+G_{m}\over{G_{p}(sC+g_{mn})}} \tag{4}$$

For a probe at {\it d. c.} and {\it at the metastable
d.c. bias point}, $V_{I}=V_{O}=V_{M}$,
$$sC\ll G_{m}\tag{5}$$

$$Y_{x}(0)=3{G_{p}g_{mn}\over G_{m}}={3\over{1/g_{mn}+1/g_{mp}}}$$

$$R_{x}(0)={1\over 3}\left({1\over{g_{mn}}}+{1\over{g_{mp}}}\right)\tag{6}$$

So formally it is the parallel of $3$ ``diodes''
${1/g_{mn}}+{1/g_{mp}}$.

It looks like each inverter is diode connected.
It is not.  The input of inverter $i$ is not its
own output but the output of $i-1$.  It is only
because at $s=0$, (1), $v_{1}=v_{2}=v_{3}$,
so $v_{i-1}\propto v_{i}$ with the same coefficient
for the three phases that $\sum i_{xi}$ looks like
three diodes in parallel.  For any $s\ne 0$,
$v_{i}\ne v_{j}$ and (4) is complex and $s$ dependent.
At $sC\sim G_{m}$, i.e. at the frequency where
${{{\rm arg}}\, G_{m}/sC\sim 60^{o}}$, the three phasors
are $120^{o}$ apart.  The Barkhausen frequency.
Then e.g. $S\approx 0$ for a probe at $\approx
\omega _{0}$ and

$$Y_{x}(j\omega _{0})\approx 3G_{p}\ne 3G_{p}g_{mn}/G_{m}$$

In general there is no single time invariant number
$R_{x}$.

That $R_{x}(0)$ is the impedance about the {\it
d.c. equilibrium} $V_{I}=V_{O}$.  The equilibrium is
unstable.  $A_{v}^{3}>1$.  The linearized time invariant
circuit has a pair of poles in the ${\rm Re}\,s>0$.
It is unobservable.  The observable steady state is
the large signal limit cycle, Fig.1, essentially
rail to rail.

Linearisation must be about the periodic trajectory,
${\rm LPTV}$ - Floquet - ${\rm PSS/PAC}$, periodic
$g_{m}(t),g_{ds}(t),C(t)$.

Instantaneously

$$R_{x}(t)\approx {1\over{g_{mp}(t)}}+{1\over{g_{mn}(t)}}
\parallel r_{o}(t)$$

and it is {\it periodically time varying} with
period $T_{0}=1/f_{0}\approx 6t_{d}$.

For most of the period a static inverter has
either its $p$ off, $v_{O}=0$, or its $n$ off,
$v_{O}=V_{DD}$.  E.g. for $v_{O}=V_{DD}$,
$r_{p}\sim r_{{\rm on\,triode}}\ll 1/g_{m}$ but
$r_{n}=\infty $, for $v_{O}=0$, $r_{p}=\infty $.
No d.c. path to ground.  The supply sees an
open except during the narrow cross over, crow bar,
where both devices are in saturation for a time
$t_{tr}\ll T_{0}$.  I.e.

$$g_{m}(t)=\cases{
g_{m} & for $t$ in $t_{tr}$\cr
0 & otherwise\cr}\tag{7}$$

Hence the {\it cycle averaged} conductance for a
low frequency probe, $\omega _{p}\ll \omega _{0}$,
where the oscillator can be regarded as quasi static,
is

$$\langle Y_{x}\rangle ={1\over{T_{0}}}\int_{0}^{T_{0}}
Y_{x}(t)\,dt \approx {t_{tr}\over T_{0}}Y_{x}(0)\ll Y_{x}(0) \tag{8}$$

$$\langle R_{x}\rangle \approx {T_{0}\over{t_{tr}}}
R_{x}(0)\gg R_{x}(0) \tag{9}$$

In the ideal square wave limit $t_{tr}\to 0$,
$\langle Y_{x}\rangle \to 0$, $\langle R_{x}\rangle
\to \infty $ except for the capacitive charging
current.  More accurately a slow, $\omega _{p}\ll
\omega _{0}$, ``d.c.'' measurement of $\langle I_{DD}
\rangle $ {\it vs} $V_{DD}$ gives the {\it incremental
large signal} resistance

$$R_{X,{inc}}^{-1}={d\langle I_{DD}\rangle \over dV_{DD}}$$

$$\langle I_{DD}\rangle =NCV_{DD}f_{0}(V_{DD})+
I_{cr}(V_{DD}) \tag{10}$$

dynamic $CVf$ plus crow bar, with

$$f_{0}\approx {1\over{NCV_{DD}/I_{Av}(V_{DD})}}\tag{11}$$

$I_{Av}\propto (V_{DD}-V_{t})^{\alpha }$.
This is not $3g_{m}$.

For $\omega _{p}\sim \omega _{0}$ the LPTV
probe suffers frequency translation.  A tone at
$\omega _{p}$ creates sidebands at $\omega_{p}\pm
n\omega _{0}$.  There is no single $Z_{x}(\omega_{p})$
but a conversion matrix $Z_{mn}=V(\omega _{p}+m\omega _{0})/
I(\omega _{p}+n\omega _{0})$.  At $\approx n\omega _{0}$
the $N=3$ currents are $\approx 120^{o}$ apart and
cancel to first order for $n\ne 3k$.  The supply
current ripple is dominantly at $3f_{0}$.  The
conventional small signal $Y_{x}$ splits into

$$Y_{x}(\omega _{p},\omega _{p}\pm \omega_{0}\dots )$$

In ${\rm PSS/PAC}$ language the $0,0$ term,
$\langle Y_{x}\rangle $ at $\omega _{p}$ is (8)-(9),
the $0,\pm 1$ terms give supply pushing, AM to PM
conversion, and can show a {\it negative} real part
about $\omega _{0}$ - the oscillator must generate
power.

Only in the limit of vanishing oscillation amplitude,
the linear limit cycle $\to $ the metastable point,
$t_{tr}\to T_{0}$, is (6) recovered as the time
average.  To first order $R_{x}=R_{x}(0)[1+O(A^{2})]$
for amplitude $A$.  For normal rail to rail CMOS
the $O(1)$ correction is $\sim T_{0}/t_{tr}\sim 5-10$.
In simulation it requires a periodic steady state
plus periodic AC, ${\rm pss+pac}$, or transient
with a small step on $V_{DD}$ averaged over many
periods, to see it.  A normal ${\rm AC}$ analysis
about the d.c. operating point gives only the
unstable (6), (4).

In the sense of ${\cal L}{\cal T}{\cal I}$
it is the resistance to common mode at the un
stable d.c. equilibrium with the loop killed.
Put

$$v_{D}=V_{DD}+v_{x}\;\;,\;\;v_{i}\;\;i=1,3$$

for the three nodes.  For the $k$th CMOS
inverter

$$i_{pk}=g_{mp}(v_{x}-v_{k-1})+g_{op}(v_{x}-v_{k})
      \tag{1a}$$
$$i_{nk}=g_{mn}v_{k-1}+g_{on}v_{k}\tag{1b}$$

with

$$v_{k}=A_{s}v_{x}-A_{v}v_{k-1}\tag{2}$$

$$A_{v}={{g_{mn}+g_{mp}}\over {g_{o}+sC}}\;\;,\;\;
  A_{s}={{g_{mp}+g_{op}}\over {g_{o}+sC}}\;\;,\;\;
  g_{o}=g_{on}+g_{op}\tag{3}$$

$1$ in, $1$ out.
Cyclic

$$\eqalign{
v_{1}+A_{v}v_{3}&=A_{s}v_{x}\cr
v_{2}+A_{v}v_{1}&=A_{s}v_{x}\cr
v_{3}+A_{v}v_{2}&=A_{s}v_{x}\cr}\tag{4}$$

and, e.g. at $s=0$,

$$v_{1}=v_{2}=v_{3}={{A_{s}}\over {1+A_{v}}}v_{x}\tag{5}$$

i. e. $v_{k-1}=v_{k}$ to ${\cal O}(g_{o}/g_{m})$.
For $s=0$, $A_{s}/A_{v}=g_{mp}/(g_{mn}+g_{mp})$,

$$v_{k}={{g_{mp}}\over {g_{mn}+g_{mp}}}v_{x}+{\cal O}(g_{o}/g_{m})
\tag{6}$$

so that for a perturbation with $\omega \ll
\omega _{p}=g_{o}/C\ll \omega _{0}$ all
three nodes move together.  In small signal

$${\rm gate}={\rm drain}\tag{7}$$

for every device and the device looks diode
connected ${1/g_{m}}$.

Total current taken from the $V_{DD}$ terminal,
with (1),

$$I_{x}=\sum_{k}i_{pk}
      =3(g_{mp}+g_{op})v_{x}-(g_{mp}+g_{op})\sum v_{k}
        -g_{mp}\sum v_{k-1}\tag{8}$$

$$I_{x}=3(g_{mp}+g_{op})\left[v_{x}-v_{1}\right]\tag{9}$$

with (5)

$$I_{x}=3{{(g_{mp}+g_{op})(g_{mn}+g_{on})}\over
       {g_{o}+g_{mn}+g_{mp}}}\,v_{x}\tag{10}$$

For $g_{o}\ll g_{m}$

$$G_{x}={1\over R_{x}}={{I_{x}}\over {v_{x}}}
      =3\,{{g_{mn}g_{mp}}\over {g_{mn}+g_{mp}}}\tag{11}$$

$$R_{x}={1\over 3}\left[{1\over {g_{mn}}}+{1\over {g_{mp}}}\right]
      \tag{12}$$

in parallel of three

$$R_{1}={1\over {g_{mn}}}+{1\over {g_{mp}}}=\left[
     g_{mp}\vert \vert g_{mn}\right]^{-1} \tag{13}$$

diode resistances in series between $V_{DD}$ and
$GND$.  This is the ${\cal L}{\cal T}{\cal I}$
incremental resistance linearised about the
metastable $V_{1}=V_{2}=V_{3}\approx V_{DD}/2$
d.c. equilibrium, $g_{m}=g_{m}(V_{DD}/2)$, with
the loop gain ${\cal L}_{0}=-A_{v}^{3}(0)\gg 1$
but the circuit constrained not to leave the
equilibrium - the normal small signal resistance
with the ring killed.  It is valid for a test
frequency

$$|s|\ll \omega _{p}\ll \omega _{0}\approx 
      \sqrt{3}\,\omega _{p}\tag{14}$$

$\omega _{0}$ the normal mode frequency,
$(-A_{v}(j\omega _{0}))^{3}=1$, and for
$|v_{x}|\ll V^{\ast}$ so that (1) is valid.

Once the loop is closed and the circuit is
allowed to go to the stable large signal limit
cycle (14) is no longer the linearisation point.
The operation becomes large signal,
rail to rail to ${\cal O}(V_{DD})$, and the
linearised circuit becomes linear periodically
time varying, ${\cal L}{\cal P}{\cal T}{\cal V}$.
Formally there is no single ${\cal L}{\cal T}{\cal I}$
$R_{x}$.  E.g. with $v_{D}=V_{DD}+v_{x}(t)$

$$i_{x}=G_{x}(t)v_{x}+{\cal O}(v_{x}^{2})\tag{15}$$

$$G_{x}(t+T_{0})=G_{x}(t)\;\;,\;\;T_{0}=2\pi /\omega _{0}\tag{16}$$

with

$$G_{x}(t)=\sum_{k} {{g_{mp,k}(t)g_{mn,k}(t)}\over
                {g_{mp,k}(t)+g_{mn,k}(t)}}\tag{17}$$

$$g_{m,k}(t)=g_{m}\left(V_{GS,k}(t)\right)\tag{18}$$

the instantaneous large signal, cyclostationary
transconductance at the phase of the limit
cycle.  In particular $v_{k-1}(t)\ne v_{k}(t)$.
At $\omega \approx \omega _{0}$

$$v_{k}(t)=V_{k}(t)+{\rm Re}\,{\hat v}_{k}e^{j\omega t}\tag{19}$$

$${\hat v}_{k-1}={\hat v}_{k}e^{\pm j2\pi /3}\tag{20}$$

the three small signal phasors are $120^{o}$
apart and the gate is no longer ${\cal A}{\cal C}$
shorted to the drain.  Putting $s=j\omega $ in
(4)

$${\bf v}={A_{s}(s)\over {1+A_{v}(s)}}{\bf 1}v_{x}
      \tag{21}$$

for the common mode, and ${\bf v}=
[1+A_{v}^{3}(s)]^{-1}\cdots v_{x}$ for the
differential mode.  The denominator $1+A_{v}(s)$
is not $1+A_{v}^{3}(s)$ but e.g.

$$R_{x}(s)={v_{x}\over I_{x}(s)}
        ={1\over {3(g_{mp}+g_{op})}}
         {{1+A_{v}(s)}\over {1+A_{v}(s)-A_{s}(s)}}\tag{22}$$
$$={1\over 3}{{g_{o}+sC+g_{mn}+g_{mp}}\over
               {(g_{mp}+g_{op})(g_{mn}+g_{on})}}\tag{23}$$

which at $s=j\omega _{0}$ is complex,
${\rm Arg}\,R_{x}\approx -60^{o}$, and in the
sideband picture

$$v_{x}(t)={\rm Re}\,{\hat v}_{x}e^{j(\omega _{0}+\Delta \omega )t}
      \tag{24}$$

creates currents at $\omega _{0}+\Delta\omega\pm
n\omega _{0}$.  I. e. the impedance is a
harmonic transfer matrix $Z_{mn}(\Delta\omega)$,
$m,n\in {\bf Z}$, with frequency conversion.
Its $0,0$ element for $|\Delta\omega|\ll
\omega _{0}$ can exhibit ${\rm Re}\,Z<0$ and an
inductive component because of the active loop.
That is the normal Floquet or Hajimiri-Lee
conversion matrix.  A single real $R_{x}$
is meaningless at ${\cal R}{\cal F}$.

What is normally quoted as ``$R_{x}$ while
oscillating'' is either

* (a) the derivative of the {\it averaged},
  ${\cal D}{\cal C}$, supply current

  $$\bar I_{x}={1\over {T_{0}}}\int_{0}^{T_{0}}I_{x}(t)dt
        \approx 3C_{L}V_{DD}f_{0}\tag{25}$$

  with respect to the ${\cal D}{\cal C}$ supply,

  $$R_{x,av}^{-1}={{\partial \bar I_{x}}\over {\partial V_{DD}}}
                =\langle G_{x}(t)\rangle
                ={1\over {T_{0}}}\int_{0}^{T_{0}}G_{x}(t)dt
                \tag{26}$$

  or
* (b) the $0,0$ element of the conversion
  matrix at $\Delta\omega\to 0$, i. e. the
  response to a perturbation $\omega _{x}\ll
  \omega _{0}$ averaged over many oscillation
  periods.

In both cases (12) survives {\it in form} with
$g_{m}$ replaced by the effective, conduction
angle averaged, describing function
transconductance,

$$R_{x,av}={1\over 3}\left[{1\over {\langle g_{mn}\rangle}}+
                         {1\over {\langle g_{mp}\rangle}}\right]
        ={R_{x,0}\over \eta}\tag{27}$$

$$\langle g_{m}\rangle ={1\over {T_{0}}}\int_{0}^{T_{0}}
                       g_{m}(t)dt =\eta\,g_{m0}\tag{28}$$

$\eta<1$ the duty factor during which the
inverter is in the high gain crowbar region.
For a conventional rail to rail hard switched
ring $\eta = \tau _{r,f}/T_{0}\ll 1$, typically
$0.1-0.3$, and

$$R_{x,av}\approx {1\over \eta}R_{x,0}\gg R_{x,0}\tag{29}$$

Ideally, zero rise-fall time, $\langle G_{x}\rangle
\to 0$, $R_{x,av}\to\infty$ at ${\cal D}{\cal C}$.
No ${\cal D}{\cal C}$ path exists between
$V_{DD}$ and $GND$ except during the transition:
for half the period the PMOS is off, for half
the period the NMOS is off,

$$G_{x}(t)\approx \cases{
        g_{mp}\vert \vert g_{mn}&{\rm in\;transition}\cr
        0&{\rm otherwise}}\tag{30}$$

so the instantaneous supply sees an open circuit
about $1-\eta$ of the time and ${1/g_{m}}$ about
$\eta$ of the time.  For a sinusoidal
describing function approximation
$v_{k}= (V_{DD}/2)\cos\omega _{0}t$,
$\langle g_{m}\rangle = (2/\pi)g_{m0}$ so that
e.g.

$$R_{x,av}\approx {\pi\over 2}R_{x,0}\approx 1.57R_{x,0}\tag{31}$$

more generally $1.5-3\times R_{x,0}$, and
$\to\infty$ for square wave switching.
In most hand calculations the factor $\eta^{-1}$
is ignored and (12) is still quoted as the
order of magnitude low frequency averaged supply
pushing resistance.

In short: the ${\cal L}{\cal T}{\cal I}$ (12)
is the small signal resistance {\it about the
unstable equilibrium with oscillation suppressed}.
About the stable limit cycle the circuit is
${\cal L}{\cal P}{\cal T}{\cal V}$; the
instantaneous $R_{x}(t)$ is periodically
modulated between $R_{x,0}$ and $\infty$,
its low frequency time average is (27), a factor
$1/\eta={\cal O}(2-\infty)$ larger than (12),
and its ${\cal R}{\cal F}$ impedance is a
complex frequency converting impedance with
${\rm Re}\,Z_{x}(\omega _{0}+\Delta\omega)$
that can become negative.  To ${\cal O}(1)$
the {\it form} (12) with $g_{m}\to\langle g_{m}\rangle$
remains a useful estimate for
$|s|\ll\omega _{0}$ after averaging over
$T_{0}\gg 2\pi/|s|$.  Neglecting the averaging
the claim ``each inverter is two diodes in
series'' fails because $v_{in}\ne v_{out}$ when
the ring is oscillating.

With ${\rm S}_{3}{\rm S}_{4}$ OFF the
conventional quasi static small signal gain at the
high ${\cal Z}$ nodes is the normal

$${{A}_{v}}(s)\approx {{g}_{m1}}{r_{o}}\approx
{{g}_{m1}}\left[ {{g}_{ds1}}+{{g}_{ds3}}+{{g}_{ds5}}
\right]^{-1}\tag{1}$$

so that with the conventional

$${{I}_{T}}\approx {{I}_{D7}}={{1\over {2}}}
{\mu}_{n}{C_{ox}}{{W_{7}}\over {L_{7}}}{\left[
{V_{GS7}}-{V_{T}}\right]^{2}}\tag{2}$$

in strong inversion

$${{g}_{{m1}}}\approx \sqrt{2{k_{1}}{{I}_{D1}}}}=
\sqrt{{k_{1}}{{I}_{T}}} \propto \sqrt{{W_{7}}}\tag{3}$$

in weak inversion ${{g}_{{m1}}}={{I}_{D1}}/n{V_{T}}\propto
{{W}_{7}}$ so that in the normal text book sense

$${{A}_{v}}\propto {{g}_{{m1}}}\propto \sqrt{{{W}_{7}}}
\;\;{\rm in\;strong\;inversion}\propto {{W}_{7}}\;\;
{\rm in\;weak\;inversion}\tag{4}$$

in so far as ${{g}_{ds}}\propto {{I}_{T}}$.
That is the ``${{g}_{m}}$ goes up'' statement that is
normally quoted.

For the clocked operation the figure of merit is not
(1) but the charge that can be integrated on the
parasitic capacitance ${{C}_{P}}\approx {{C}_{X}}$ in
the time the circuit is allowed to stay in the high
impedance amplifying region.  In the normal
StrongArm timing, Fig.1, with $CK=0$
${\rm S}_{1}-{\rm S}_{4}$ ON, $P,Q,X,Y={V_{DD}}$,
${\rm M}_{7}$ OFF.  With $CK:0\to 1$, ${\rm S}_{1}-
{\rm S}_{4}$ OFF, ${\rm M}_{7}$ ON, $P$ and $Q$ are
discharged through ${\rm M}_{1}{\rm M}_{2}$ with

$${{C}_{P}}{{d{{V}_{P,Q}}}\over {dt}}=-{{I}_{D1,2}}\tag{5}$$

$${{I}_{D1}}={{I_{T}}\over 2}+{{1\over 2}}{{g}_{{m1}}}
{{v}_{id}}\qquad {{I}_{D2}}={{I_{T}}\over 2}-{{1\over 2}}
{{g}_{{m1}}}{{v}_{id}} \tag{6}$$

so that differentially

$${d\over {dt}}\left( {{V}_{P}}-{{V}_{Q}}\right)=
-{{{{g}_{{m1}}}{{v}_{id}}}\over {{{C}_{P}}}}\tag{7}$$

and, for a time ${{T}_{{\rm int}}}$,

$$\Delta {{V}_{PQ}}({{T}_{{\rm int}}})=
{{{{g}_{{m1}}}{{v}_{id}}{{T}_{{\rm int}}}}\over
{{{C}_{P}}}}\tag{8}$$

i. e. $q=Cv$ gain

$${{A}_{{\rm int}}}={{\Delta {{V}_{PQ}}}\over {{{v}_{id}}}}
={{1\over {{{C}_{P}}}}\int_{0}^{{{T}_{{\rm int}}}}
{{{g}_{{m1}}}dt}\approx {{{{g}_{{m1}}}{{T}_{{\rm int}}}}
\over {{{C}_{P}}}}\tag{9}$$

${{T}_{{\rm int}}}$ is not a free variable.  The
circuit stays high ${\cal Z}$ only until the common
mode of $P,Q$ has fallen enough to turn ${\rm
M}_{3}{\rm M}_{4}$ on, $\Delta {{V}_{CM}}\approx
{{V}_{TN}}$, and then until the common mode of $X,Y$
has fallen enough to turn ${\rm M}_{5}{\rm M}_{6}$ on,
$\Delta {{V}_{CM}}\approx \left| {{V}_{TP}}\right|$.
To first order

$${{T}_{1}}\approx {{{{C}_{P}}{{V}_{TN}}}\over
{{{I}_{T}}/2}}\qquad {{T}_{2}}-{{T}_{1}}\approx
{{{{C}_{X}}\left| {{V}_{TP}}\right|}\over {{{I}_{T}}/2}}
\tag{10}$$

so that, e. {\rm g.} at the moment ${\rm M}_{3}$ turns
on,

$${{A}_{{\rm int}}}({{T}_{1}})\approx
{{{{g}_{{m1}}}}\over {{{C}_{P}}}}{{2{{C}_{P}}{{V}_{TN}}}
\over {{{I}_{T}}}}=2{{V}_{TN}}{{{{g}_{{m1}}}}\over
{{{I}_{T}}}}\tag{11}$$

and with (3) in square law strong inversion
${{g}_{{m}1}}=2{{I}_{D1}}/{{V}_{ov1}}={{I}_{T}}/
{{V}_{ov1}}$

$${{A}_{{\rm int}}}({{T}_{1}})\approx
2{{{{V}_{TN}}}\over {{{V}_{ov1}}}}\tag{12}$$

$${{V}_{ov1}}=\sqrt{{{2{{I}_{D1}}}\over {{k_{1}}}}}\propto
\sqrt{{{I}_{T}}}\propto \sqrt{{{W}_{7}}}\tag{13}$$

In weak inversion ${{g}_{{m1}}}/{{I}_{T}}=1/n{{V}_{T}}=
{\rm const}$ and

$${{A}_{{\rm int}}}({{T}_{1}})\approx {{{{V}_{TN}}}\over
{n{{V}_{T}}}}={\rm const.}\tag{14}$$

More completely, including the ${\rm M}_{3}{\rm M}_{4}$
positive feedback between ${{T}_{1}}$ and ${{T}_{2}}$,
Razavi, JSSC 92,

$$\Delta {{V}_{XY}}({{T}_{2}})\approx \Delta
{{V}_{PQ}}({{T}_{1}})\exp \left[ {{{{T}_{2}}-{{T}_{1}}}
\over {{{\tau }_{{\rm reg}}}}}\right]\tag{15}$$

$${{\tau }_{{\rm reg}}}\approx {{{{C}_{X}}}\over
{{{g}_{{m3}}}}}\propto 1/\sqrt{{{I}_{T}}}$$

$${{A}_{{\rm int}}}({{T}_{2}})\approx
{{{{g}_{{m1}}}}\over {{{g}_{{m3}}}}}\;
{\rm or}\;2{{{{V}_{TN}}}\over {{{V}_{ov1}}}}\;
{{{{V}_{TP}}}\over {{{V}_{ov3}}}}\;{\rm etc.}\tag{16}$$

i. e. the normal $1/{{V}_{ov}}\propto 1/\sqrt{{{I}_{T}}}$
voltage gain.  The ${\rm dc}$ ${{g}_{m}}{{r}_{o}}$ goes
up with ${{I}_{T}}$ but the integration time (10) goes
down $\propto 1/{{I}_{T}}$ and, because

$${{T}_{{\rm int}}}\propto 1/{{I}_{T}}\qquad
{{g}_{{m}}}\propto \sqrt{{{I}_{T}}}\;\;{\rm s.i.}\;
\propto {{I}_{T}}\;\;{\rm w.i.}\tag{17}$$

$${{A}_{{\rm int}}}\propto {{{{g}_{m}}{{T}_{{\rm int}}}}
\over C}\propto {{{{g}_{m}}}\over {{{I}_{T}}}}\propto
\cases{
{\rm const.}&w. i.\cr
1/\sqrt{{{I}_{T}}}\propto 1/\sqrt{{{W}_{7}}}&s. i.\cr}\tag{18}$$

In words: in weak/moderate inversion the useful
pre-regeneration, offset determining, ``initial'' gain is
to first order independent of the tail device size; in
conventional strong inversion sizing it falls as
$1/\sqrt{{W_{7}}}$, $1/{{V}_{ov1}}$.  The curve is
very flat, it exhibits a shallow maximum for a small
tail device, ${{V}_{ov1}}\approx 0.1-0.2\,{\rm V}$, and
then falls monotonically.  If ${\rm M}_{7}$ is made so
wide that ${\rm M}_{1}{\rm M}_{2}$ - and then ${\rm
M}_{3}{\rm M}_{4}$ - are driven into the triode region
before ${\rm M}_{5}{\rm M}_{6}$ can turn on, ${{r}_{o}}$
collapses and ${{A}_{{\rm int}}}\to 0$.  Neglecting the
${{T}_{{\rm int}}}\propto 1/{{I}_{T}}$ factor this is
normally quoted simply as (4), ${{A}_{v}}\propto
\sqrt{{W_{7}}}$, ${{A}_{v}}\propto {W_{7}}$ in weak
inversion.

The total latch gain after the regeneration interval
${{T}_{ev}}$

$${{G}_{{\rm tot}}}({{T}_{ev}})\approx {{A}_{{\rm int}}}
\exp \left[ {{{{T}_{ev}}-{{T}_{{\rm int}}}}\over
{{{\tau }_{{\rm reg}}}}}\right]\qquad 
{{\tau }_{{\rm reg}}}\approx C/{{g}_{m,{\rm latch}}}
\propto 1/\sqrt{{{W}_{7}}}\tag{19}$$

can still increase with ${{W}_{7}}$ because
${{\tau }_{{\rm reg}}}$ shrinks, i. e. the usual
speed - offset, ${{A}_{{\rm int}}}-{{\tau }_{{\rm
reg}}}$, trade-off: wide ${\rm M}_{7}$ is fast, narrow
${\rm M}_{7}$ is sensitive, low offset.  With
${{T}_{{\rm int}}}$ neglected this is quoted as
``the initial - low frequency - gain increases with
${{W}_{7}}$''.

> {\it Remark:} In many text books the
> ${{T}_{{\rm int}}}$ shortening is neglected and (1) is
> quoted as the ``initial gain'' : ${{A}_{v0}}\approx
> {{g}_{{m1}}}{{r}_{o1}}|\,|{{r}_{o3}}|\,|{{r}_{o5}}\propto
> {{g}_{{m1}}}\propto \sqrt{{W_{7}}}$, $\propto {W_{7}}$
> sub-threshold, i. e. widening ${\rm M}_{7}$ nominally
> increases the small signal gain until velocity
> saturation/sub-threshold is reached.  The clocked,
> integrating, offset setting gain (9)--(12) does the
> opposite.

In the Long Chanel, square law, ${\rm sat.}$
approximation the circuit can be reduced for
${\rm CK}=1$ to the ${\rm n}$ - channel pair ${\rm M1-M2}$
loaded by the ${\rm n}$ - chanel latch ${\rm M3-M4}$,
${\rm M5-M6}$ is {\it off}, $C_{P}$ is the capacity at
$P,Q$, $C_{X}$ the capacity at $X,Y$, Fig.1,

$${\rm M1:}\;\;i_{d1}=g_{m1}v_{i1}+g_{d1}(v_{P}-v_{S})$$
$${\rm M3:}\;\;i_{d3}=g_{m3}(v_{Y}-v_{P})+g_{d3}(v_{X}-v_{P}) \tag{*}$$

etc.  For the differential half circuit $v_{S}\approx 0$
for ${\rm M7}$ a good ${\rm C.S.}$

$${{v_{x}}\over {v_{i}}}{\Bigl |}_{0}\approx
{{g_{m1}}\over {g_{d1}+g_{d3}+g_{d5}}}=
{{2}\over {(\lambda _{n}+\lambda _{p})V_{ov1}}}\tag{1}$$

$$V_{ov1}=V_{GS1}-V_{T}= \sqrt{{{2I_{D1}}\over
{\mu _{n}C_{ox}W_{1}/L_{1}}}} \tag{2}$$

$$I_{D1}\approx {\textstyle{1\over 2}}I_{T}\qquad 
I_{T}= {\textstyle{1\over 2}}\mu _{n}C_{ox}{{W_{7}}\over {L_{7}}}
\left( V_{CK}-V_{T}-V_{S}\right)^{2}\;\;{\rm sat.}\tag{3}$$

$${{W_{7}}\!\uparrow}\;\; I_{T}\!\uparrow\;\;V_{ov1}\!\uparrow
\;\;A_{v0}\!\downarrow \tag{4}$$

and, e. {\it g.} in the conventional ``integrating''
picture, with ${\rm M3-M4}$ {\it off} for
$0<t<t_{1}$,

$$C_{P}{{dV_{P}}\over {dt}}=-I_{D1}\qquad 
C_{P}{{d\Delta V_{P}}\over {dt}}=-g_{m1}\Delta V_{i} \tag{5}$$

$$\Delta V_{P}(t)=-{{g_{m1}\Delta V_{i}}\over {C_{P}}}\,t \tag{6}$$

So that at the moment $t_{1}$ at which $V_{P}=V_{DD}-
V_{Tn}$ and ${\rm M3-M4}$ come on

$$t_{1}\approx {{C_{P}V_{Tn}}\over {I_{0}}}\qquad 
I_{0}={\textstyle{1\over 2}}I_{T} \tag{7}$$

$$\Delta V_{P1}= {{g_{m1}V_{Tn}}\over {I_{0}}}\Delta V_{i}
= {{2V_{Tn}}\over {V_{ov1}}}\Delta V_{i}\tag{8}$$

$$G_{P}\equiv {{\Delta V_{P1}}\over {\Delta V_{i}}}=
{{2V_{Tn}}\over {V_{ov1}}}\propto I_{T}^{-1/2}\propto
W_{7}^{-1/2}\;\;{\rm l.ch.}\tag{9}$$
$$\propto W_{7}^{-1}\;\;{\rm w.i.}\tag{9a}$$

For $t_{1}<t<t_{2}$ the same thing happens at $X,Y$,

$$C_{X}{{d\Delta V_{X}}\over {dt}}\approx -g_{m1}^{\ast}
\Delta V_{i}\tag{10}$$

$$t_{2}-t_{1}\approx {{C_{X}V_{Tp}}\over {I_{0}}}\tag{11}$$

and, to within a factor of order unity,

$$\Delta V_{X2}\approx 
{{g_{m1}^{\ast}\left( t_{2}-t_{1}\right)}\over {C_{X}}}
\Delta V_{i}+ \Delta V_{P1}\approx 
\left[{{g_{m1}^{\ast}V_{Tp}}\over {I_{0}}}+
{{g_{m1}V_{Tn}}\over {I_{0}}}\right]\Delta V_{i} \tag{12}$$

i. e. the large signal differential voltage that is
presented to the back to back inverters ${\rm M3-M6}$
when the ${\rm p}$ - channel cross coupled pair comes
on,

$$G_{0}\equiv {{\Delta V_{X2}}\over {\Delta V_{i}}}
\approx {{V^{\ast}}\over {V_{ov1}}}\propto 
{{g_{m1}}\over {I_{T}}}\propto 
I_{T}^{-1/2}\propto W_{7}^{-1/2}\tag{13}$$

In the velocity saturated, short chanel limit
$g_{m1}\propto W_{1}$ , $I_{T}\propto W_{7}$,

$$G_{0}\propto W_{7}^{0}\tag{14}$$

more generally $G_{0}\propto W_{7}^{-1/4\div 1/2}$.
If the output resistance in (1) is artificially kept
constant

$$|A_{v0}|\propto g_{m1}\propto \sqrt{I_{T}}\propto
\sqrt{W_{7}}\;\;{\rm s.i.}\tag{15}$$
$$\propto I_{T}\propto W_{7}\;\;{\rm w.i.}\tag{15a}$$

is the conventional low frequency, small signal voltage
gain.  In words: the ${\rm a.c.}$ $g_{m}R_{0}$ gain
formally goes up as $\sqrt{W_{7}}$, $W_{7}$ in weak
inversion, while the time the circuit has to integrate
that $g_{m}$ on $C_{P},C_{X}$ goes down as
$1/I_{T}$.  The net, usable, dynamic or integrating
gain handed to the regenerative latch goes as
$g_{m}T_{int}/C\propto g_{m}/I_{T}\propto 1/V_{ov1}$,
i. e. to first order it is independent of the tail
current and to second order it falls as $W_{7}^{-1/2}$,
$W_{7}^{-1}$ in weak inversion.

With the finite headroom included the $G_{0}(W_{7})$
curve is ${\rm n}$ - shaped.  For a very narrow
${\rm M7}$ the common source node $S$ sits high,
$V_{ov1}$ is small but ${\rm M1-M2}$ hit the triode
region after a very small drop of $V_{P,Q}$ and (9)
(13) collapse.  Widening ${\rm M7}$ pulls $S$ down,
${\rm M1-M2}$ stay saturated for the whole
$V_{Tn}+V_{Tp}$ swing and $G_{0}$ rises a little to a
broad maximum, typically a few times $(W_{7})_{\min}$,
and then follows (9)(13), i. e. falls as
$W_{7}^{-1/2}$, more or less flat in the fully
velocity saturated limit.  Once ${\rm M7}$ itself is
driven into the triode region $I_{T}$ ceases to go as
$W_{7}$, $R_{T}=1/g_{d7}$ collapses, the differential
tail ceases to be a virtual ground and (1)(9)(13) fall
much more rapidly.  To within the usual engineering
accuracy the circuit is normally operated at or beyond
the maximum and the statement is normally abbreviated
to: to first order the initial, integrating gain is
independent of $W_{7}$, in normal design it goes
weakly down with $W_{7}$.  With $R_{0}=$ const. the
text book $A_{v0}=g_{m1}R_{0}$ of course goes as
(15).

> {\it Remark:}  In the conventional square law notation
> the textbook small signal gain (1) is often quoted
> simply as $A_{v0}\propto g_{m1}\propto \sqrt{W_{7}}$.
> That is the $R_{0}=$ const. form of (15).

With the (square law) counting the circuit is
essentially a ${\rm G}_{m}\int {\rm d}t/{\rm C}$ amplifier

$${\rm G}_{0}={{g_{m1,2}T_{a}}\over {{\rm C}_{{\rm X,Y}}}}
\tag {*}$$

$T_{a}$ is the time that you have to integrate on
${\rm C}_{{\rm X,Y}}$ before the $n$ - latch, ${\rm M}_{3}
{\rm -M}_{4}$, and the $p$ - latch, ${\rm M}_{5}{\rm
-M}_{6}$, can take over.  In reset, ${\rm CK}=0$,
${\rm S}_{1}\dots {\rm S}_{4}$ on, $P\approx Q\approx
X\approx Y\approx V_{DD}$.  ${\rm M}_{1}{\rm -M}_{4}$ are
off.  Put ${\rm CK}=1$, ${\rm M}_{7}$ saturated

$${\rm I}_{T}\approx {1\over 2}\mu _{n}{\rm C}_{ox}
{W_{7}\over {\rm L}_{7}}\left(V_{DD}-V_{T}\right)^{2}
\propto W_{7}\tag{1}$$

at $t=0^{+}$ ${\rm X,Y}$ stay at $V_{DD}$ and
$P,Q$ are discharged with

$${{\rm d}V_{P,Q}\over {\rm d}t}=-{{\rm I}_{D1,2}\over
{\rm C}_{P}}\qquad {\rm I}_{D1,2}\approx {\rm I}_{T}/2 \tag{2}$$

so that, for a differential input $\Delta V_{i}$,

$$\Delta V_{P,Q}(t)={{g_{m1,2}\Delta V_{i}}\over 
{\rm C}_{P}}t \tag{3}$$

$${\rm M}_{3}{\rm -M}_{4}$$ get ${\rm V}_{GS}>0$ when
$P$($Q$) has fallen by $|V_{Tn}|$,

$$T_{1}\approx {{{\rm C}_{P}|V_{Tn}|}\over {{\rm I}_{D1,2}}}
\propto {1\over {\rm I}_{T}}\propto {1\over W_{7}} \tag{4}$$

and, for $t>T_{1}$, $X,Y$ are discharged through
${\rm M}_{1}{\rm -M}_{3}$ and ${\rm M}_{2}{\rm -M}_{4}$
with, to first order,

$$\Delta V_{XY}(t)\approx {{g_{m1,2}\Delta V_{i}}\over
{\rm C}_{X}}(t-T_{1})\tag{5}$$

Regeneration can start when $\Delta V_{XY}\sim V_{Tp}$
or, in any case, after a time

$$T_{a}\approx T_{1}+{{{\rm C}_{X}|V_{Tp}|}\over 
{\rm I}_{D1,2}}\propto {1\over {\rm I}_{T}} \tag{6}$$

So that the differential voltage that is presented
to the back to back inverters ${\rm M}_{3}{\rm -M}_{6}$
at the moment they go into the high gain region is,
from (*) (5) (6),

$${\rm G}_{0}={{\Delta V_{XY}(T_{a})}\over {\Delta V_{i}}}
\approx {{g_{m1,2}T_{a}}\over {\rm C}_{X}}
\approx {{g_{m1,2}}\over {{\rm I}_{T}}}{{{\rm C}_{X}|V_{T}|
+{\rm C}_{P}|V_{T}|}\over {\rm C}_{X}} \tag{7}$$

For a conventional square law ${\rm M}_{1,2}$ in saturation

$$g_{m1,2}= \sqrt{2\mu _{n}{\rm C}_{ox}{W_{1}\over
{\rm L}_{1}}{\rm I}_{D1}}\propto \sqrt{{\rm I}_{T}}
\propto \sqrt{W_{7}} \tag{8}$$

$${\rm G}_{0}\propto {{g_{m1,2}}\over {{\rm I}_{T}}}
\propto {1\over {\sqrt{{\rm I}_{T}}}}\propto
{1\over {\sqrt{W_{7}}}}\tag{9}$$

i. e. $g_{m}$ goes up as $\sqrt{W_{7}}$ but the time
you have to use it goes down as $1/W_{7}$.  E.G.

> {\it double $W_{7}$ $\rightarrow$ ${\rm I}_{T}\times 2$,
> $g_{m}\times 1.4$, $T_{a}/2$, net sampled gain
> $/1.4$.}

Formally the ordinary small signal voltage gain of the
cascode ${\rm M}_{1}{\rm -M}_{3}$,

$${\rm A}_{v0}={{g_{m1}}\over {g_{ds1}+g_{ds3}+g_{m3}}}\approx
{{g_{m1}}\over {g_{ds1}}}\approx {2\over {\lambda V_{ov1}}}
\propto {1\over {\sqrt{{\rm I}_{D1}}}}\propto {1\over
{\sqrt{W_{7}}}} \tag{10}$$

also falls as ${\rm I}_{T}^{-1/2}$.

In a modern velocity saturated short channel technology

$$g_{m}\approx W_{1}{\rm C}_{ox}v_{sat}\propto {\rm I}_{D}$$

so that $g_{m}/{\rm I}_{T}={\rm const.}$ and (7) becomes
to first order independent of $W_{7}$,

$${\rm G}_{0}\approx {{v_{sat}{\rm C}_{ox}W_{1}}\over
{{\rm I}_{T}}}T_{a}\approx {\rm const.}\tag{11}$$

In no case do you {\it gain} (sampled) voltage gain
by widening the tail device.  The text book shorthand
is often quoted as

> {\it The (dynamic) voltage gain of the Strong ARM is,
> to first order, independent of the tail current.  With
> square law counting it falls as $W_{7}^{-1/2}$.}

What you gain by $W_{7}\uparrow $ is speed,
$latch$ time

$$T_{latch}\propto {{\rm C}_{XY}\over {g_{m3,5}}}\log
{{\Delta V_{logic}}\over {\Delta V_{XY}(T_{a})}}$$

at the expense of pre amplifier gain, input referred
offset

$$V_{os}\propto {\rm G}_{0}^{-1}\propto \sqrt{W_{7}}$$

input referred noise, power, clock loading and kick back.
If the ${\rm M}_{1,2}$ current is made large enough to
drive ${\rm M}_{1,2}$ into the triode region at $T_{a}$,
${\rm G}_{0}$ collapses even faster.  There is an optimum
$W_{7}$ for minimum $V_{os}$.

If by ${\rm A}_{v}$ you mean the conventional LTI
${\rm A}_{v}=g_{m}r_{o}$ with $r_{o}$ held fixed,
${\rm A}_{v}\propto g_{m}\propto \sqrt{W_{7}}$ naively
{\it increases} as $\sqrt{W_{7}}$.  The quantity that is
normally quoted as the {\it initial}, {\it pre amp.} or
{\it integration} gain of the Strong ARM, Eq.(*), is the
decreasing, at best flat, function (9) (11).

In a conventional reset it is the so called
{\it Strong Arm} latch, Fig.1 in

\vbox{\ninerm J. Montanaro {\it et al.} {\it A $160{\rm MHz}$
$32{\rm b}\;0.5{\rm W}$ CMOS RISC microprocessor},
{\ninerm ISSCC 1996} }

\vbox{\ninerm
T. Kobayashi {\it et al.} {\it A current controlled latch sense
amplifier and a static power saving input buffer for low power
architecture}, {\ninerm JSSC 28, 523 1993 }}

It can be considered as a dynamic
$T_{int}$ integrator followed by a regenerative latch.
With $CK=0$ $M_{7}$ is off and $S_{1}-S_{4}$ put

$$V_{P}=V_{Q}=V_{X}=V_{Y}=V_{DD}\tag{1}$$

With $CK\uparrow $ $M_{7}$ goes on with

$$I_{T}=I_{1}+I_{2}\tag{2}$$

$S_{1}-S_{4}$ go off.  For

$$0<t<t_{1}\qquad |V_{GS3}|\approx |V_{GS4}|\approx 0\tag{3}$$

$X$ and $Y$ stay at ${{V_{DD}}}$ on the ${\rm C}_{x}=
C_{X}=C_{Y}$ and $P$ and $Q$ integrate the signal
current of $M_{1}-M_{2}$ on the ${{C_{p}}=C_{P}=C_{Q}}$,

$$C_{p}{\dot V}_{P}=-I_{1}\qquad C_{p}{\dot V}_{Q}=-I_{2}
\tag{4}$$

$$V_{P}=V_{DD}-I_{1}t/C_{p}\qquad V_{Q}=V_{DD}-I_{2}t/C_{p}
\tag{5}$$

so that for a differential signal

$$I_{1}-I_{2}=g_{m1}\Delta V_{in}\tag{6}$$

$$\Delta V_{PQ}(t)=V_{P}-V_{Q}=-g_{m1}\Delta V_{in}t/C_{p}
\tag{7}$$

is the usual $g_{m}/sC_{p}$ integrator.
In small signal language

$${\cal A}_{p}(s)={{g_{m1}}\over{sC_{p}}}\parallel r_{o1}\qquad
\omega _{p}={1\over {r_{o1}C_{p}}}\qquad
{\rm GBW}={g_{m1}\over {C_{p}}}\tag{8}$$

and for a fixed integration time $T_{{\rm int}}$

$${\cal A}_{1}=g_{m1}T_{{\rm int}}/C_{p}\propto 1/C_{p}\tag{9}$$

is the ''initial'' or ''pre amplification'' gain, bandwidth
$\propto 1/C_{p}$.

In normal operation $T_{{\rm int}}$ is not fixed.  $M_{3}$
with $V_{G}=V_{Y}$, $V_{S}=V_{P}$ and $M_{4}$ with
$V_{G}=V_{X}$, $V_{S}=V_{Q}$ stay off until

$$V_{P}(t_{1})=V_{Q}(t_{1})=V_{DD}-V_{Tn}\tag{10}$$

i. {\it e.}

$$t_{1}=C_{p}V_{Tn}/I_{cm}\qquad I_{cm}=I_{T}/2 \tag{11}$$

linearly increasing with $C_{p}$ and

$$\Delta V_{PQ}(t_{1})=-{{g_{m1}V_{Tn}}\over{I_{cm}}}\Delta V_{in}
\tag{12}$$

$${\cal A}_{1}={{\Delta V_{PQ}(t_{1})}\over{\Delta V_{in}}}=
{{g_{m1}V_{Tn}}\over{I_{cm}}}\tag{13}$$

nominally $C_{p}$ independent {\it at the trip point}.
In normal text book language the ''initial gain'' is
$C_{p}$ independent to first order.

For $t>t_{1}$ put, for the increments,

$$\eqalign{
C_{p}\dot v_{p}&=-g_{m1}v_{in1}+g_{m3}(v_{y}-v_{p})\cr
C_{p}\dot v_{q}&=-g_{m1}v_{in2}+g_{m3}(v_{x}-v_{q})\cr
C_{x}\dot v_{x}&=-g_{m3}(v_{y}-v_{p})\cr
C_{x}\dot v_{y}&=-g_{m3}(v_{x}-v_{q})\cr}\tag{14}$$

with $g_{m3}=g_{m4}$.  For the differential quantities
$\Delta v_{p}=v_{p}-v_{q}$, $\Delta v_{x}=v_{x}-v_{y}$,
$\Delta v_{in}=v_{in1}-v_{in2}$,

$$\eqalign{
C_{p}\Delta \dot v_{p}&=-g_{m1}\Delta v_{in}-g_{m3}
\left(\Delta v_{p}+\Delta v_{x}\right)\cr
C_{x}\Delta \dot v_{x}&=+g_{m3}\left(\Delta v_{p}+\Delta v_{x}
\right)\cr}\tag{15}$$

Put $S=\Delta v_{p}+\Delta v_{x}$,

$$\dot S-{{g_{m3}}\over{C_{x}}}{{C_{p}-C_{x}}\over{C_{p}}}S=
-{{g_{m1}}\over{C_{p}}}\Delta v_{in}\tag{16}$$

$$a=g_{m3}\left({1\over{C_{x}}}-{1\over{C_{p}}}\right) \tag{17}$$

$$S(t)=\left[S(t_{1})+b/a\right]e^{a(t-t_{1})}-b/a\tag{18}$$

$$b=-g_{m1}\Delta v_{in}/C_{p}\qquad S(t_{1})=\Delta V_{PQ}(t_{1})
\tag{19}$$

$$C_{x}\Delta \dot v_{x}=g_{m3}S\tag{20}$$

so that

$$\Delta v_{x}(t)={{g_{m3}}\over{C_{x}}}\int_{t_{1}}^{t}S(t')dt'
\tag{21}$$

For $C_{p}\gg C_{x}$, $a\approx g_{m3}/C_{x}>0$ and

$$S(t)\approx S(t_{1})e^{g_{m3}(t-t_{1})/C_{x}}\tag{22}$$

$$\Delta v_{x}(t)\approx S(t_{1})\left[e^{g_{m3}(t-t_{1})/C_{x}}-1
\right]\tag{23}$$

the normal regenerative exponential with

$$\tau _{n}=C_{x}/g_{m3}\tag{24}$$

For $C_{p}\approx C_{x}$, $a\approx 0$,

$$S(t)\approx S(t_{1})-g_{m1}\Delta v_{in}(t-t_{1})/C_{p}\tag{25}$$

$$\Delta v_{x}(t)\approx {{g_{m3}}\over{C_{x}}}S(t_{1})(t-t_{1})
\tag{26}$$

In either case if the circuit is allowed to go to the
second trip point where

$$\eqalign{
V_{X}(t_{2})&=V_{Y}(t_{2})=V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}|\cr
t_{2}-t_{1}&\approx C_{x}|V_{Tp}|/I_{cm}\cr}\tag{27}$$

when $M_{5}-M_{6}$ go on, the voltage that has been
developed differentially at $X-Y$ at $t=t_{2}$, {\it i. e.} the
normally quoted {\it available} small signal gain before the
PMOS latch regenerates, is, to first order,

$${\cal A}_{2}={{g_{m3}(t_{2}-t_{1})}\over{C_{x}}}=
{{g_{m3}|V_{Tp}|}\over{I_{cm}}}\tag{28}$$

again $C_{x}$ independent, so that the total nominal
pre regenerative gain

$${\cal A}_{0}={\cal A}_{1}{\cal A}_{2}\approx
{{g_{m1}V_{Tn}}\over{I_{cm}}}{{g_{m3}|V_{Tp}|}\over{I_{cm}}}
\tag{29}$$

in the $a\to 0$ linear limit and

$${\cal A}_{0}\propto {{g_{m1}V_{Tn}}\over{I_{cm}}}
\exp \left[{{g_{m3}|V_{Tp}|}\over{I_{cm}}}
\left(1-{{C_{x}}\over{C_{p}}}\right)\right]\tag{30}$$

in the $C_{p}\gg C_{x}$ exponential limit, is nominally
independent of $C_{p},C_{x}$ and depends only on
$g_{m}/I$ and $V_{T}$.  The $C_{p}$ dependence in (30) is

$${\cal A}_{0}(C_{p})\propto 
\exp \left[{{g_{m3}|V_{Tp}|}\over{I_{cm}}}{{C_{x}}\over{C_{p}}}
\right]^{-1}\tag{31}$$

monotonically increasing with $C_{p}$, $\to \exp
\left[g_{m3}|V_{Tp}|/I_{cm}\right]$ for $C_{p}\gg C_{x}$,
$\to 1$ for $C_{p}=C_{x}$, {\it i. e.} a very weak,
logarithmic increase of the available trip point voltage
with added $C_{p}$.

What does increase linearly with $C_{p}$ is the time
needed to get there, (11), and the pole frequency (8)
moves down as $1/C_{p}$.  The gain band width product

$${\rm GBW}_{p}=g_{m1}/C_{p}\tag{32}$$

goes as $1/C_{p}$.  For a given clock frequency, {\it i. e.}
for fixed $T_{{\rm int}}$, (9) the usable initial
integration gain goes as $1/C_{p}$, the $-3{\rm dB}$
band width goes as $1/C_{p}$ and the decision delay

$$T_{d}\approx t_{1}+(t_{2}-t_{1})+\tau_{0}\ln {{V_{DD}}\over
{\Delta V_{X}(t_{2})}}\tag{33}$$

$$\tau_{0}^{-1}\approx {{g_{m3}}\over{C_{x}}}+{{g_{m5}}\over{C_{x}}}
\tag{34}$$

goes up $\propto C_{p}$.  In everyday language: you
lose speed, you lose gain per unit time and you increase
the $kT/C_{p}$, clock feed through $C_{gd}/C_{p}$ and
$C_{p}$ mismatch $\Delta C_{p}/C_{p}$ offset for
practically no increase in DC trip point voltage.

That is why in text books the statement is normally
shortened to: {\it the initial $g_{m}/C$ gain goes down as
$1/C_{p}$}, or, with the trip point definition, {\it the
initial gain is to first order $C_{p}$ independent and any
added $C_{p}$ just slows the comparator}.  If you insist
on waiting until $M_{5}-M_{6}$ switch, the small signal
voltage that is present at $X-Y$ at that instant does go
up slowly with $C_{p}$ as (30)–(31), which is sometimes
used intentionally, $5-20{\rm fF}$ at $P-Q$, to get a few
${\rm dB}$ more pre amp. gain and less kick back at the
expense of $C_{p}V_{T}/I_{T}$ more delay.  The conventional
way to cure it is the double tail or Elzakker latch which
isolates $C_{p}$ from $C_{x}$.  Cf. any text on the
Strong Arm latch, {\it e. g.} Razavi, {\it Design of Analog
CMOS Integrated Circuits}, Chap. 12.

At the transition it is a
$${g_{m}VT^{-1}}$$
integrator.  In the familiar piece wise linear
picture, Fig. 12.20 of Razavi, with ${\rm CK}=0$

$$V_{P,Q}=V_{X,Y}=V_{DD}\tag{reset}$$

$$M_{7}={\rm OFF}\qquad S_{1-4}={\rm ON}$$

with ${\rm CK}=1$

$$S_{1-4}={\rm OFF}\tag{evaluate}$$
$$M_{7}={\rm ON}$$

let

$$I_{0}=I_{7}\qquad I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{0}/2\tag{1}$$

$${{dV_{P}}\over {dt}}=-{{I_{D1}}\over {C_{P}}}\qquad
  {{dV_{Q}}\over {dt}}=-{{I_{D2}}\over {C_{Q}}} \tag{2}$$

so that for a differential input

$$\Delta V_{PQ}(t)=V_{P}-V_{Q}=-{{I_{D1}-I_{D2}}\over {C_{P}}}t
        \approx -{{g_{m1}\Delta V_{in}}\over {C_{P}}}t \tag{3}$$

$X,Y$ stay at $V_{DD}$ because for

$$V_{GS3}=V_{Y}-V_{P}<V_{TN}\qquad V_{GS4}=V_{X}-V_{Q}<V_{TN}\tag{4}$$

$M_{3},M_{4}$ are off.  $M_{3}$ {\it resp.} $M_{4}$
comes on when

$$V_{Y}-V_{P}=V_{TN}\tag{5}$$

i. e. when the common mode at $P,Q$ has fallen by

$$|\Delta V_{CM}|=V_{TN}\tag{6}$$

$$T_{1}=\int_{V_{DD}}^{V_{DD}-V_{TN}}{{C_{P}dV_{P}}\over {I_{0}/2}}
      ={{2C_{P}V_{TN}}\over {I_{0}}}\propto C_{P}\tag{7}$$

and, from (3),

$$|\Delta V_{PQ}(T_{1})|={{g_{m1}T_{1}}\over {C_{P}}}|\Delta V_{in}|
   ={{2g_{m1}V_{TN}}\over {I_{0}}}|\Delta V_{in}|\tag{8}$$

$C_{P}$ cancels.  To first order the differential voltage
sampled on $P,Q$ at the instant the nMOS cross coupled pair
fires is $C_{P,Q}$ independent.  That is the {\it sampled}
{\it seed} voltage that is normally quoted as the {\it
initial voltage gain}

$$A_{v0}^{(P)}={{\Delta V_{PQ}(T_{1})}\over {\Delta V_{in}}}
        \approx {{g_{m1}V_{TN}}\over {I_{0}/2}}\approx {{g_{m1}}\over
        {g_{m3}}} \tag{9}$$

in small signal form

$$R_{P}\approx {1\over {g_{m3}}},\qquad A_{v0}\approx -g_{m1}R_{P}
\tag{10}$$
