$$ \omega _{pP}\approx {{g_{m3}}\over {C_{P}}}\tag{11}$$

so that the low frequency small signal voltage gain at $P,Q$
is $C_{P}$ independent, $C_{P}$ only moves the dominant pole
at $P,Q$ down as $1/C_{P}$ and adds the delay (7).

For $t>T_{1}$ $M_{3},M_{4}$ are on.  With $C_{X}=C_{Y}$,
$C_{P}=C_{Q}$ the incremental circuit for the differential
signals $v_{p}=V_{P}-V_{Q}$, $v_{x}=V_{X}-V_{Y}$ is, to
$g_{m}$ order,

$$\eqalign{
C_{P}{\dot v}_{p}&=-g_{m3}v_{x}-g_{m3}v_{p}-g_{m1}v_{in}\cr
C_{X}{\dot v}_{x}&=g_{m3}v_{x}+g_{m3}v_{p}\cr} \tag{12}$$

i. e.

$$\left[ \matrix{C_{P}p+g_{m3}&g_{m3}\cr -g_{m3}&C_{X}p-g_{m3}\cr}
        \right]\left[ \matrix{v_{p}\cr v_{x}\cr}\right]=
        \left[ \matrix{-g_{m1}v_{in}\cr 0\cr}\right] \tag{13}$$

$$\left(C_{P}C_{X}p^{2}+g_{m3}(C_{X}-C_{P})p\right)v_{x}
        =-g_{m1}g_{m3}v_{in} \tag{14}$$

For Laplace $v_{in}(s)=V_{in}/s$

$$V_{x}(s)=-{{g_{m1}g_{m3}V_{in}}\over
          {C_{P}C_{X}s^{2}\left(s+a\right)}},\qquad 
          a={{g_{m3}(C_{X}-C_{P})}\over {C_{P}C_{X}}}\tag{15}$$

$$v_{x}(t)=-{{g_{m1}g_{m3}V_{in}}\over {C_{P}C_{X}a^{2}}}
          \left[at-1+e^{-at}\right] \tag{16}$$

For $at\ll 1$, $C_{P}\approx C_{X}$,

$$v_{x}(t)\approx -{{g_{m1}g_{m3}}\over {2C_{P}C_{X}}}V_{in}t^{2}
                \tag{17}$$

i. e. a $t^{2}$ integrator with incremental gain

$$\left|A_{v}(t)\right|=\left|{{v_{x}(t)}\over {V_{in}}}\right|
        \approx {{g_{m1}g_{m3}t^{2}}\over {2C_{P}C_{X}}}
        \propto {1\over {C_{P}C_{X}}}\tag{18}$$

for a {\it given\/} evaluation interval.  For $C_{X}>C_{P}$ and
$at\gg 1$

$$v_{x}(t)\approx -{{g_{m1}}\over {C_{X}-C_{P}}}V_{in}t
                \tag{19}$$

$$\left|A_{v}(t)\right|\approx {{g_{m1}t}\over {C_{X}-C_{P}}}
        \propto {1\over {C_{X}-C_{P}}}\tag{20}$$

For $C_{P}>C_{X}$, $a<0$, put $b=-a=g_{m3}(C_{P}-C_{X})/C_{P}C_{X}
>0$,

$$v_{x}(t)\approx -{{g_{m1}C_{P}C_{X}}\over
                {g_{m3}(C_{P}-C_{X})^{2}}}V_{in}e^{bt}\tag{21}$$

an exponential regeneration with

$$\tau _{n}={1\over b}={{C_{P}C_{X}}\over {g_{m3}(C_{P}-C_{X})}}
        \tag{22}$$

In ordinary use the integration is stopped when the common
mode at $X,Y$, which for $t>T_{1}$ falls with the total
capacitance $C_{P}+C_{X}$,

$${{dV_{CMX}}\over {dt}}\approx -{{I_{0}}\over {C_{P}+C_{X}}} \tag{23}$$

reaches $V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|$ and the pMOS pair $M_{5}M_{6}$
fires,

$$T_{2}\approx T_{1}+{{C_{X}|V_{TP}|+C_{P}V_{TN}}\over {I_{0}}}
      \propto C_{P}+C_{X}\tag{24}$$

so that the self timed differential seed at the onset of
full CMOS regeneration is, from (16) with $t=T_{2}$,

$$|\Delta V_{X}(T_{2})|\propto {{(C_{P}+C_{X})^{2}}\over
        {C_{P}C_{X}}}|\Delta V_{in}|={{C_{P}}\over {C_{X}}}+
        {{C_{X}}\over {C_{P}}}+2\tag{25}$$

for the $t^{2}$ regime and

$$|\Delta V_{X}(T_{2})|\propto {{C_{P}+C_{X}}\over {C_{X}-C_{P}}}
        |\Delta V_{in}|\tag{26}$$

for the linear regime, i. e. to first order $C_{P}$
independent and to second order a very weak increase with
$C_{P}$, $C_{P}/(C_{X}-C_{P})$, tending to the limit
$g_{m3}/C_{X}$ for $C_{P}\gg C_{X}$.

In engineering terms: the $DC$ $g_{m}R$ gain
$g_{m1}/g_{m3}$ does not change.  The $GBW$,
$g_{m}/C_{P}$, goes down as $1/C_{P}$, the dominant pole
$\omega _{p}=g_{m3}/C_{P}$ moves in, and for a {\it fixed\/}
clock evaluation time the large signal integration gain
(17)–(20) falls as $1/C_{P}$, $1/C_{P}C_{X}$.  The price for
any extra seed voltage (25)–(26) is a linear increase of the
evaluation delay (7), (24),

$$\Delta T_{D}\approx {{V_{TN}}\over {I_{0}/2}}\Delta C_{P}
        \approx {{C_{P}V_{T}}\over {I_{0}}}\tag{27}$$

and a corresponding increase of the input referred offset,
thermal noise and kick back for a given throughput.

It is customary to summarise this as {\it the usable
initial, pre-regeneration, voltage gain falls,
$\propto 1/C_{P}$, $1/C_{P}C_{X}$, and the latch slows down
$\propto C_{P}$}.  In the idealised $\int g_{m}dt/C$
picture the $C_{P}$ cancels at the sampling instant,
Eq.\,{\rm (8)}, so the textbook shorthand is {\it no first
order change in the sampled seed voltage, at best a
marginal $\propto (C_{P}+C_{X})/(C_{X}-C_{P})$ increase
bought with a $\propto C_{P}$ delay penalty; for any
practical fixed rate clock the effective gain is reduced}.
With the usual $C_{P}<C_{X}$ design the often quoted
result is simply

$$A_{v,{\rm int}}(t)\approx {{g_{m1}t}\over {C_{X}}}\;\;{\rm or}\;\;
  {{g_{m1}g_{m3}t^{2}}\over {2C_{P}C_{X}}}\;\;{\rm decreases\;with\;}
  C_{P}$$

and the $-3\,{\rm dB}$ gain $g_{m1}/g_{m3}$ stays put while
$GBW\approx g_{m1}/C_{P}$ falls.  Hence the comparator
appears as lower gain, higher input referred offset,
$\propto 1/A_{v0}$, and slower regeneration,
Eqs.\,(22),(27).  Minimising $C_{P,Q}$ is the normal
speed optimisation; a small intentional $C_{P,Q}$ is
sometimes added to trade speed for improved isolation,
kick back and a $\sim (C_{P}+C_{X})^{2}/C_{P}C_{X}$
increase of the self timed seed, up to the
$g_{m}/C_{X}$ limit.

With the conventional linearised, self timed,
integration picture the circuit is two cascaded $g_{m}-C$
integrators.  For the ${\rm M}_{1}-{\rm M}_{2}$ pair, Fig.Razavi

$${\rm S}_{1}-{\rm S}_{4}\;\;{\rm on}\;\;
V_{P}=V_{Q}=V_{X}=V_{Y}=V_{DD}\qquad {\rm M}_{7}\;\;{\rm off}$$

on ${\rm CK}\uparrow \;{\rm S}_{i}\;{\rm off}\;{\rm M}_{7}\;{\rm on}$

$$\eqalign{
C_{P}{\dot V}_{P}&=-I_{D1}-I_{D3}\cr
C_{P}{\dot V}_{Q}&=-I_{D2}-I_{D4}\cr
C_{X}{\dot V}_{X}&=-I_{D3}\cr
C_{Y}{\dot V}_{Y}&=-I_{D4}\qquad {\rm M}_{5,6}\;\;{\rm off}}$$

put $\Delta I=I_{D1}-I_{D2}=g_{m1}\Delta V_{in}$,
$\;p=(V_{P}-V_{Q})/2$, $x=(V_{X}-V_{Y})/2$, $x(0)=p(0)=0$,
linearise ${\rm M}_{3}$ about $V_{GS}=V_{DD}-V_{P}$,

$$i_{d3}=g_{m3}(y-p)+g_{o3}(x-p)\tag{1}$$

etc. and for the normal $g_{o}\ll g_{m}$,

$$\eqalign{
C_{P}s\,p+g_{m3}p+g_{m3}x&=-g_{m1}\Delta V_{in}/2\cr
C_{X}s\,x-g_{m3}x-g_{m3}p&=0} \tag{2}$$

so that, $D(s)=C_{P}C_{X}s^{2}+g_{m3}(C_{X}-C_{P})s$,

$${{x}\over{\Delta V_{in}}}(s)=
-{{g_{m1}g_{m3}}\over{2D(s)}}\tag{3}$$

i. e. for $|s|\gg g_{m}/C$

$${{x}\over{\Delta V_{in}}}(s)\approx -{{g_{m1}g_{m3}}\over
{2C_{P}C_{X}s^{2}}}\tag{4}$$

in the time domain, for a $\Delta V_{in}u(t)$,

$$p(t)={{g_{m1}\Delta V_{in}}\over {C_{P}}}t \tag{5}$$

$$C_{X}{\dot x}=g_{m3}p\;\;,\;\;x(t)={{g_{m1}g_{m3}\Delta V_{in}}
\over{2C_{P}C_{X}}}t^{2}\tag{6}$$

i. e. $A_{v}(t)=x(t)/\Delta V_{in}\propto 1/C_{P}C_{X}$ for
a prescribed interrogation time $T_{int}$.  In the normal
text book shorthand

$$A_{v0}(T_{int})={1\over {C_{P}}}\int_{0}^{T_{int}}g_{m1}dt
\approx {{g_{m1}T_{int}}\over {C_{P}}}\propto {1\over {C_{P}}}
\tag{7}$$

for a fixed clock, the ``initial'' small signal gain goes
down like $1/C_{P}$ and the input referred contribution of
any offset in the regenerative latch goes up like $C_{P}$,
the regeneration time constant $\tau _{r}=C/g_{m}$ goes up
like $C_{P}$.

If you let the latch time itself the $1/C_{P}$ is to first
order cancelled by the $C_{P}$ dependence of the time at
which the ${\rm n}$ -latch fires.  With (5) the $P$ node
falls

$$V_{P}(t)=V_{DD}-{{I_{0}}\over{C_{P}}}t\tag{8}$$

$I_{0}=I_{tail}/2$, so that ${\rm M}_{3}$ turns on for

$$V_{DD}-V_{P}=V_{THN}\;\;,\;\;T_{1}={{C_{P}V_{THN}}\over{I_{0}}}
\tag{9}$$

and

$$\Delta V_{P}(T_{1})={{g_{m1}\Delta V_{in}}\over{C_{P}}}T_{1}
={{g_{m1}V_{THN}}\over{I_{0}}}\Delta V_{in}\tag{10}$$

$C_{P}$ independent to first order.  Carrying the second
integration (6) to the point where the ${\rm p}$ -latch fires,

$$V_{X}(t)=V_{DD}-{{I_{0}}\over{C_{X}}}(t-T_{1})\tag{11}$$

$$|V_{THP}|={{I_{0}}\over{C_{X}}}T_{2}\;\;,\;\;T_{2}=
{{C_{X}|V_{THP}|}\over{I_{0}}}\tag{12}$$

and from (6) with (9)(12)

$$x(T_{1}+T_{2})={{g_{m1}g_{m3}\Delta V_{in}}\over{2C_{P}C_{X}}}
T_{2}\left( 2T_{1}+T_{2}\right) \tag{13}$$

i. e. in the linear $g_{m}$ model

$$A_{vX}\equiv {{x(T_{1}+T_{2})}\over{\Delta V_{in}}}
={{g_{m1}g_{m3}}\over{2I_{0}^{2}}}
\left[2V_{THN}|V_{THP}|+{{C_{X}}\over{C_{P}}}|V_{THP}|^{2}
\right]\tag{14}$$

$c$.f. Razavi, {\it The StrongARM Latch} ISSCC 2015.
To the order most text books quote the $2V_{THN}|V_{THP}|$
term is the $C$ independent ``$P$ gain'' (10) and the
normally dominant $C_{X}/C_{P}$ term makes the usable
pre-regeneration gain at the output, $X-Y$, go as
$C_{X}/C_{P}\propto 1/C_{P}$.

With the more correct square law
$I_{D3}=(\beta _{3}/2)(V_{GS3}-V_{TH})^{2}$,

$$I_{D3}(t)={\beta_{3}\over 2}\left({{I_{1}t}\over{C_{P}}}-V_{THN}
\right)^{2}\;,\;t>T_{1}\tag{15}$$

$$C_{X}{\dot V}_{X}=-I_{D3}\;,\;
V_{X}(t)=V_{DD}-{\beta_{3}\over{6C_{X}}}
\left({{I_{0}}\over{C_{P}}}\right)^{2}(t-T_{1})^{3}\tag{16}$$

$$|V_{THP}|={\beta_{3}\over{6C_{X}}}
\left({{I_{0}}\over{C_{P}}}\right)^{2}(T_{2}-T_{1})^{3}\tag{17}$$

$$T_{2}-T_{1}= \left({{6C_{X}|V_{THP}|}\over{\beta_{3}}}\right)^{1/3}
\left({{C_{P}}\over{I_{0}}}\right)^{2/3}\propto
C_{P}^{2/3}C_{X}^{1/3}\tag{18}$$

and for the differential signal $\Delta I=g_{m1}\Delta V_{in}$,

$$\Delta I_{D}=I_{D3}-I_{D4}
={\beta_{3}\Delta I\,I_{0}\over{C_{P}^{2}}}\,t\,(t-T_{1})\tag{19}$$

$$|\Delta V_{X}(T_{2})|={1\over{C_{X}}}\int_{T_{1}}^{T_{2}}
|\Delta I_{D}|dt
={{2|V_{THP}|}\over{I_{0}}}\Delta I
+{1\over2}\beta_{3}^{1/3}6^{2/3}
{{V_{THN}|V_{THP}|^{2/3}}\over{I_{0}^{4/3}}}
{{C_{P}^{1/3}}\over{C_{X}^{1/3}}}\Delta I\tag{20}$$

i. e.

$$A_{vX}={{|\Delta V_{X}|}\over{\Delta V_{in}}}
=g_{m1}{{2|V_{THP}|}\over{I_{0}}}
+{1\over2}g_{m1}\beta_{3}^{1/3}6^{2/3}
{{V_{THN}|V_{THP}|^{2/3}}\over{I_{0}^{4/3}}}
{{C_{P}^{1/3}}\over{C_{X}^{1/3}}}\tag{21}$$

apart from the $C_{P}^{1/3}C_{X}^{-1/3}$ correction the
normally quoted term is $C$ independent.  In either model
no appreciable increase of the voltage division
$V_{os,latch}/A_{v0}$ of the latch offset is obtained by
making $C_{P}$ large.  The $1/C_{P}$ in (7) is cancelled to
first order by $T_{1}\propto C_{P}$ ( $T_{2}\propto
C_{P}^{2/3}$ in the square law model) and, for the
conventional fixed $T_{int}$ definition, $A_{v0}\propto
1/C_{P}$; for the complete $X-Y$ signal (14) $A_{vX}\propto
C_{X}/C_{P}$.  For very large $C_{P}$ the cubic law (16)
indeed makes $A_{vX}$ collapse $\propto 1/C_{P}$.

In the usual one line text book shorthand this is quoted as

> {\it the (fixed time) initial $g_{m}-C$ integrator gain
> falls as $1/C_{P}$ - and in the self timed latch it is
> to first order $C_{P}$ independent, Eq.\,10, so that adding
> $C_{P}$ buys you, at best, no extra pre-amplification.
> The normally dominant $X-Y$ gain, Eq.\,14, goes as
> $C_{X}/C_{P}$ and therefore goes down with $C_{P}$;
> with the square law correction Eq.\,21 it goes as
> $C_{P}^{1/3}C_{X}^{-1/3}$ before it eventually goes
> $\propto 1/C_{P}$.  In all cases the evaluation time
> $T_{int}=T_{1}+T_{2}\propto C_{P}\,(C_{P}^{2/3})$ and the
> regeneration time constant $\tau_{r}=C/g_{m}\propto C$
> grow linearly with $C_{P}$, so the comparator is made
> slower, noisier and more power hungry for (at best) the
> same input referred latch offset.}

With the conventional $A_{v0}=g_{m}T_{int}/C_{P}$ language
this is normally abbreviated to ``$A_{v0}$ goes down $\propto
1/C_{P}$'' - the input referred offset
$V_{os}^{in}=V_{os}^{latch}/A_{v0}$ goes up and the latch
gets slower.  To first order the self timed sampled
$\Delta V_{P}(T_{1})=g_{m}V_{TH}|\Delta V_{in}/I_{0}$ is
$C_{P}$ independent, so the more precise statement is
``to first order the $P$ gain does not increase at all and
the $X-Y$ gain decreases as $C_{X}/C_{P}$ $(C_{P}^{1/3})$;
you pay a $\propto C_{P}$ increase in $T_{int}$ and in
$\tau _{r}=C/g_{m}$ for no (or negative) improvement in
offset.''  This is why $C_{P},C_{Q}$ are normally kept as
small as parasitics allow and, if peaking is required,
$C_{X},C_{Y}$ is increased, not $C_{P},C_{Q}$.

In the normal sizing the circuit is the
so called Strong Arm latch. With

$${\cal S}_{1}\sim {\cal S}_{4}$$
the precharge switches, ${\cal M}_{7}$ the tail
device

* $${t_{1}}:CK=0\;\;P=Q=X=Y=V_{DD}\;\;,{\cal M}_{7}
{\rm \;off}$$
* $${t_{2}}:CK=1\;\;{\cal S}_{i}{\rm \;off\;,}{\cal M}_{7}
{\rm \;on\;,}\;P,Q\;{\hbox{fall with}}\;dV/dt=I_{D1,2}/C_{P,Q}$$
  the $\Delta V_{in}=V_{{in}1}-V_{{in}2}$ is integated as
  $\Delta V_{PQ}(t)=g_{m1,2}\Delta V_{in}t/C_{P,Q}$,
* $${t_{3}}:V_{PQ}<V_{DD}-V_{Tn}\;\;{\cal M}_{3},{\cal M}_{4}
{\rm \;on\;,\;}X,Y\;{\rm fall with}\;
dV/dt=I_{D3,4}/C_{XY}$$
* $${t_{4}}:V_{XY}<V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}|\;\;{\cal M}_{5},{\cal M}_{6}
{\rm \;on}$$

and the back to back inverters ${\cal M}_{3}{\cal M}_{5}$,
${\cal M}_{4}{\cal M}_{6}$ regenerate with

$$\eqalign{
V_{o}(t)&=\Delta V_{0}{\rm e}^{t/\tau}\cr
\tau^{-1}&={{G_{mN}+G_{mP}}\over {C_{XY}}}\cr
C_{XY}&=C_{0}+C_{gd5,6}^{\prime}W_{5,6}+C_{db5,6}^{\prime}
W_{5,6}+C_{gs5,6}^{\prime}W_{6,5}+C_{gd3,4}+C_{db3,4}
+C_{gs3,4}\cr
G_{mN}&=g_{m3}=g_{m4}\propto W_{3,4}\cr
G_{mP}&=g_{m5}=g_{m6}\propto W_{5,6}}$$

and, to first order,

$${\cal D}=t_{CK-Q}=t_{0}+t_{latch}$$

$$\eqalign{
t_{0}&\approx {{C_{XY}|V_{Tp}|}\over {I_{D1,2}}}
+{{C_{PQ}V_{Tn}}\over {I_{D1,2}}}\cr
t_{latch}&=\tau \log {{V_{DD}}\over {\Delta V_{0}}}\cr
\Delta V_{0}&\approx {{g_{m1,2}\Delta V_{in}}\over {C_{XY}}}t_{0}}$$

so that for $C_{XY}$ constant

$$t_{latch}\propto {1\over {G_{mN}+G_{mP}}}\propto {1\over {W_{5,6}}}$$

{\it i. e.} in small signal the p -latch {\it does}
latch faster the bigger $W_{5,6}$ is made.

With the self loading put in

$$\tau ={{C_{0}+C_{p}^{\prime}W_{5,6}}\over {G_{mN}+g_{mP}^{\prime}
W_{5,6}}}$$

and

$$t_{0}\propto C_{XY}\propto C_{0}+C_{p}^{\prime}W_{5,6}$$

$${\cal D}(W_{P})=A\left(C_{0}+C_{p}^{\prime}W_{P}\right)
+{{C_{0}+C_{p}^{\prime}W_{P}}\over {G_{mN}+g_{mP}^{\prime}W_{P}}}
\log {{V_{DD}}\over {\Delta V_{0}(W_{P})}}$$

has a shallow optimum at

$${{d{\cal D}}\over {dW_{P}}}=0\;\;,\;\;W_{P,opt}\approx
{C_{0}\over {C_{p}^{\prime}}}{{G_{mN}}\over {G_{mN}+{\rm log\;term}}}
\approx {\cal O}(1)\times W_{N}$$

in most technologies essentially the minimum $W_{P}$ that
still gives regenerative switching, normally
$W_{5,6}\approx 0.5-1.0\,W_{3,4}$ and in absolute value
$1-4\mu $ in $0.18\mu $, {\it i. e.} close to minimum
geometry.

* Starting from minimum geometry a modest increase of
$W_{5,6}$ does decrease the exponential time constant
$\tau $ by $\Delta \tau /\tau \approx -g_{mP}^{\prime}
\Delta W_{P}/(G_{mN}+G_{mP})$ and in the textbook
``$C_{XY}={\rm const.}$'' sense the comparator can be
said to get faster, of the order of $10-20\%$ for a
factor $2$ in $W_{P}$.

* The same $\Delta W_{P}$ increases the capacitance that
has to be discharged in $t_{0}$ and in reset,
$\Delta t_{0}/t_{0}\approx C_{p}^{\prime}\Delta W_{P}/C_{XY}$,
and increases $\tau $ through the numerator.  For any
appreciable widening $C_{p}^{\prime}W_{P}\sim C_{0}$,
$C_{p}^{\prime}\Delta W_{P}/C_{XY}>g_{mP}^{\prime}
\Delta W_{P}/(G_{mN}+G_{mP})$ and

$${{d{\cal D}}\over {dW_{P}}}>0$$

the conventional clock to $Q$ propagation delay,
$${\cal D}\approx C_{XY}|V_{Tp}|/I_{tail}+
\left(C_{XY}/G_{m}\right)\log \left(V_{DD}/\Delta V_{0}\right)$$
goes {\it up}} with $W_{5,6}$ and the maximum clock rate
$$f_{max}^{-1}\approx t_{reset}+{\cal D}\;\;,\;\;
t_{reset}\propto R_{{\cal S}3,4}C_{XY}$$
goes down.  The power $C_{XY}V_{DD}^{2}f$ goes up as
$W_{P}$.  In the normal, already optimum, sizing this is
normally quoted as ``making ${\cal M}_{5}{\cal M}_{6}$
bigger slows the comparator down''.

In round numbers in e. {\rm g.} $65{\rm nm}$ with
$W_{3,4}=4-8\mu $, $W_{5,6}=2-4\mu $, $C_{XY}\approx
10-20{\rm fF}$, $\tau \approx 15-25{\rm ps}$,
doubling $W_{5,6}$ lowers $\tau $ by $\sim 15\%$ but
raises $t_{0}$ by $\sim 20-30\%$ for a net $5-15\%$
{\it increase} of $t_{CK-Q}$ for small $\Delta V_{in}$
and a $\sim W_{P}$ increase of $t_{reset}$.  For
$W_{P}\gg W_{P,opt}$ the delay grows $\propto W_{P}$.

> {\it Remark:} If the self loading $C_{p}^{\prime}W_{P}$ is
> neglected, the usual textbook statement is: $G_{mP}\propto
> W_{P}$ so $\tau \propto 1/W_{P}$ and the latch regenerates
> faster, {\it i. e.} the {\it small signal regeneration
> speed}} improves with $W_{5,6}$.

With the usual abuse of language the ``speed'' is
two speeds.  Put ${\rm CK}=0$ for reset, ${\rm CK}=1$ for
evaluate.  During reset

$${\rm S}_{1}\!\cdot\! {\rm S}_{2}\;:\;P,Q\to V_{DD}\qquad
  {\rm S}_{3}\!\cdot\! {\rm S}_{4}\;:\;X,Y\to V_{DD}\qquad 
  {\rm M}_{7}\;\;{\rm OFF}$$

$$V_{GS3}=V_{Y}-V_{P}=0\;\;V_{GS4}=0\;\;V_{SG5}=V_{SG6}=0$$

on ${\rm CK}\uparrow $ ${\rm S}_{1}-{\rm S}_{4}$ go open,
${\rm M}_{7}$ goes on and $I_{D1,2}$ starts to discharge
$C_{P,Q}$ at a rate $\Delta I/g_{m1,2}$,

$${{dV_{P}}\over {dt}}=-{{I_{1}}\over {C_{P}}}\qquad
  {{dV_{Q}}\over {dt}}=-{{I_{2}}\over {C_{Q}}}\tag{1}$$

till

$$V_{P}<V_{Y}-V_{Tn}\tag{2}$$

and ${\rm M}_{3}$ or ${\rm M}_{4}$ comes on.  From then on
$X,Y$ are discharged through the ${\rm M}_{1}{\rm -M}_{3}$
${\rm M}_{2}{\rm -M}_{4}$ cascode at a rate $I_{1,2}/C_{X,Y}$
until

$$V_{X,Y}<V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}|\tag{3}$$

and the ${\rm M}_{5}{\rm -M}_{6}$ $p$ -pair comes on.
With both pairs on the small signal circuit at $X,Y$ is,
differentially,

$$C_{X,Y}{{d\Delta V}\over {dt}}=(g_{m3}+g_{m5})\Delta V,
\qquad \Delta V=V_{X}-V_{Y} \tag{4}$$

so that, with

$$\Delta V_{0}=\Delta V(t=t_{0})\tag{5}$$

the initial unbalance put on $C_{X,Y}$ by the $I_{1}-I_{2}$
integrator (1)-(3) before the $p$ devices come on,

$$\Delta V(t)=\Delta V_{0}
      \exp \left[{{g_{m3}+g_{m5}}\over {C_{X,Y}}}(t-t_{0})\right] \tag{6}$$

and, e.g. for $|\Delta V|=V_{DD}/2$,

$$t_{latch}={{C_{X,Y}}\over {g_{m3}+g_{m5}}}
            \ln {{V_{DD}/2}\over {\Delta V_{0}}}\tag{7}$$

and, to first order, from (1)-(3)

$$\eqalign{
t_{0}&=t_{0P}+t_{0X}\cr
     &={{C_{P}|V_{GS3}-V_{Tn}|}\over {I_{D1,2}}}
      +{{C_{X,Y}|V_{Tp}|}\over {I_{D1,2}}}+{\cal O}(1/g_{m}) \cr
     &={{C_{X,Y}}\over {I_{D1,2}}}|V_{Tp}|+{\rm etc.}} \tag{8}$$

$$t_{d}=t_{0}+t_{latch}\approx 
{{C_{X,Y}|V_{Tp}|}\over {I_{D}}}
+{{C_{X,Y}}\over {g_{m3}+g_{m5}}}
  \ln {{V_{DD}/2}\over {\Delta V_{0}}}\tag{9}$$

which is normally quoted in the Razavi form

$$t_{d}\approx 2{{C_{X}V_{Tp}}\over {I_{D}}}
+{{C_{X}}\over {g_{m,{\rm eff}}}}
 \ln \left[{{V_{DD}}\over 2}{\sqrt{{2C_{X}}\over {\beta_{1}}}}
           {{g_{m,{\rm eff}}}\over {I_{D}\Delta V_{in}}}\right]
\tag{10}$$

with $g_{m,{\rm eff}}=g_{m3}+g_{m5}$, $\Delta V_{0}\propto
g_{m1}\Delta V_{in}t_{0}/C_{X}\propto \Delta V_{in}I_{D}^{-1}
\sqrt{\beta_{1}/C_{X}}$, cf. {\it e.g.} Razavi, {\it Design
of Analog CMOS Integrated Circuits}, Chap. 8.

$$C_{X,Y}=C_{X0}+C_{j,db5}+C_{ov5}+C_{gs5}+ \cdots 
        =C_{X0}+W_{5}c_{j}^{\prime}+{2\over 3}W_{5}L_{5}C_{ox}
          +W_{5}C_{ov}^{\prime}+ \cdots \propto W_{5}\tag{11}$$

$$g_{m5}\propto \cases{
        \sqrt{W_{5}} & square law\cr
        W_{5} & {\rm short\; channel,\; }v_{sat}\cr}\tag{12}$$

So that for the regeneration proper

$$\tau _{l}= {{C_{X,Y}}\over {g_{m3}+g_{m5}}}\tag{13}$$

a small increase of $W_{5,6}$ from minimum size {\it decreases}
$\tau _{l}$ because the denominator increases faster than the
numerator.  E.g. square law

$$\tau _{l}={{C_{X0}+k_{c}W_{5}}\over {g_{m3}+k_{g}\sqrt{W_{5}}}}\tag{14}$$

$${{d\tau _{l}}\over {dW_{5}}}=0\;\;{\rm for}\;\;
  k_{c}(g_{m3}+k_{g}\sqrt{W_{5}})-{{k_{g}}\over {2\sqrt{W_{5}}}}
        (C_{X0}+k_{c}W_{5})=0\tag{15}$$

i.e. a shallow optimum at

$$g_{m5,opt}\approx g_{m3}{{1}\over {1+C_{X0}/k_{c}W_{5}}}\tag{16}$$

normally quoted as $g_{m5}\approx g_{m3}$ or $W_{5}\approx
W_{3}$ for matched layout, $\mu _{n}\approx 2\mu _{p}$, etc.
Up to about a factor $1.5-2$ increase from minimum $W_{5}$
$\tau _{l}$ can be reduced by $10-20\%$.  Normal textbook
shorthand: ``the latch gets faster''.

The price is (11).  The initial unbalance $\Delta V_{0}$
that the latch has to regenerate goes as $1/C_{X,Y}$ and the
``integrator'' time $t_{0}\propto C_{X,Y}$ (8) goes {\it up}
linearly with $W_{5,6}$.  The logarithmic term in (9) also
goes as $\ln C_{X,Y}^{1/2}$.  Hence the {\it total}
StrongArm delay (9)-(10) has a shallow optimum and then {\it
increases}} with $W_{5,6}$,

$${{dt_{d}}\over {dW_{5}}}={{|V_{Tp}|}\over {I_{D}}}{{dC_{X}}\over {dW_{5}}}
+{{1}\over {g_{m,{\rm eff}}}}{{dC_{X}}\over {dW_{5}}}
  \ln(\cdots)+C_{X}{{d(1/g_{m,{\rm eff}})}\over {dW_{5}}}\ln(\cdots)
  +\cdots >0\tag{17}$$

for any appreciable widening beyond the $g_{m5}\approx g_{m3}$
optimum.  In the normally sized circuit the $t_{0}$ term
dominates, so the usual loose statement is that widening
${\rm M}_{5}{\rm -M}_{6}$ {\it slows the comparator down}},
increases the reset, $R_{on,{\rm S}_{3,4}}C_{X,Y}$, time and
increases the dynamic power $C_{X,Y}V_{DD}^{2}f_{CK}$ for no
appreciable gain in regeneration speed.  With $C_{X,Y}\propto
W_{5}$ and $g_{m}\propto \sqrt{W}$ the often quoted result is

$$t_{d}\to {\cal O}(W_{5})\tag{18}$$

so that for $W_{5}\gg W_{5,opt}$ the comparator is decidedly
slower.  In the limit $W_{5}\to \infty $, $\tau _{l}\to
k_{c}W_{5}/k_{g}\sqrt{W_{5}}\propto \sqrt{W_{5}}\to \infty $.

If the $1/C_{X}$ dependence of $\Delta V_{0}$ and the $t_{0}$
term are neglected the latch itself can be said to get
marginally faster, $d\tau _{l}/dW_{5}<0$, up to the optimum
(16).  That is the ``speed improves'' quoted in some notes.

For mismatch the $p$ -pair offset contribution goes as
$1/\sqrt{W_{5}L_{5}}$, so widening ${\rm M}_{5,6}$ does
reduce the input referred offset due to ${\rm M}_{5,6}$ at the
expense of power and, beyond the optimum, of speed.  The
conventional optimum is $W_{5}\approx (0.5-1.0)W_{3}$,
$g_{m5}\approx g_{m3}$, giving the minimum $t_{d}$ in (10).

With the usual ${\rm {{S{'}}s}}$ the ${\rm {{S{'}}s}}$
open the operation is sometimes divided into an
e. g. {\it after} ${\rm {S_{1}S_{2}}}$ open {\it
e. g.} as

* {\it {\rm {P\,Q}} discharge:} ${\rm {M_{7}}}$ on
${\rm {S_{1}S_{2}}}$ off
$${{V}_{P,Q}(t)={{V}_{DD}}-{{I}_{1,2}\over
{{C}_{P,Q}}}t\tag{1}}$$
so that a

$$\eqalign{
\Delta {{V}_{PQ}}(t) &={{g_{m1}}\over {{C}_{PQ}}}\Delta
{{V}_{{\rm {in}}}}t \cr
\Delta {{V}_{i}}&={{g_{m1}}\over {{C}_{PQ}}}{{V}_{THN}\over
{{I}_{1}}}\Delta {{V}_{{\rm {in}}}}{{C}_{PQ}} \tag{2}}$$

is built up on ${{C}_{PQ}}$ before
${{V}_{P,Q}}={{V}_{DD}}-{{V}_{TN}}$ and ${{M}_{3}},
{{M}_{4}}$ can come on,

* {\it {\rm {X\,Y}} fall:} ${{M}_{3,4}}$ on
$${{V}_{X,Y}(t)={{V}_{DD}}-{{I}_{3,4}\over {{C}_{XY}}}t\tag{3}}$$
$$\Delta {{V}_{XY}}(t)={{g_{m3}}\over {{C}_{XY}}}
\int \Delta {{V}_{PQ}}dt\approx 
{{g_{m1}}g_{m3}\over {{C}_{PQ}}{{C}_{XY}}}{{t^{2}}\over 2}
\Delta {{V}_{{\rm {in}}}} \tag{4}$$
with an {\it amplification}

$${{A}_{0}}\propto {{g_{m1}}\over {{C}_{PQ}}}
{{g_{m3}}\over {{C}_{XY}}}{{t_{a}}^{2}} \tag{4a}$$

until ${{V}_{X,Y}}={{V}_{DD}}-\left| {{V}_{TP}}\right|$ and
the ${\rm {p}}$ -channel cross coupled pair can come
on.

* {\it latch:} ${{M}_{5}}{{M}_{6}}-{{M}_{3}}{{M}_{4}}$
closed.  In small signal

$${{d\over {dt}}}\Delta {{V}_{XY}}={{g_{m3}}+g_{m5}\over
{{C}_{XY}}}\Delta {{V}_{XY}}\tag{5}$$

so that with (2)(4) as the initial condition

$$\Delta {{V}_{XY}}(t)=\Delta {{V}_{0}}
\exp \left[{{t-t_{a}}\over {{\tau }_{R}}}\right]\tag{6}$$

$${{\tau }_{R}}\approx {{{C}_{XY}}\over {{g_{m3}}+g_{m5}
-g_{ds3}-g_{ds5}}}\tag{7}$$

and, to conventional first order,

$${{t}_{{\rm {CK-Q}}}}\approx {{t}_{a}}+{{\tau }_{R}}
\ln {{ {{V}_{DD}}}\over {\Delta {{V}_{0}}}}\tag{8}$$

$${{t}_{a}}\propto {{C}_{XY}}\left| {{V}_{TP}}\right|
/{{I}_{3}}+{{C}_{PQ}}{{V}_{TN}}/{{I}_{1}}\tag{9}$$

${{C}_{XY}}$ is

$${{C}_{XY}}={{C}_{gd3}}+{{C}_{db3}}+{{C}_{db5}}+{{C}_{gd5}}
+{{C}_{gs5}}+{{C}_{gs6}}+{{C}_{dS3}}+{{C}_{w}}\tag{10}$$

$${{C}_{gs5,6}}\approx {2\over 3}{{W}_{5,6}}{{L}_{5,6}}
{{C}_{ox}}\;\;,\;\;{{C}_{db5,6}}\propto {{W}_{5,6}}\;\;,
\;\;{{C}_{gd5,6}}\propto {{W}_{5,6}}\tag{11}$$

i. e. to first order ${{C}_{XY}}={{C}_{0}}+{{C}_{ox}}^{{\prime
}}{{W}_{5,6}}$ while, square law long channel,

$${{g}_{m5,6}}\propto \sqrt{{{W}_{5,6}}{{I}_{5,6}}}\tag{12}$$

and short channel $g_{m}\propto {{W}_{5,6}}$.

Hence

* ${{t}_{a}}$ (1)(3)(9) - the time to generate the
seed voltage $\Delta {{V}_{0}}$ for the latch and to
bring ${{M}_{5,6}}$ to the edge of conduction - goes
{\it linearly} with ${{C}_{XY}}$, i. e. linearly with
${{W}_{5,6}}$;

* ${{\tau }_{R}}$ goes as ${{C}_{XY}}/\left(
{{g}_{m3}}+{{g}_{m5}}({{W}_{5}})\right)$.  Long
channel

$${{\tau }_{R}}\propto {{ {{C}_{0}}+{{C}_{ox}}^{{\prime
}}{{W}_{5}}}\over {{{g}_{m3}}+{{g}_{m0}}\sqrt{{{W}_{5}}}}}\tag{13}$$

and short channel

$${{\tau }_{R}}\propto {{ {{C}_{0}}+{{C}_{ox}}^{{\prime
}}{{W}_{5}}}\over {{{g}_{m3}}+{{g}_{m0}}{{W}_{5}}}}\tag{14}$$

so that

$$\left.{{\partial {{\tau }_{R}}}\over {\partial
{{W}_{5}}}}\right|_{\rm lc}\propto 
{1\over {\sqrt{{{W}_{5}}}}}\left[1-{{{C}_{0}}\over {2
{{C}_{ox}}^{{\prime }}{{W}_{5}}}}+{\cal O}(1)\right]>0
\;\;{\rm for}\;\;{{W}_{5}}>{{W}_{5,{\rm opt}}}\tag{15}$$

and

$${{W}_{5,{\rm opt}}}^{\rm lc}\approx 
{{{C}_{0}}\over {{{C}_{ox}}^{{\prime }}}}\;,\qquad
{{W}_{5,{\rm opt}}}^{\rm sc}\approx {{{g}_{m3}}\over
{{{g}_{m0}}}}{{C}_{ox}^{{\prime }}{{W}_{3}}\over {{C}_{0}}}$$

in round numbers ${{W}_{5,{\rm opt}}}\approx
(0.5-1.0){{W}_{3}}$ to $\approx 2{{W}_{3}}$, depending
on the fixed capacitance ${{C}_{0}}$.

In words: ${{M}_{5,6}}$ help the positive feed back once
it has started, Eq. 5, but they load the very node they
have to help, Eq. 10, and while they are still off they
do nothing but add ${{C}_{XY}}$ to be discharged by the
${{n}}$ -channel side, Eq. 3--4, and fight the
${{n}}$ -channel pull down once they do come on.

For ${{W}_{5,6}}<{{W}_{5,{\rm opt}}}$ the
$\Delta {{g}_{m}}/\Delta {{C}}$ is $>0$ and the latch
can be made marginally faster by fattening ${{M}_{5,6}}$,
for

$${{W}_{5,6}}>{{W}_{5,{\rm opt}}}\;\;,\qquad 
{{d{{t}_{{\rm {CK-Q}}}}}\over {d{{W}_{5,6}}}}>0\tag{16}$$

the normal, well sized, Strong Arm is already at or
past ${{W}_{{\rm opt}}}$ so that any {\it appreciable}}
increase of ${{W}_{5,6}}$ increases ${{C}_{XY}}$
essentially linearly while ${{g}_{m5}}$ increases only as
$\sqrt{W}$ - ${\rm {SC}}$ as $W$ - and

$${{t}_{{\rm {CK-Q}}}}\approx 
\left[{{C}_{0}}+{{C}_{p}}{{W}_{5,6}}\right]
\left[{{\left|{{V}_{TP}}\right|}\over {{{I}_{av}}}}+
{1\over {{{g}_{m,av}}}}\ln {{V}_{{\rm logic}}\over
{\Delta {{V}_{0}}({{C}_{XY}})}}\right]\tag{17}$$

goes up.  In conventional language the circuit gets
{\it slower}}, its ${\rm {CK-Q}}$ propagation - regeneration
- time constant ${{\tau }_{R}}$ gets larger and its
precharge time ${{t}_{{\rm {pch}}}}\approx
0.69{{R}_{S3,4}}{{C}_{XY}}$ gets larger.  The
${\rm {p}}$ -channel pair going to a low ${{V}_{DS}}$ also
reduces its output resistance and the small signal gain
${{A}_{v}}={{g}_{m}}{{r}_{o}}$ of the back to back
inverters stops increasing and eventually falls with $W$.

The usual textbook shorthand is therefore: ``widening
${{M}_{5}}{{M}_{6}}$ degrades the speed'' - more precisely
the delay versus ${{W}_{5,6}}$ is ${\rm {U}}$ shaped
with a shallow minimum at about the normal design value,
${{W}_{5}}\approx {{W}_{3}}$, ${{W}_{6}}\approx
{{W}_{4}}$, so that a small increase from the minimum
geometry will speed the latch up by 10--20\% while any
large increase makes ${{t}_{a}}$ and ${{\tau }_{R}}$
capacitance dominated and makes the comparator slower,
more power hungry and harder to precharge, and, because
the ${{M}_{5,6}}$ drain capacitance now dominates
${{C}_{XY}}$, more sensitive to dynamic offset.

> {\it Remark:} If the $W$ is increased keeping the
> $S_{3}S_{4}$ precharge devices constant the
> precharge - reset - time increases as
> ${{R}_{S}}{{C}_{XY}}$.  If $S_{3}S_{4}$ are widened
> with $M_{5,6}$ the clock load increases. {\it Mutatis
> mutandis} for $M_{3,4}$.

In the literature this is the Kobayshi-Cho-Gray StrongArm
optimisation, see e. g. B. Razavi, {\it Design of Analog
CMOS Integrated Circuits}, Chap. 13, and Nikolic {\it et
al.}, {\it JSSC} {\bf 35}, 944 (2000).  Naive ``more
$g_{m}$ is faster'' ignores the self loading
${{C}_{gs}}+{{C}_{gd}}+{{C}_{db}}\propto W$.

With the ideal clock the circuit is the
${\cal C}^{2}{\rm MOS}$ ${\rm TR}$ divider of Fig.1.
The two ${\cal C}^{2}$ inverters plus ${\rm Inv}_{3}$

$$\eqalign{
Z&\to X=\bar Z{\rm ~if~}{\tt CK}=1\cr
X&\to Y=\bar X{\rm ~if~}{\tt CK}=0\cr
Y&\to Z=\bar Y}$$

so that with

$${\tt CK}=1~~~~\left\{\eqalign{
M_{D}&:Z\to X\cr
M_{R}&:X{\rm ~stored~on~}C_{Y}\cr}\right.
\qquad 
{\tt CK}=0~~~~\left\{\eqalign{
M_{D}:&{\rm stored~on~}C_{X}\cr
M_{R}:&X\to Y\to Z\cr}\right.$$

the circuit divides by two.
Free running with ${\tt CK}\equiv 1$ it is the
common three inverter ring.  Let

$R_{D}\propto 1/W_{D}$ , $R_{{\tt CK}}\propto 1/W_{{\tt CK}}$
be the on resistance of the normal, $M_{1}$, and of the
clock device and

$$C_{X,Y}=C_{0}+C_{{\rm diff},{\tt CK}}+C_{g,{\tt CK}}
       \approx C_{G,M_{1}}+C_{w}+W_{{\tt CK}}C_{j}+W_{{\tt CK}}C_{g}$$

the capacitance on the two dynamic nodes.
$C_{0}$ is the gate capacitance of the next
${\cal C}^{2}$ inverter plus wiring, $W_{{\tt CK}}C_{j}$
the ${\tt CK}$ drain diffusion capacitance on $X,Y$
and $W_{{\tt CK}}C_{g}$ the gate capacitance that
loads the ${\tt CK}$ driver.

For the transparent latch

$$t_{pD}\approx \left(R_{D}+R_{{\tt CK}}\right)C_{X,Y}\tag{1}$$

$$t_{p}\approx t_{pM}+t_{pR}+t_{{\rm Inv}_{3}}\approx
2t_{pD}+t_{{\rm Inv}_{3}} \tag{2}$$

is the period of the ring, $f_{0}\propto 1/t_{p}$, and,
more important, $1/2t_{p}$ is the maximum ${\tt CK}$
frequency that the divider will follow.
In the ideal clock, $t_{r,{\tt CK}}=t_{f,{\tt CK}}=0$,
approximation (1) is often written $t_{pD}\propto 
R_{{\tt CK}}C_{0}$, i. e. $t_{pD}\propto 1/W_{{\tt CK}}$,
fattening the ${\tt CK}$ device lowers the stack
resistance and the circuit goes faster, saturating
at

$$t_{pD}({\rm min})\approx R_{D}C_{0}\tag{3}$$

the delay of the unclocked inverter.

Put in the $W_{{\tt CK}}$ dependence of $C_{X,Y}$

$$\eqalign{
t_{pD}&=\left(R_{D}+{a\over {W_{{\tt CK}}}}\right)
        \left(C_{0}+bW_{{\tt CK}}\right) \cr
      &=R_{D}C_{0}+ab+R_{D}bW_{{\tt CK}}+a{{C_{0}}\over {W_{{\tt CK}}}} \cr}\tag{4}$$

$$a\propto R_{\square},\qquad b\propto C_{j}+C_{g}\;.$$

(4) has the usual self loaded shallow minimum

$${{dt_{pD}}\over {dW_{{\tt CK}}}}=0:\qquad 
W_{{\tt CK}}^{{\rm opt}}=\sqrt{{{aC_{0}}\over {R_{D}b}}}
      \propto \sqrt{{{C_{0}}\over {R_{D}}}} \tag{5}$$

For $W_{{\tt CK}}<W_{{\tt CK}}^{{\rm opt}}$

$${{dt_{pD}}\over {dW_{{\tt CK}}}}<0$$

and the normal $1/W_{{\tt CK}}$ speed up is observed;
for

$$W_{{\tt CK}}>W_{{\tt CK}}^{{\rm opt}}\qquad 
{{dt_{pD}}\over {dW_{{\tt CK}}}}>0\tag{6}$$

the $R_{D}bW_{{\tt CK}}$ self loading term dominates.
In the limit

$$t_{pD}\to R_{D}bW_{{\tt CK}}\to \infty \qquad W_{{\tt CK}}\to \infty \tag{7}$$

the dynamic node has to be charged through the
{\it normal} device $R_{D}$ onto the ${\tt CK}$
diffusion capacitance, and the extra $R_{{\tt CK}}$
reduction is immaterial.

For a modern process $C_{0}\approx C_{j}W_{D}$ and
$R_{D}\propto 1/W_{D}$ so that (5) is

$$W_{{\tt CK}}^{{\rm opt}}\approx W_{D}\sqrt{{{R_{\square ,{\tt CK}}C_{j,D}}
\over {R_{\square ,D}C_{j,{\tt CK}}}}}\approx (0.5-1.0)W_{D}\tag{8}$$

i. e. the minimum is essentially at minimum geometry.
Any ``normal'' ${\cal C}^{2}$ divider is normally
designed with $W_{{\tt CK}}\approx W_{{\tt CK}}^{{\rm opt}}
\approx W_{D,min}$ for minimum clock load and minimum
area.  On that design

$${{dt_{p}}\over {dW_{{\tt CK}}}}>0\tag{9}$$

fattening the clock devices puts more diffusion
capacitance on the high impedance dynamic nodes $X$
and $Y$ than it takes out in stack resistance.
E. g. with $W_{D}=W_{min}$

$$\left.{{t_{pD}(2W_{{\tt CK}})}\over {t_{pD}(W_{{\tt CK}})}}\right|
      \approx 1.1-1.3\tag{10}$$

in SPICE, i. e. essentially no speed up and for
$W_{{\tt CK}}\gtrsim 2W_{min}$ a distinct slow down.

If the finite rise and fall time of the ${\tt CK}$
driver is included the effect is much more marked.
$C_{{\tt CK}}=W_{{\tt CK}}C_{g}$ loads the ${\tt CK}$
buffer,

$$t_{r,{\tt CK}},t_{f,{\tt CK}}\propto R_{{\tt CK}buf}C_{{\tt CK}}
      \propto W_{{\tt CK}}\tag{11}$$

and $t_{r,{\tt CK}},t_{f,{\tt CK}}$ add directly to the
setup and hold time of the latches and to (2).
The clock power

$$P_{{\tt CK}}\propto C_{{\tt CK}}V_{DD}^{2}f_{{\tt CK}}
      \propto W_{{\tt CK}}\tag{12}$$

goes up linearly with $W_{{\tt CK}}$ for essentially no
improvement in $f_{max}$ and, for $W_{{\tt CK}}>
W_{{\tt CK}}^{{\rm opt}}$, for a decrease in $f_{max}$.

used as a $:2$.

$${\rm Inv}_{1}:Z\to X\;\;{\rm passes}\qquad

and with ${\cal CK}=0$, ${\overline {\cal CK}}=1$

$${\rm Inv}_{1}:Z\not\to X\;\;{\rm off}\qquad

so that for the toggle $f_{{\rm max}}$

$${{1}\over {f_{{\rm max}}}}\approx

$$t_{{\rm M,S}}\approx 0.7R_{{\rm eff}}C_{{\rm L}}$$

$$R_{{\rm eff}}=R_{{\rm I}}+R_{{\rm sw}}$$
$$\eqalign{
R_{{\rm I}}&\propto 1/W_{{\rm I}}\cr
R_{{\rm sw}}&\propto 1/W_{{\rm sw}}\cr}$$
is the series combination of the normally driven
device, the $M_{1}$ in the figure, and the ${\cal
CK}$ switch and

$$C_{{\rm L}}=C_{X,Y}=C_{{db}I}+C_{{db}{\rm sw}}
+C_{gI}^{\prime}+C_{W}\propto W_{{\rm sw}}+{\rm const.}$$

is the capacitance of the dynamic node $X$ resp. $Y$:
the drain diffusion of the switch itself, the gate
capacitance of the following ${\rm C^{2}MOS}$ inverter
and wiring.  E. {\it g.} for the master

$$C_{X}=C_{d}\left( W_{{\rm swM}}\right)+C_{g}\left(
W_{{\rm IS}}\right)+C_{0}\tag{1}$$

$$R_{{\rm M}}=R_{0}/W_{{\rm IM}}+R_{0}/W_{{\rm swM}}\tag{2}$$

so that, with ${\cal CK}$ ideal, the Elmore delay
of the transparent latch is, to first order,

$$t_{{\rm M}}\propto \left({{R_{0}}\over {W_{{\rm IM}}}}
+{{R_{0}}\over {W_{{\rm sw}}}}\right)
\left( C_{0}^{\prime}+C_{0}^{\prime\prime}W_{{\rm sw}}
\right) \tag{3}$$

$$t_{{\rm M}}= {{A}\over {W_{{\rm sw}}}}+BW_{{\rm sw}}+C\tag{4}$$

$${{dt_{{\rm M}}}\over {dW_{{\rm sw}}}}=0:
\qquad W_{{\rm sw}}^{{\rm opt}}\approx 
\sqrt{{{A}\over {B}}}= \sqrt{{{R_{0}C_{0}^{\prime}}
\over {R_{0}C_{0}^{\prime\prime}/W_{{\rm IM}}}} }
\approx \sqrt{{{C_{0}^{\prime}W_{{\rm IM}}}\over
{C_{0}^{\prime\prime}}}} \tag{5}$$

Neglecting the self loading $C_{db{\rm sw}}\propto
W_{{\rm sw}}$ in (1) $B=0$ and

$$t_{{\rm M,S}}\propto {{1}\over {W_{{\rm sw}}}}$$

{\it i. e.} in the conventional text book
approximation with $C_{{\rm L}}={\rm const.}$ and
${\cal CK}$ ideal the latch looks faster and $(*)$
looks faster the larger you make the pass transistor,
$t_{pd}\propto R_{{\rm sw}}C_{{\rm L}}\propto
1/W_{{\rm sw}}$; you just lower the series resistance
in the signal path.

With the self loading retained (3)--(4) has a shallow
minimum (5).  Normally $R_{{\rm I}}\gg R_{{\rm sw}}$,
$C_{0}^{\prime\prime}W_{{\rm sw}}\sim C_{0}^{\prime}$
already for $W_{{\rm sw}}=W_{{\rm min}}$ so that
$W_{{\rm sw}}^{{\rm opt}}$ is essentially $W_{{\rm min}}$
and for any appreciable $W_{{\rm sw}}>W_{{\rm sw}}^{{\rm
opt}}$

$$t_{{\rm M,S}}\approx BW_{{\rm sw}}\propto W_{{\rm sw}}$$

the delay {\it increases} about linearly with the
width of the ${\cal CK}$ device hung on the dynamic
nodes $X$ and $Y$.  The same $W_{{\rm sw}}$ hangs a
gate capacitance

$$C_{{\cal CK}}=C_{g{\rm swM}}+C_{g{\rm swS}}\propto
W_{{\rm swM}}+W_{{\rm swS}}$$

on the ${\cal CK}$ and ${\overline {\cal CK}}$ nets.
With a realistic ${\cal CK}$ driver of finite
$R_{{\cal CK}}$ the ${\cal CK}$ rise and fall time

$$t_{r{\cal CK}}\propto R_{{\cal CK}}C_{{\cal CK}}
\propto W_{{\rm sw}}$$

goes up $\propto W_{{\rm sw}}$ degrading $t_{su}$,
$t_{h}$ and adding $t_{r{\cal CK}}$ to $(*)$.  In
addition the overlap $C_{gd{\rm sw}}\propto W_{{\rm
sw}}$ couples the ${\cal CK}$ transition onto the
floating dynamic node $X$ resp. $Y$,

$$\Delta V_{X,Y}\approx {{C_{gd{\rm sw}}}\over
{C_{X,Y}}}\;V_{{\cal CK}}$$

and the charge sharing between

$$C_{{\rm int}}=C_{s{\rm sw}}+C_{d{\rm I}}$$

the inter series device node, and $C_{X,Y}$ gets worse
$\propto W_{{\rm sw}}$.

In normal design language the divider is said to get
slower, more power hungry, $P_{{\cal CK}}=C_{{\cal
CK}}V_{DD}^{2}f_{{\cal CK}}\propto W_{{\rm sw}}$,
and more feed through sensitive when you up size the
${\cal CK}$ switches.  The $1/W_{{\rm sw}}$ resistive
improvement is normally already saturated with the
${\cal CK}$ devices at $W_{{\rm min}}$.  E. {\it g.}
in $0.18\mu $ SPICE $W_{{\rm sw}}^{{\rm opt}}\approx
1$--$2\,W_{{\rm min}}$.

It is the well known frequency divider/ring.
$C^{2}MOS$.

$$\vcenter{
\hbox{${\rm Inv}_{1}\equiv Z+{\bar C}_{K}\to X$}
\hbox{${\rm Inv}_{2}\equiv X+{C}_{K}\to Y$}
\hbox{${\rm Inv}_{3}\equiv Y\to Z$}
}$$

$$\eqalign{
{C}_{K}=0 & {\rm Inv}_{1}~~{\rm HZ}~~ {\rm Inv}_{2}~~{\rm ON}\cr
& Y=\bar X\;\;Z=\bar Y =X\cr
{C}_{K}=1 & {\rm Inv}_{1}~~{\rm ON}~~{\rm Inv}_{2}~~{\rm HZ}\cr
& X=\bar Z\;\;Z^{*}= \bar Y^{*} }$$

In the phase in which it is ${\rm ON}$ the
inverter is a normal $CMOS$ inverter with a $n$ and a $p$
in series

$$\eqalign{
R_{X}&=R_{p{\rm D}}+R_{p{\rm C}}~~{\rm pull\;up}\cr
     &=R_{n{\rm D}}+R_{n{\rm C}}~~{\rm pull\;down}\cr
R_{Y}&={\rm ditto}}$$

in Elmore sense, Fig.1,

$${\cal T}_{X}\approx \left(R_{D}+R_{C}\right)C_{X}\tag{1}$$
$${\cal T}_{Y}\approx \left(R_{D}+R_{C}\right)C_{Y}\tag{2}$$
$$f_{osc}\approx \left[2\left({\cal T}_{X}+{\cal T}_{Y}
+{\cal T}_{3}\right)\right]^{-1}\propto 
{\cal T}^{-1}\tag{3}$$

and, for a divider, the maximum usable ${C}_{K}$
frequency is $\propto {\cal T}^{-1}$.

$$R_{C}=R_{C0}{W_{C0}\over W_{C}}\propto {1\over W_{C}}\tag{4}$$

$$C_{X}=C_{X0}+C_{dC}\tag{5}$$

$$C_{dC}=C_{j}+C_{jsw}+C_{ov}\propto W_{C}\tag{6}$$

So that {\it e. g.} for the pull down

$${\cal T}_{Xf}\approx \left(R_{n1}+R_{nC0}{W_{0}\over W_{C}}\right)
\left[C_{Xf0}+C_{nC}^{\prime}W_{C}+C_{pC}^{\prime}W_{C}\right]
\tag{7}$$

with

$$C_{Xf0}\approx C_{g,p2}+C_{g,n1,2}+C_{w}\tag{8}$$

the {\it fixed} gate load of the next $C^{2}MOS$
inverter plus wiring, {\it i. e.} independent of $W_{C}$.

$${d{\cal T}\over dW_{C}}=-{R_{C0}W_{0}\over W_{C}^{2}}
\left(C_{0}+C^{\prime}W_{C}\right)+
\left(R_{D}+R_{C0}{W_{0}\over W_{C}}\right)C^{\prime}=0\tag{9}$$

$$W_{C,opt}\approx \sqrt{{R_{C0}W_{0}C_{0}\over
R_{D}C^{\prime}}}\tag{10}$$

${\cal T}(W_{C})$ is $1/W_{C}$ for $W_{C}$ small,
$R_{C}\gg R_{D}$, and $\propto W_{C}$ for $W_{C}$
large $R_{C}\ll R_{D}$

$${\cal T}\approx R_{C}C_{0}\propto 1/W_{C}\;\;W_{C}\to 0\tag{11}$$
$${\cal T}\approx R_{D}C_{0}+R_{D}C^{\prime}W_{C}
\propto W_{C}\;\;W_{C}\to \infty \tag{12}$$

In words: as soon as $R_{C}<R_{D}$ making $W_{C}$
larger does not make the $RC$ product any smaller.
It is dominated by the {\it data} device $M_{1}$ and
its complementary $p$ , $R_{D}\approx $ constant.
You continue to pay linearly the drain junction,
side wall and overlap capacitance of the clock
device on the very critical dynamic nodes $X$ and $Y$
and its gate capacitance

$$C_{CK}=C_{gCK}=C_{ox}W_{C}L_{C}\tag{13}$$

on the clock distribution.

For an ideal, zero impedance, ${C}_{K}$ source (9)
has a shallow optimum at $R_{C}\approx R_{D}$,
{\it i. e.} $W_{C}\approx W_{D}$, normally
$W_{pC}\approx 2W_{nC}$, of the order of the
minimum width device.  Normalised to that optimum
the improvement you get by going from $W_{C}=W_{min}$
to $W_{C,opt}$ is $10$ to $20\%$.  Any substantial
factor $>2-3$ increase in $W_{C}$ makes $C_{X},C_{Y}$
in (5)-(6) dominate and

$${\cal T}\approx {\cal T}_{min}+R_{D}C^{\prime}\Delta W_{C}\tag{14}$$

increase , {\it i. e.} decrease the oscillation
frequency, decrease the divider $f_{max}$, increase
${\rm CK\to Q}$.

With a realistic clock driver

$${\cal T}_{CK}=R_{CK,drv}C_{CK}\propto R_{CK,drv}W_{C}\tag{15}$$

has to be added to (1)-(2).  Unless the clock
driver is scaled up in proportion to $W_{C}$ , with
all the power $P_{CK}=C_{CK}V_{DD}^{2}f_{CK}$ penalty
that that entails, (15) degrades $t_{r},t_{f}$ of
${C}_{K}$ directly.

That is normally quoted as: {\it widening the clock
devices beyond minimum to  $1.5\times$ {\rm self loads}
the $C^{2}MOS$ latch and makes it slower.}

Up sizing for speed has to be done on $M_{1}$ and on
its $p$ complement.  $W_{C}$ is normally left at
$W_{min}$ or $1-2\,W_{min}$.  In text book form:

> {\it The $C^{2}MOS$ is {\rm clock self loaded}. 
> Making the clock transistors fat does not speed the
> circuit up.  For any useful increase it slows it
> down.}

With an ideal clock the conventional $1/W_{C}$
speed up saturates at $R_{C}\approx {1\over 3}-
1\,R_{D}$ and is then swamped by the $W_{C}$
capacitance.  With a normal clock driver the
circuit is slower for essentially {\it any}
increase of $W_{C}$ if the driver is not also
widened.

In any physical implementation (10)-(11) is
corrupted to first order by

* (a) the conventional $CK$ to $Q$ delay,
$t_{CQ}^{M}\ne t_{CQ}^{S}$;

* (b) the extra delay of ${\rm Inv}_{3}$,
$t_{p}({\rm Inv}_{3})$,
so that, e. g.

$$Z(t)=Y\left(t-t_{p3}\right)\tag{13}$$

and

$$\Delta \phi _{X-Z}= \pi /2 \pm 
\omega _{d}t_{p3}+{\cal O}(\Delta t_{CQ})\tag{14}$$

whereas

$$\Delta \phi _{X-Y}= \pi /2+{\cal O}(\Delta t_{CQ})\tag{15}$$

is to first order independent of $t_{p3}$;

* (c) any deviation of $D_{CK}$ from $50\%$,

$$\Delta \phi =\pi /2\pm \pi \left(D_{CK}-1/2\right)
\tag{16}$$

* (d) $t_{pLH}\ne t_{pHL}$ so that $D_{X}\ne D_{Y}
\ne 50\%$ even for $D_{CK}=50\%$;

* (e) the fact that $X$ and $Y$ are {\it
dynamic\/} storage nodes.  Loading $X$ or $Y$
with anything more than a minimum size,
matched, dummy compensated inverter
destroys the charge hold and the division
ratio.  Normally $X$ and $Y$ have to be
buffered with a pair of {\it matched\/}
inverters $X\to I,\bar I$, $Y\to Q,\bar Q$,
which then have to be ratioed so as not to
destroy the loop gain, and the systematic
mismatch of the two buffers adds directly to
(14)-(16).

Because of (a)-(e) the circuit as drawn,
without matched symmetrical re timing and
buffering, is normally not usable as a
precision $I/Q$ generator.  With a pair of
matched output inverters/buffers on $X$ and
on $Y$ \lbrack $Z$\rbrack  it can be used as a
low accuracy, $f_{CK}/2$, nominal $50\%$ duty,
$90^{\rm o}$ quadrature generator, quadrature
error, Fig.1,

$$\epsilon _{\phi }\approx 
\omega _{d}\left[t_{p3}+\Delta t_{CQ}+
\Delta t_{pLH-pHL}\right]+
\pi\left(D_{CK}-1/2\right) \tag{17}$$

typically a few degrees to more than $10^{\rm
o}$ in a conventional CMOS process, plus the
normal ${\rm PRBS}$ jitter.  For precision
quadrature the conventional remedy is to go
to a fully static, or better a differential
${\rm CML}$-${\rm M/S}$ latch pair, or to a
Johnson counter $\div 4$ and re time, where
the $I$ to $Q$ delay is set by geometry not
by $D_{CK}$ and $t_{p3}$.  In that strict
sense the answer is ``no''.

+{{\omega _{\div 2}}t_{p{\rm Inv3}}}\tag{10}$$

stage.

The well known ${\rm C^{2}MOS}$ {\it a k a\/}
${\rm NORA}$,{\it a k a\/} ${\rm TSPC}$ latching
inverter is

$${\cal I}_{C}=
{{M_{pC}}\over {M_{pS}}}\left |
\begin{matrix}
G_{p}\\
G_{n}
\end{matrix} \right |{{M_{nS}}\over {M_{nC}}}$$

with $${R_{C}=1/\beta _{C}\Delta V\;\;,\;\;C_{C}=C_{ox}W_{C}L+C_{ov}W_{C}
+C_{j}W_{C}}$$
$${R_{S}=1/\beta _{S}\Delta V\;\;,\;\;C_{S}=C_{ox}W_{S}L+C_{ov}W_{S}
+C_{j}W_{S}\tag{1}}$$
so that conventionally

$$t_{pLH}\approx 0.69\left[ R_{pC}C_{x}+(R_{pC}+R_{pS})C_{L}
\right] \tag{2}$$
$$t_{pHL}\approx 0.69\left[ R_{nC}C_{x}^{\prime}+
(R_{nC}+R_{nS})C_{L}\right] $$

$C_{x}=C_{dpC}+C_{spS}$ is the capacitance of the
intermediate node $x\equiv D_{pC}=S_{pS}$,
$C_{L}=C_{dpS}+C_{dnS}+C_{gpS}^{\prime}+C_{gnS}^{\prime}+C_{w}$
is the capacitance of the ``output'' node of the
cell. Fig.1 is two such cells on opposite phases
$+{\cal I}_{S}$

$${\overline {CK}}\;{\cal I}_{C,1}\;-\;CK\;{\cal I}_{C,2}\;-\;
{\cal I}_{S}\;-\;{\overline {CK}}\;{\cal I}_{C,1}\tag{3}$$

i. e. the conventional dynamic divide by two, master
and slave latches made out of a single ${\rm C^{2}MOS}$
inverter plus storage capacitance plus static inverter.
Call $C_{1}$ the storage node $Q_{m}={\cal I}_{C,1}/{\cal I}_{C,2}$,
$C_{2}$ the storage node $Q_{s}={\cal I}_{C,2}/{\cal I}_{S}$.
On phase $CK=1\;,\overline{CK}=0$ ${\cal I}_{C,1}$ is
transparent and ${\cal I}_{C,2}$ is tri stated, $C_{1}$
is driven through ${\cal I}_{C,1}$, $C_{2}$ is holding.
On phase $CK=0\;,\overline{CK}=1$ ${\cal I}_{C,2}$ is
transparent and ${\cal I}_{C,1}$ is holding and $C_{2}$ is
driven through ${\cal I}_{C,2}+{\cal I}_{S}$ back to
${\cal I}_{C,1}$. Up to clock non overlap the loop gain
is ${\cal I}_{C,1}\times {\cal I}_{C,2}\times {\cal I}_{S}$.

Neglecting for a moment the cost of generating $CK,
\overline{CK}$ put $R_{C}\propto 1/W_{C}$,
$C_{x}=C_{x0}+k_{x}W_{C}$,
$C_{L}\approx C_{L0}+k_{L}W_{S}$ independent of $W_{C}$
to first order. From (2)

$$\eqalign{
t_{p}&\approx 0.69\left[ {a\over {W_{C}}}\left(C_{x0}+k_{x}W_{C}\right)
+\left({a\over {W_{C}}}+R_{S}\right)C_{L0}\right] \cr
&\approx 0.69\left[ ak_{x}+R_{S}C_{L0}+{a\left(C_{x0}+C_{L0}\right)
\over {W_{C}}}\right] \tag{4}}$$

i. e. $t_{p}(W_{C})$ is monotonic decreasing. You
get less $R_{C}$ but you pay more $C_{x}$. For
$W_{C}\rightarrow \infty $

$$t_{p,min}\rightarrow 0.69\left(ak_{x}+R_{S}C_{L0}\right) \tag{5}$$

the delay of the data device alone plus the self
loading $R_{C}C_{x}$ of the clock device on itself.
With normal layout $C_{x0}\sim C_{L0}$, $ak_{x}\sim
R_{S}C_{L0}$ going e. g. from $W_{C}=W_{S}$ to
$W_{C}=2W_{S}$ buys you $10-20\%$ on $t_{p}$,
going from $2W_{S}$ to $4W_{S}$ buys you a few
percent, E.E. The unloaded, ideal voltage source
clock, divider toggle frequency $f_{T}\approx
\left[t_{p,1}+t_{p,2}+t_{p,S}\right]^{-1}$ improves
monotonically but essentially saturates.

That is the {\it unloaded\/} block.  In any real
system you have to make $CK$.

$$C_{CK}= \sum W_{C}L\,C_{ox}+C_{ov}W_{C}+C_{w,CK}\propto W_{C}\tag{6}$$
$$t_{r,CK}\approx 0.69R_{CKd}C_{CK}\propto W_{C}\tag{7}$$
$$T_{min}\approx t_{p,1}(W_{C})+t_{r,CK}(W_{C})+t_{f,CK}(W_{C})
+t_{su}+t_{margin}\tag{8}$$

The transparency window is $T_{CK}/2-t_{r,f}$.
Increasing $W_{C}$ steals transparency window as fast
as it reduces $t_{p}$.  The conventional figure of
merit for the system, $f_{max}$ at which the loop
will still regenerate, Fig.1,

$$f_{max}^{-1}\approx t_{DQ}+t_{su}\propto 
\left[{k_{1}\over {W_{C}}}+k_{2}W_{C}\right] +c^{st}\tag{9}$$

has a minimum

$${{dT_{min}}\over {dW_{C}}}=0\;:\;W_{C,opt}\approx
\sqrt{{k_{1}\over {k_{2}}}}\approx W_{S}\tag{10}$$

For $R_{CKd}$ normalized to a ${\rm FO4}$ inverter
$W_{C,opt}$ is about $0.8-1.0\,W_{nS}$ for the $n{\rm C}$
device and $1.5-2.0\,W_{nS}$ for the $p{\rm C}$ device
to equalise $R_{nC}=R_{pC}$. Normal design keeps
$W_{C}\approx W_{S,min}$. Up to $\sim 2\times $ you win
a little, beyond that

$$C_{L,eff}=C_{L0}+C_{dpS}+C_{dnS}\propto W_{S}+W_{C}$$
clock feed through $\Delta V_{CF}=C_{ov}W_{C}/
\left(C_{L}+C_{ov}W_{C}\right)\Delta V_{CK}$ and charge
sharing between $C_{x}$ and $C_{L}$,
$\Delta V_{CS}=C_{x}/\left(C_{x}+C_{L}\right)\Delta V_{x}$,
sub threshold leakage $\propto W_{C}$ and the
cross conduction current during the $CK \slash
\overline{CK}$ overlap $\propto W_{C}$ all increase
$\propto W_{C}$.

So with the customary abuse of language: you {\it degrade\/}
the usable speed.  In round numbers a ${\rm C^{2}MOS}$
divider with minimum geometry clock devices will toggle
at $f_{T0}$. Doubling the clock devices will get you
$f_{T}\approx 1.1-1.2f_{T0}$ ideal clock, essentially
no improvement at system level, at twice the clock
power, twice the clock routing capacitance and much
worse clock slope, feed through and charge sharing
robustness.  Quadrupling them makes the divider slower
at $R_{CKd}\ne 0$.

> {\it In the text book sense of ``make $W_{C}\gg W_{S}$,
> does it get faster?'' the answer is NO. There is a
> shallow optimum at about minimum width. Any substantial
> increase is a net loss on $f_{max}$, on power and on
> robustness. If you want it faster make $W_{S}$,
> $W_{{\cal I}_{S}}$ bigger, make $C_{L}$ smaller, keep
> $W_{C}$ minimum. Low $V_{t}$, forward body bias or
> TSPC$^{\ast}$ helps much more than blowing up the
> clock FETs.}

$^{\ast}$ TSPC keeps only one clock FET per cell,
halving (6).

If $CK,\overline{CK}$ are taken as ideal zero impedance
voltage sources the pedantic answer is (4)-(5): $t_{p}$
decreases monotonically as $1/W_{C}$ to the asymptote
(5). Normally quoted as ``improves but saturates''.

With an ideal 0 impedance generator on ${\cal C}K$
the circuit is just the closed loop

$$A\equiv {{W_{p}^{a}}\over {W_{n}^{a}}}
\;\;\xrightarrow[W_{CKp}\atop W_{CKn}]{}\;B
\;\;\xrightarrow[W_{\bar CKp}\atop W_{\bar CKn}]{}\;C
\;\;\xrightarrow{A_{0}}\;A\tag{*}$$

$m\equiv A$ is the {\it master} tr. gate inverter,
$s\equiv B$ the {\it slave} tr. gate inverter, $A_{0}$ the
conventional inverter and $(^{*})$ is normally connected
${\cal D}\equiv \bar {\cal Q}$ to make the conventional
${\cal C}^{2}{\rm MOS}$ ${\cal D}$ ${\cal F}{\cal F}$ and
${\cal Q}\to \bar {\cal Q}\to {\cal Q}$ divider.  With
${\cal D}={\cal Q}$ it is the 3 inverter ring.
In either case with

$${\cal C}K =1\qquad W_{CK}^{a}{\rm \;on\;}W_{CK}^{s}{\rm
\;off\;}$$

the $a$ inverter is low impedance, $R_{a}=R_{inv}^{a}+
R_{CK}^{a}$ and the $s$ inverter is ${\rm Hi}{\rm Z}$, the
signal propagates $A\to B$.  With ${\cal C}K=0$ $R_{s}=
R_{inv}^{s}+R_{\bar CK}^{s}$ and the signal propagates
$B\to C\to A$.  The period of the closed loop is

$$T_{0}\approx \tau _{a}+\tau _{s}+\tau _{0}\tag{1}$$

With the conventional Elmore  model Fig.2 for e. {\it g.} the
$n$ side

$$\eqalign{
\tau _{a}&=(R_{n,inv}^{a}+R_{n,CK}^{a})C_{L}^{a}+
           R_{n,CK}^{a}C_{I}^{a}\cr
C_{I}^{a}&=C_{db,CK}^{a}+C_{db,inv}^{a}\cr
C_{L}^{a}&=C_{db,inv}^{a}+C_{g,inv}^{s}\cr} \tag{2}$$

and the same with $p\leftrightarrow n$, $a\leftrightarrow
s$, $CK\leftrightarrow \bar CK$.
${\cal C}_{L}$ is the useful load, the gate load of the
following inverter plus the drain load of the inverter
{\it per se}.  ${\cal C}_{I}$ is the parasitic internal
node between the ${\cal C}K$ switch and the inverter
device, Fig.2.

$${{R_{CK}\propto {1\over {W_{CK}}}} \qquad 
  {C_{I}\propto W_{CK}+W_{inv}}\qquad 
  {C_{L}\approx {\rm cst.}(W_{CK})}} \tag{3}$$

so that, for given $W_{inv}$,

$$\tau _{a,s}= {{R_{0}C_{L}}\over {W_{inv}}}+
            {{R_{0}C_{L}}\over {W_{CK}}}+
            {{R_{0}k(W_{CK}+W_{inv})}\over {W_{CK}}} \tag{4}$$

$$= \tau _{inv}+{{R_{0}(C_{L}+kW_{inv})}\over {W_{CK}}}+R_{0}k \tag{5}$$

Formally $\partial \tau /\partial W_{CK}<0$.  For an ideal,
zero impedance, ${\cal C}K$ source the forward delay of the
transparent latch falls as $1/W_{CK}$ towards the
asymptotic intrinsic inverter delay

$$\tau _{a,s}\to \tau _{inv}+R_{0}k = R_{inv}C_{L}+{\rm cst.}\tag{6}$$

The ${\cal C}K$ device is just a series switch.
Normally $R_{CK}<R_{inv}$ already for $W_{CK}=W_{inv}$
so you gain at most

$${{\Delta \tau}\over {\tau _{inv}}}\approx
{{R_{CK}}\over {R_{CK}+R_{inv}}}< {1\over 2} \tag{7}$$

and very rapidly saturates.  In first order the
conventional ${\cal C}^{2}{\rm MOS}$ latch propagates with
a delay essentially independent of $W_{CK}$.

If the finite impedance of the ${\cal C}K$ generator and
the load it sees is taken into account

$$\tau _{CK}=R_{CK}^{drv}C_{g,CK}\qquad C_{g,CK}\propto
W_{CK}\tag{8}$$

has to be added to (1).  $\tau _{CK}\propto W_{CK}$,
$\tau _{a,s}\propto 1/W_{CK}$, so that the {\it usable}
cycle time

$$T_{c}=T_{0}(W_{CK})+\tau _{CK}(W_{CK})\tag{9}$$

has a shallow minimum for

$$W_{CK}^{opt}\approx \sqrt{{{R_{0}(C_{L}+kW_{inv})}\over
{R_{CK}^{drv}k_{g}}}}\sim (0.5-1.0)W_{inv}\tag{10}$$

normally quoted as ``minimum size''.  For all practical
purposes putting $W_{CK}=2\div 3\,W_{\min }$ buys you
$10-20\,{\rm pS}$ of forward delay at the expense of a
factor $2\div 3$ in ${\cal C}K$ power,
$P_{CK}\propto C_{g,CK}V_{DD}^{2}f$, a factor $2\div 3$
in clock feed through

$$\Delta V_{H}\approx {{C_{ov,CK}}\over {C_{H}}}\Delta V_{CK}
\propto W_{CK}\tag{11}$$

on the high impedance storage node $H\equiv B$ when the
switch goes ${\rm Hi}{\rm Z}$ and the extra diffusion
capacitance that the {\it on} inverter has to charge
through $R_{CK}$.  Beyond the optimum (10) the circuit
gets slower, more power hungry and considerably less
robust versus charge sharing and race through on the
${\cal C}K\leftrightarrow \bar {\cal C}K$ overlap.
That is why in the text books the ${\cal C}K$ switches of
a ${\cal C}^{2}{\rm MOS}$ - ${\rm TSPC}$ latch - divider
- ring are always drawn minimum size.  With the usual
abuse of language the operation is said to ``degrade with
$W_{CK}$''.

by 2, the frequency of the gated ring,

f_{{\cal C}{\cal K}}\propto W_{{\cal C}{\cal K}} \tag{10}$$

is restored to full swing. This is the normal
logic form of the divider. Price:

* $C_{M}\to C_{M}+C_{gR}+C_{jR}$ and $C_{\bar M}\to
C_{\bar M}+C_{dR}$, typically $10-30\%$ extra load
on the high speed loop {\it in addition} to the
active fight during the write phase $CK=1$.

During $CK=1$, $I_{in}=I_{Qb}$ through the two slave
inverters must {\it overpower} $I_{R}$ to force $M$
to the new value. For a time $\sim t_{p}$ there is a
crow bar current $I_{1}-I_{R}$ between $V_{DD}$ and

$g_{m1}-g_{mR}$.

$$t_{p,stat}\approx t_{p,dyn}\left(1+\frac{C_{R}}{C_{M}}\right)
 \frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m1}-g_{mR}} > t_{p,dyn}$$

$$t_{CQ,stat}>t_{CQ,dyn}\qquad f_{max,stat}<f_{max,dyn}$$

in the conventional $\sim 15-25\%$ for minimum
size keeper. Dynamic power $CV^{2}f$ goes up with
$C_{R}$ and short circuit power $I_{sc}V_{DD}t_{sc}f$
during the contention goes up. Area goes up.

For that reason ${\rm Inv_{R}}$ is always made
{\it weak}, long $L$, small $W$,

$$\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_{R}\approx \frac{1}{5}-\frac{1}{3}
 \left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_{1}$$

just strong enough to compensate $I_{leak}$ and
noise but weak enough to be overpowered with little
penalty. With correct ratioing the $f_{max}$ penalty can be
kept to $<10\%$ while $f_{min}$ is brought from
${\rm MHz}$ to $0$, e. g. $8{\rm GHz}$ dynamic to
$7.0-7.5{\rm GHz}$ pseudo static in $65{\rm nm}$,
at $\sim 10-20\%$ power and area cost.

Unratioed, $g_{mR}\ge g_{m1}$ the master cannot be
written, the divider sticks and/or draws large DC
current.

In the figure only the master is staticized, the
slave, the two inverters on the right, is still
dynamic, {\it half static} TSPC. With a second keeper
on the slave it becomes fully static.

It is the classical {\it weak keeper\/} ,
{\it staticizer\/} , {\it bleeder\/}
of the {\tt TSPC} $\div 2$.

$$D= \bar Q\;\;{\rm so}\;\;Q_{n+1}= \bar Q_{n}$$

with master made of $TG_{1}+{\rm Inv}_{1}$
and slave $TG_{2}+{\rm Inv}_{2}+{\rm Inv}_{3}$
closed in a ring is normally {\it all dynamic}.

In the ideal $CK/\bar {CK}$ non overlap case
with $C_{gs}$ alone:

* $CK=1\;,\;\bar {CK}=0$ : $Y=X$, $Z=\bar Y$,
$W=$ floating, $V=\bar W$, $X=\bar V$ holds

* $CK=0\;,\;\bar {CK}=1$ : $Y=$ floating, $Z=\bar Y$
holds, $W=Z$, $V=\bar W$, $X=\bar V=Z$ copied

so on every $0\to 1\to 0$ {\it full} period

$$Z_{n+1}= \bar Z_{n}\qquad X_{n+1}= \bar X_{n}$$

$\div 2$ only so long as the charge on the
floating node, $Y$ in $\Phi_{1}=0$ and $W$ in
$\Phi_{1}=1$, does not leak away. In normal
CMOS

$$\tau _{leak}\approx C_{node}V_{DD}/I_{leak}\approx
10^{-13}/10^{-9}\approx 10^{-4} {\rm s}$$

so

$$f_{min}\approx 10^{4}-10^{6}{\rm Hz},\;\;
f_{max}\approx 1/3t_{p}$$

any stop of the clock, any slow clock, any
coupling noise, clock feed through, charge
sharing on $Y,W$ destroys the state. It is
normally called {\it dynamic\/} and {\it
ratioless\/}:

$$P_{dyn}=C_{L}V_{DD}^{2}f\;\;,\;\;t_{CQ}=t_{TG}+t_{Inv}$$
minimum.

Putting the red ${\rm Inv}$ in the master, in
sign as a {\it cross coupled latch} with
${\rm Inv}_{1}$

$$Y \xrightarrow{{\rm Inv}_{1}} Z
 \xrightarrow{{\rm red}}X \xrightarrow{TG_{1}}Y$$

in the drawing as a {\it parallel} driver
$$X\;\xrightarrow[{\rm red}]{{\rm Inv}_{1}}\;Z$$
it is the same thing {\it modulo} $TG_{1}$,
makes the master {\it pseudo static}, {\it
ratioed}.

In the transparent phase, $CK=1$, the two
${\rm Inv}$ drive $Z$ in {\it parallel}, {\it
a fortiori} faster. In the hold phase,
$CK=0$, $\bar {CK}=1$,

$$Z =\bar Y\;\;{\rm from\;Inv}_{1}\;\;{\rm with\;\;}
Y=Q_{n}={\rm floating\;capacitor}$$

is now held by

$$Z =\bar X\;\;{\rm from\;red\;\;with\;\;}
X= W = Z\;\;{\rm from\;slave}$$

{\it i. e.} the red ${\rm Inv}$ fights
${\rm Inv}_{1}$ on $Z$, or, if you draw it as
$Z\to X$, it fights the slave on $X$.

So for DC:

* Pro: the loop gain $>1$ holds $Y/Z$
for $f\to 0$. No $f_{min}$. The node is
low impedance, restored to $V_{DD}/V_{SS}$,
noise margin goes from $\approx 0$ dynamic
to $NM_{H,L}\approx V_{DD}/3$, clock feed

rail, can be stopped. In modern jargon the
conventional TSPC becomes the E-TSPC,
extended TSPC, and can even be made faster
because the series ${\rm MOS}$ in the
clocked ${\rm Inv}$ can be suppressed.

* Contra: ratioed logic. During the {\it
write} the driver must over power the keeper.

For the master to be writable

$$ \left({W\over L}\right)_{red}<<
   \left({W\over L}\right)_{Inv_{1}},
   \left({W\over L}\right)_{slave}$$

normally $1/3$ to $1/10$ and long $L$,
high $V_{t}$ if possible.  If that ratio is
not respected the latch cannot be flipped,

does not $\div 2$.

Even correctly ratioed:

* added $C_{g}+C_{d}$ on $X,Y,Z$, about

$$t_{CQ}^{stat}=t_{CQ}^{dyn}+ \Delta t_{red}

$$f_{max}^{stat}\approx 0.7-0.9\,f_{max}^{dyn}$$

in $0.18\mu$ e. {\it g.} $5.0{\rm GHz}
\to 3.5-4.5{\rm GHz}$.

* a direct $V_{DD}\to V_{SS}$ short circuit
current during the fight

$$I_{sc}\approx {1\over 2}\mu C_{ox}{W\over L}

$$P =C_{L}V_{DD}^{2}f +V_{DD}I_{sc}t_{sc}f$$

$10-30\%$ more power, static power
$\ne 0$ during transition, $PDP$ worse.

* $t_{setup},t_{hold}$ of the equivalent
$D\,{\rm FF}$ are degraded, essentially the
hold time must cover the fight time.

* process, $V_{DD}$, $T$ variation of the
ratio can make it fail at low $V_{DD}$ or
high $T$.

In one sentence: you buy DC, leakage and
noise robustness and rail to rail operation
for area, for a small to large, depending on
sizing, loss in $t_{p}$, $f_{max}$ and
$P_{dyn}+P_{sc}$ and you make the circuit
ratioed. Made weak enough it is a negligible
penalty, made as strong as ${\rm Inv}_{1}$
it kills the divider.

This is the conventional CMOS ${\rm TG}/{\rm C^{2}MOS}$
{\it pseudo static} $T$ divide by 2 turned into the
conventional dynamic figure and somebody has tried to
``staticize" it. It is wrong in two ways.

Let

* $A$ = to the left of the $CK$ ${\rm TG}$
* $M$ = to the right of the $CK$ ${\rm TG}=$ input of
${\rm Inv}_{1}$
* $B$ = output of ${\rm Inv}_{1}=$ to the left of the
$\bar {CK}$ ${\rm TG}$
* $C$ = to the right of the $\bar {CK}$ ${\rm TG}$
  $=$ input of the slave ${\rm inv}$
* $E$ = output of the slave $=$ $A$ by the
global wiring.

Without colour the circuit is the dynamic
$T$~FF:

$$A\stackrel{CK}{\to}M\stackrel{{\rm Inv}_{1}}{\to}
B\stackrel{\bar {CK}}{\to}C\stackrel{{\rm Inv}}{\to}
\stackrel{{\rm Inv}}{\to}E=A\tag{*}$$

$3$ inversions round the loop. Closed on
$CK=1$ open on $\bar {CK}=0$ and vice versa.
It is an edge triggered $D$ with $D=\bar Q$.
$M$ and $C$ are {\it storage} nodes. On

* $CK=1$, $\bar {CK}=0$ $M=A=E$, $B=\bar A$,
$C$ is floating on $C_{C}$.
* $CK=0$, $\bar {CK}=1$ $M$ is floating on $C_{M}$,
$B={\rm Inv}_{1}(M)$, $C=B$, $E=\bar B=A$.

$C_{M}$ drives ${\rm Inv}_{1}$ and $C_{C}$ drives the
slave. In hold they leak with $I_{\rm off}$ so

$$ \Delta V = I_{\rm leak}T_{H}/C_{M,C} $$

must be $\ll V_{DD}/2$. I.e. $f_{CK}>f_{\min }
\approx I_{\rm leak}/C_{M,C}V_{DD}$, normally
${\rm kHz}$ to ${\rm MHz}$ with modern leakage.
That is the ``minimum frequency'' of a dynamic
divider.

A conventional weak keeper for a ${\rm TG}$
latch is

$${\rm Inv}_{1}:M\to B\,\;\;{\rm Keeper}:\;B\to M$$

with the ${\rm TG}$ {\it in series} with the loop.
With $CK=1$ the loop is transparent and $A$
overwrites it. With $CK=0$ the ${\rm TG}$ is
open and ${\rm Inv}_{1}+{\rm keeper}$ is a
cross coupled bistable holding $M/B$ statically.
It must be ratioed: keeper $W/L \ll {\rm Inv}_{1}$
and $\ll$ driver $E$ so it can be over written.

Normally you need {\it two} keepers: $B\to M$ for
the master and $E\to C$ or $D\to C$ for the slave.
With one keeper only the circuit is half static.
It still has a $f_{\min }$ for the other phase.

As drawn the {\it red} inverter is $A\to B$ in the
drawing, $B\to A$ if you reverse the symbol. In
either case it is {\it not} $B\to M$.

* If $A\to B$ it is a second feed forward
${\rm inv}$ in {\it parallel} with $CK+{\rm Inv}_{1}$.
With $\bar {CK}=1$ you have

$$A\stackrel{\rm red}{\to}B \to C \to\bar C\to E=A$$

$3$ inversions round a {\it combinational} loop:
a gated ring oscillator. With $\bar {CK}=0$ $B=
\bar A$ combinationally. There is no latch at
all.

* If $B\to A$, as normally intended as a keeper,
it goes to $A$, not to $M$.

$$ {\rm loop}: A\stackrel{CK}{\to} M\stackrel{{\rm Inv}_{1}}
{\to} B\stackrel{\rm red}{\to}A \tag{**}$$

i.e. ${\rm Inv}_{1}+{\rm red}$ is a latch {\it only}
with $CK=1$ closed. That is the {\it transparent}
phase, when you do {\it not} need it. With $CK=0$
open $M$ is disconnected. $(**)$ is open.
$M$ is left floating on $C_{M}$ driving ${\rm Inv}_{1}$.
${\rm Red}$ holds $A/B$ not $M/B$. $M$ still leaks and
will flip ${\rm Inv}_{1}$ after $T_{H}=C_{M}\Delta V/
I_{\rm leak}$.

In the other phase $\bar {CK}=1$

$$B\stackrel{\bar {CK}}{\to}E=B\;{\rm via\; slave}\qquad
B\stackrel{\rm red}{\to}A=E=\bar B\;{\rm via\; red}$$

the slave non inverting path $B\to E$ fights the
inverting path $B\stackrel{\rm red}{\to}E$ on the
same node $A=E$.

So at best ${\rm red}$ is a weak bus holder for the
{\it global} $A$ node. It will hold $A/B$ statically
when the slave is opaque, $CK=1$, but it does not
hold $M$ when the master is opaque and it does not
hold $C$ at all. The circuit stays dynamic.
$C$ is always dynamic. $M$ is dynamic for half
the period. The $f_{\min}$ for $T_{H}({\rm low})$
and for $f_{CK}$ is essentially unchanged.

What it does do is put a DC fight on $A=E$.
On $CK=0\to 1$ $E$ must overwrite the keeper to
write new data into the master and on $CK=1\to
0$ ${\rm red}$ must fight $E$ while the slave is
trying to toggle. If ${\rm red}$ is made with a
normal strong $W/L$ the divider will not toggle
at all - it is a ratioed latch stuck in the old
state. If made weak, long $L$ small $W$, the
divider can be made to work but with large crow
bar current during the write, degraded noise
margin, slower $f_{\max }$ and still dynamic
leakage on $M$ and $C$.

> with ${\rm Inv}_{1}$ is a cross coupled keeper
> that makes the divider static and removes the
> $f_{\min}$'' is false as drawn. Correctly wired
> it would be $B\to M$, not $B\to A$, and even then
> it would make only the master static. You need a
> second keeper $E\to C$ to make the whole
> divider static. As drawn it is a miswired
> half keeper that leaves the critical storage node
> $M$ and the slave node $C$ floating, does not
> remove the leakage induced $f_{\min}$, makes the
> latch ratioed and can destroy the divide by two
> function if not made weak.} 

In textbooks this is exhibited as the classic
``keeper on the wrong side of the ${\rm TG}$''
mistake. The correct staticizer is to move the
left terminal of the red inverter from $A$ to $M$.
Then with a weak $W/L$ and a second weak
feredback inverter $E\to C$ you get the usual
``weak feedback'' pseudo static TSPC divider
with no $f_{\min }$ at the expense of ratioed
static power during switching.

With the wiring as shown it is at most a
pseudo static bus holder for $A$ that has to be
overpowered on every toggle.

No. It is a {\it half} keeper.

$$CK~{\rm TG} + {\rm Inv}_{1} = {\rm master~~latch} \qquad 
\bar {CK}~{\rm TG}+2{\rm Inv} = {\rm slave~~latch}$$

with $Q=D\!=\!\bar Q$ i. e. $T$-FF/$\div 2$.

* With $CK=0$,$\bar {CK}=1$:

$$D_{M}\equiv B\;\;{\rm open}\;\;,
\;\;C\leftrightarrow B\;{\rm by\; Inv_{1}+red}$$
master opaque, stored on $B-C$.
$C$ drives $D$ drives $E$ drives $F$,
slave transparent:
$$F=C,\;\;E=\bar D, \;\;D=C\;{\rm driven}$$
whole ring closed $B-C-D-E-F$ and ${\rm DC}$
static.

* With $CK=1$,$\bar {CK}=0$:

$$D\;{\rm open},\;B\!-\!F\;{\rm closed}$$
master transparent $B=F$, $C=\bar B$,
slave opaque, $D$ high impedance

$$\eqalign{
B &=F \cr
C &=\bar B\cr
D &= {\rm float}\cr
E &=\bar D\cr
F &=\bar E = D\cr}$$

i. e. the master is still held by the
${\rm Inv}_{1}\leftrightarrow {\rm red}$ cross couple,
the slave storage node $D$, the input of the
slave inverter, is {\it dynamic}, on its
diffusion + gate $C_{p}$.

So ``red + ${\rm Inv}_{1}$'' is indeed a
cross coupled latch - normally drawn as a
{\it clocked} feedback inverter - here drawn
as a direct weak feedback inverter, a weak
keeper, trickle inverter, bleeder,
staticizer, level restorer, ``semi-static'',
``pseudo static'' latch.

When the master is opaque, $CK=0$, it is held
statically against leakage, charge sharing,
coupling noise, power supply droop, etc. by
the red inverter.

When the master is transparent, $CK=1$, the
red inverter is overdriven by the $F$ driver
through the $CK$ transmission gate.
I. e. it {\it must} be ratioed weak, long $L$
small $W$, high $R_{out}$, so it can be
overpowered for a correct write. While it is
being overpowered it draws $I_{sc}$ crowbar
current. It is a ratioed pseudo NMOS latch.
If it is made normal strength the divider
jams and will not toggle, $B=\bar F$ cannot be
written.

It does {\it not} make the whole master-slave
FF/divider static. For $CK=1$ the $D$ node is
floating. If you stop the clock with $CK=1$,
$\bar {CK}=0$, for

$$t_{H} > {C_{p}\Delta V\over I_{leak}} \approx
10^{-13}\times 0.5/10^{-9} \sim 10-100\mu {\rm s}$$

$D$ leaks to $V_{DD}$ or $V_{SS}$,
$E,F$ follow, the next $CK=0$ loads the
wrong $F$ and the $\div 2$ loses state.

So conventionally the circuit is still
regarded as {\it dynamic}. There is a maximum
allowable $CK=1$ pulse width, i. e. a minimum
operating frequency if the clock has $50\%$
duty cycle, or more precisely still a
minimum clock frequency for $DC$ high
operation. You can stop the circuit
indefinitely only with $CK=0$.

To make it truly single phase fully static,
$F_{min}=0$ for either phase, you need a
second, normally clocked, weak feedback
inverter round the slave, $F\rightarrow D$
or $E\rightarrow D$.

In text books the circuit as drawn is often
called the Yuan-Svensson True Single Phase
Clock, TSPC, pseudo static or half static
divide by two, master pseudo static, slave
dynamic, $T$-FF. The red inverter is the
master staticizer - it lets you run the
divider down to low frequency {\it and} holds
the master node while the master is opaque
so you do not have to refresh it every cycle -
but at the price of a ratioed contention write
and without staticizing the slave.

> {\it Remark:} With ordinary sizing the divider will
divide correctly as a dynamic divider even
without the red inverter. The red inverter is
not logically necessary, it is there for
robustness at low speed, noise, soft error
and start up.

It is ``keeper'' in name only. Let

* $N_{1}$ be the node to the {\it right} of the $CK$
  transfer gate $=$ input of $Inv_{1}$
* $N_{2}$ be the node to the {\it left} of the $\bar {CK}$
  transfer gate $=$ output of $Inv_{1}$
* $N_{3}$ be the node to the {\it right} of the $\bar {CK}$
  transfer gate $=$ input of the $slave$ $2\;Inv.$
* $N_{0}$ be the common node $=$ left of $CK$ $=$ output
  of the $slave$ $=Q$.

Without the red $Inv.$

* $CK=1$ , $\bar {CK}=0$: $N_{1}=N_{0}$, $N_{2}=\bar N_{1}$,
  transparent, $N_{3}$ $Z$
* $CK=0$, $\bar {CK}=1$: $N_{1}$ $Z$, $N_{2}= \bar N_{1}$
  memorised on $C_{N1}$, $C_{N2}$, $N_{3}=N_{2}$ transparent.
* $CK=1$, $\bar {CK}=0$: $N_{3}$ $Z$ memorised on $C_{N3}$.

So the toggle ${\rm DFF}$ with ${\rm D}=\bar Q$ is two
{\it dynamic} latches. The state is the charge on the
high $Z$ nodes $N_{1}$ and $N_{3}$ and to a lesser
extent $N_{2}$ which follows $N_{1}$. ${\rm d}V/{\rm d}t=
I_{leak}/C\sim $msec. The clock must be re-circulated
before that. There is a minimum $f_{ck}$.

A conventional weak keeper for the ${\rm M}$ latch is

$$N_{2} \rightarrow Inv_{w} \rightarrow N_{1}\tag{*}$$

with $Inv_{w}$ weak, so that when $CK=0$ the loop
$Inv_{1}+Inv_{w}$ is {\it closed} and isolated from $N_{0}$.
$N_{1}$ is always driven, either by $N_{0}$ through $CK=1$ or
by $Inv_{w}$ through $(*)$ for $CK=0$. $Inv_{1}$ can
overpower $Inv_{w}$ when $CK=1$ to write. Ditto for
the ${\rm S}$ latch $N_{5}\rightarrow Inv_{w}\rightarrow N_{3}$.

What is drawn in red is {\it not} $(*)$. Up to orientation,

$$\;N_{2}\; {\rm or}\; N_{0} \rightarrow Inv_{red} \rightarrow
  N_{0}\; {\rm or}\; N_{2}\; \tag{**}$$

in the drawing the left plate of the red $Inv.$ is
$N_{0}$ , the right plate, bubble, is $N_{2}$. So at
best

$$N_{0}\rightarrow Inv_{red}\rightarrow N_{2} $$

or vice versa $N_{2}\rightarrow Inv_{red}\rightarrow N_{0}$.
In either case the left plate is {\it not} $N_{1}$.

In particular the often quoted $N_{2}\rightarrow Inv_{red}
\rightarrow N_{1}$ ``cross coupled latch with $Inv_{1}$''
does not exist. $N_{1}$ and $N_{0}$ are the same node
only when $CK=1$. When the latch is supposed to hold,
$CK=0$, $N_{1}$ is open. The red loop is open. The
charge on $N_{1}$ is still left on a $Z$ node and will
leak through the $n$ - or $p$ - diffusion of the $TG$
and of $Inv_{1}$ with time constant $C_{N1}/I_{off}$.

$$N_{1}\;\;{\rm is\;still\;dynamic}$$

The only thing the red $Inv.$ does keep is $N_{2}$.
For $CK=0$, $N_{1}$ $Z$, $Inv_{1}$ is driving $N_{2}$
to $\bar N_{1}$ on the basis of a leaking input, $N_{2}$
would follow the leak. The red $Inv.$ now drives $N_{2}$
from $N_{0}=Q$ which is low impedance. So $N_{2}$ is
never $Z$, it is always driven either by $Inv_{1}$ or
by $Inv_{red}$. But it is driven to the {\it wrong}
value in hold.

Normal hold: with $CK=0$, $\bar {CK}=1$, $Q=N_{2,old}$,
$N_{3}=N_{2,old}$.

With $N_{0}\rightarrow N_{2}$ red: $N_{2,red}= \bar N_{0}
= \bar Q = \bar N_{2,old}$. The red $Inv.$ fights the
value the ${\rm M}$ latch is supposed to hold. Normal
operation is only possible as {\rm ratioed} logic: the
red $Inv.$ must be made weak $W/L \ll W/L_{Inv1}$,
$W/L_{Q\;driver}$ so that during the phase in which it
fights it is overpowered. We get

* $CK=1$: $CK$ closed, $Inv_{1}$ and $Inv_{red}$ both drive
$N_{2}$ to $\bar N_{0}$ - no fight.
* $CK=0$: $CK$ open, $Inv_{1}$ drives $N_{2}$ to the
old $\bar N_{1,old}$, $Inv_{red}$ drives $N_{2}$ to
$\bar N_{0}= \bar N_{2,old}$, opposite, $Inv_{1}$ must win
if the leak has not yet moved $N_{1}$.

The complementary case $N_{2}\rightarrow N_{0}$ is the
dual: the loop $N_{1}-CK-Inv_{1}-Inv_{red}$ is a latch
{\it closed when $CK=1$}, i.e. precisely when the ${\rm M}$
latch should be transparent. It holds when it should sample
and is open when it should hold. Again it only works
ratioed.

In either description it is not a conventional keeper/
cross coupled bistable isolated when $CK=0$. It is a
weak feed through, half keeper, pseudo-NMOS, contention
latch. It gives a DC path $V_{DD}-V_{SS}$ through
$Inv_{1}/Inv_{red}/Q$ driver for half the cycle and
static power.

Even if you accept to call the $N_{0}-N_{2}$ loop a
weak pseudo latch that keeps $N_{2}$ defined, the
circuit {\it as a frequency divider} is still dynamic:

* $N_{1}$ still $Z$ for $CK=0$
* $N_{3}$ still $Z$ for $\bar {CK}=0\;(CK=1)$

One weak inverter on the master can at most pseudo-
staticize the master intermediate node $N_{2}$, it cannot
staticize the true storage node $N_{1}$ nor the slave
storage node $N_{3}$. The divider will still lose state
if $\bar {CK}=0$ is kept too long, $C_{N3}$ leaking, and
if $CK=0$ is kept too long $C_{N1}$ leaking will flip
$Inv_{1}$ and, even though $N_{2}$ is weakly held, the
contention current will eventually be won by the leak if
you wait long enough. So a minimum $f_{ck}$ remains,
at best moved by the ratio.

A truly static toggle ${\rm DFF}$ needs {\it two}
keepers, $(*)$ for the master and the equivalent for the
slave, both weak and isolated behind the $TG$, e.g. clocked
feedback inverter. Moving the left plate of the red
$Inv.$ from $N_{0}$ to $N_{1}$ and adding the missing
slave keeper, properly ratioed $\sim 1/5-1/10$, is the
text book static TSPC/C$^{2}$MOS latch.

Without that the 3 $Inv.$ + $2\;TG$ + global $\bar Q\rightarrow D$
connection is just the well known dynamic divide by $2$.
Adding the red $Inv.$ as drawn does not make it static,
it makes it a ratioed pseudo static divider with contention,
degraded swing, noise margin and power, and is normally
quoted as the classic {\it wrong place for the keeper}
mistake. Remove it and you recover the correct low power
dynamic divider operation.

With the bias choke ${\rm C}_{1}\to {\rm s.c.}$
for ${\rm a.c.}$ put

$${G_{F}=1/R_{F}\;\;G_{s}=1/R_{s}\;\;G_{o}=1/r_{o}\;\;
r_{o}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}\;\;g_{m}=g_{m1}+g_{m2}\;\;
i_{n}^{2}=4kT\gamma g_{m}\;{\rm A^{2}/Hz}\;\;0.7<\gamma <2$$

$$\eqalign{
i_{nF}^{2}&=4kTG_{F}\cr 
v_{ns}^{2}&=4kTR_{s}\cr}$$

$${\rm at\;\;input:}\;(V_{i}-V_{s})G_{s}+(V_{i}-V_{o})G_{F}+i_{nF}=0 \tag{1}$$
$${\rm at\;\;output:}\;(V_{o}-V_{i})G_{F}-i_{nF}+V_{o}G_{o}+g_{m}V_{i}
+i_{n}=0 \tag{2}$$

$$\left| {{V_{o}}\over {V_{i}}}\right| _{0}=
{{g_{m}-G_{F}}\over {G_{F}+G_{o}}}\approx g_{m}r_{o}\parallel R_{F}=|A_{v}|$$

$$\left| {{V_{o}}\over {V_{s}}}\right| =
