   • Without RS   :  Av ≈ – gm ( RD ‖ ro )      (ordinary common-source)
   • With RS ≫ 0  :  feedback reduces gain and
                     linearises the stage by the factor (1 + gmRS).
   • Output resistance Rout ≈ RD ‖ ro
   • Input resistance Rin ≈ ∞ (gate oxide).

5. Qualitative behaviour

   • The circuit behaves like an inverting amplifier whose gain is set
     principally by RD and gm but is tamed by the source-degeneration
     resistor RS.  
   • RS also makes the bias remarkably insensitive to threshold-voltage,
     temperature and process spreads, because any excess drain current
     immediately lifts VS and thereby reduces VSG (“local negative
     feedback”).  
   • For small gmRS (little degeneration) the stage can deliver large
     gain; for large gmRS it approaches a unity-gain (buffer-like)
     behaviour.  
   • With both RS and RD present the maximum undistorted output swing is
     roughly the rail-to-rail value multiplied by RD /( RS + RD ).

6. Summary

   The topology in the figure is a resistively biased, source-degenerated
   PMOS common-source amplifier.  It realises an analogue inverter whose

        – static transfer characteristic is monotonic and centre-biased,
        – small-signal voltage gain is           Av = – gmRD /(1+gmRS),
        – input resistance is essentially infinite, and
        – output resistance is RD (‖ ro).

   Choosing RS mainly fixes the bias current and the amount of local
   feedback, while RD determines the voltage gain and the available
   output swing.

The network is nothing more than a common-source PMOS stage whose source is “degenerated’’ by the resistor RS and whose drain is loaded by the resistor RD (figure reproduced for reference).

1.  Device orientation  

    • M1 is a PMOS transistor (arrow points into the body).  
    • The upper node (connected to RS) is the source, the lower node (connected to RD) is the drain.  
    • ID flows from the positive supply VDD through RS, the source, the channel, RD and finally to ground.

2.  Large-signal (d.c.) operation  

    a. Regions of operation  

       The controlling quantity for a PMOS device is VSG = VS – VG (all voltages measured with respect to ground).

       • Cut–off: VSG < |VT|  
         (or VS – VG < |VT|).  
         In this region ID = 0 ⇒ VS = VDD,  VD = 0 ⇒ VOUT = 0.

       • Saturation: VSG ≥ |VT|  and  VSD > VSG – |VT|  
         The channel equation (neglecting λ) is  
         ID = ½ kP (VSG – |VT|)^2,  kP = μpCox(W/L).

       • Triode: VSG ≥ |VT|  and  VSD ≤ VSG – |VT|  
         ID = kP[(VSG – |VT|)VSD – ½ VSD²].

    b. Bias (saturation assumed — the normal small-signal operating region)

         ID = ½ kP(VSG – |VT|)²  
         = ½ kP(VDD – IDRS – VG – |VT|)²        (because VS = VDD – IDRS)

         For a given VIN(=VG) this is a cubic equation in ID that can be solved numerically or graphically; once ID is known

              VS  = VDD – IDRS
              VOUT(=VD) = IDRD.

         The circuit therefore behaves as a self-biased inverter:  
         • VIN high (≈VDD) → M1 cut off → VOUT ≈ 0.  
         • VIN low (near ground) → M1 on → VOUT ≈ IDRD, a positive value that can approach VDD if RD is large.

         The presence of RS automatically sets the drain current and keeps M1 in saturation over a wide VIN range; without RS the bias would be extremely sensitive to device parameters.

3.  Small-signal model  

    With the Mosfet in saturation we use the hybrid-π model (ro may be included if high accuracy is needed).

         gm  = 2ID/(VSG – |VT|) = √(2kPID)          (no λ)  
         rs  = RS                                (external resistor)  
         rd  = RD || ro                          (ro may be large → rd ≈ RD).

    Looking into the gate the resistance is practically infinite, so the incremental source node rises by

         vS = –gm rs · vgs              (negative sign because increasing VG lowers VSG).

    The effective (degenerated) transconductance seen looking into the drain is therefore

         gmeff = gm / (1 + gmRS).

    Small-signal gain (ro neglected for clarity)

         Av = vout / vin
            = – gmeff RD
            = – gm RD / (1 + gm RS).

    Important observations

    • Because of the minus sign the stage is inverting (as in a conventional NMOS common-source amplifier).  
    • RS lowers the magnitude of the gain and at the same time linearises the transfer characteristic and greatly reduces the dependence on the exact value of |VT| or kP.  
    • The input resistance ≃ ∞ (MOS gate), the output resistance ≃ RD (‖ ro if included).

4.  Summary of key equations

    Cut-off limit: VIN > VDD – |VT| ⇒ VOUT ≈ 0.  
    Saturation current: ID = ½ kP (VDD – IDRS – VIN – |VT|)².  
    Output voltage: VOUT = IDRD.  
    Small-signal gain: AV = –gmRD / (1 + gmRS).

    By choosing RS large enough to satisfy gmRS ≫ 1, the circuit can be biased so that AV approaches –RD/RS (a convenient design guideline) and remains quite insensitive to process spreads in kP or |VT|.

Hence the figure represents a self-biased, source-degenerated PMOS common-source amplifier/inverter, and the expressions above fully describe its d.c. operating point and a.c. (small-signal) behaviour.

Circuit description  
M1 is an n-channel MOSFET whose drain is hard–wired to the positive supply VDD.  
Its source is connected to ground through a resistor RS and the output node Vout
is taken at the source.  
The gate is the signal input node Vin.  
Because the signal is taken from the source while the drain is at ac ground, the
stage is a common-drain (source-follower) amplifier, biased with a purely
resistive current source (RS).

------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Large-signal (DC) analysis
------------------------------------------------------------------
Let  

    VS  = Vout  (the dc source voltage)
    ID  = the drain/source current
    VGS = Vin – VS
    VDS = VDD – VS

Assume the MOSFET is in saturation (λ = 0 for the moment)

    ID = ½ k (VGS – VTH)^2      when  VDS ≥ VGS – VTH        (1)

The same current must flow through RS

    ID = VS / RS                                            (2)

Combining (1) and (2)

    ½ k (Vin – VS – VTH)^2 = VS / RS                        (3)

Equation (3) (or a graphical load-line drawn between the
MOSFET’s I–V curve and the straight line ID = VS/RS)
gives the operating point (VS, ID) for any Vin.

Operating regions

a. Cut-off Vin < VTH  
   VGS < VTH ⇒ ID ≈ 0 ⇒ VS ≈ 0 ⇒ Vout ≈ 0

b. MOSFET turned on  
   As soon as current flows, VDS = VDD – VS and
   VGS – VTH = Vin – VS – VTH.
   The saturation condition is

        VDS ≥ VGS – VTH
        VDD – VS ≥ Vin – VS – VTH
        Vin ≤ VDD + VTH                                       (4)

For every practical signal Vin (Vin never exceeds VDD by VTH)
inequality (4) is automatically met, so the device stays in
saturation for all conducting points and (3) is valid.

Useful closed form  
Writing a = k/2 and rearranging (3) gives a quadratic in VS

    a VS^2 – (2a(Vin – VTH) + 1/RS) VS + a(Vin – VTH)^2 = 0  (5)

The physically correct (smaller) root is

    VS = [2a(Vin – VTH) + 1/RS
          – √( (2a(Vin – VTH)+1/RS)^2 – 4a^2(Vin – VTH)^2 ) ] / (2a)

For most designs gmRS ≫ 1 (see next section); then VS is
well approximated by

    VS ≈ Vin – VTH                                           (6)

i.e. the follower reproduces the input level minus one VGS drop.

------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  Small-signal (incremental) analysis
------------------------------------------------------------------
The incremental model consists of

• gm vgs current source from drain to source  
• ro from drain to source (optional)  
• RS to ground at the source node  
• Gate open-circuited (infinite Rin).

With the supply taken as the small-signal ground, the drain node
is ac ground, so ro also connects to ground.

Nodal equation at the source (set vin = small-signal gate voltage,
vs = small-signal source/output voltage):

    vs/RS + vs/ro = gm (vin – vs)

Solve for gain  Av = vs / vin :

    Av = gm / ( gm + 1/RS + 1/ro )                          (7)

If ro ≫ RS (or if we neglect channel-length modulation)

    Av = gmRS / (1 + gmRS)                                 (8)

 therefore

    gmRS ≪ 1   ⇒ Av ≈ gmRS      (small gain)  
    gmRS ≫ 1   ⇒ Av → 1         (voltage follower)

Input resistance  Rin ≅ ∞  
Output resistance (set vin = 0) is simply

    Rout = RS ∥ ro                                          (9)

For ro → ∞, Rout = RS.

------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Qualitative behaviour
------------------------------------------------------------------
• High input impedance – the stage presents essentially a
  capacitive load to the preceding circuit.

• Voltage gain slightly less than unity; it approaches 1 when
  gmRS is made large by choosing a big RS (or large device).

• The dc output level tracks the input, shifted down by about
  one VGS (≈ 0.6–1 V for most processes).

• The maximum positive swing is limited by
  Vout,max ≈ VDD – VDS,sat (a few hundred mV below VDD).  
  The minimum swing is ground (unless the MOSFET cuts off).

• Small output resistance (RS ∥ ro) makes the stage useful as a
  buffer for driving capacitive or resistive loads.

• Using a resistor instead of an active current source is simple
  but wastes headroom: at quiescent conditions Vout sits several
  hundred millivolts above ground, so only the upper part of the
  supply range is available for signal swing.

------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  Summary
------------------------------------------------------------------
The circuit is a resistively biased NMOS source follower.

Large-signal: ½ k(Vin – VTH – Vout)² = Vout/RS (saturation for
all realistic Vin).  For gmRS ≫ 1, Vout ≈ Vin – VTH.

Small-signal:  Av = gm/(gm + 1/RS + 1/ro) ≈ gmRS/(1+gmRS) < 1,
Rin ≅ ∞,  Rout = RS ∥ ro.

It provides a high-impedance input, a low-impedance output and
unity (slightly less) voltage gain, at the cost of one threshold
voltage drop in the dc transfer and some loss of output swing.

Circuit name  
The network is a source-follower (common-drain) NMOS stage whose source is returned to ground through a resistor RS.  
Because the only dc path for the drain is the supply VDD, the MOSFET normally operates in saturation and the resistor supplies the channel current.

1. Regions of operation  

a. Cut-off Vin ≤ Vth  
 VGS < Vth ⇒ ID = 0,    Vout = 0.

b. Saturation Vth < Vin < VDD + Vth  
 VDS = VDD – Vout ≥ VGS – Vth, so the device is in saturation for the whole useful input range.

c. Triode Vin ≥ VDD + Vth (rarely used)  
 The device leaves saturation because VDS < VGS – Vth; Vout then cannot rise appreciably above VDD – VDS,sat.

The useful operating range is therefore condition (b).

2. DC (large-signal) relationship  

With M1 in saturation and neglecting channel-length modulation

 ID = ½ β (Vin – Vout – Vth)²  β = μn Cox (W/L) .

The same current flows through RS:

 ID = Vout / RS.

Equating the two currents gives the dc transfer equation

 ½ β RS (Vin – Vout – Vth)² = Vout   (1)

or, solved explicitly for Vout

 Vout = Vin – Vth – ΔV  
 ΔV = [ –1 + √(1 + 2 β RS (Vin – Vth) ) ] / (β RS).

Equation (1) is the load-line intersection of the MOSFET square-law curve with the straight line ID = Vout/RS.

Practical observations
• As soon as Vin rises a little above Vth, Vout grows almost linearly with Vin.  
• The gate–source overdrive Vov = Vin – Vout – Vth is automatically adjusted by the feedback through RS, reducing sensitivity to β and Vth variations.

3. Small-signal (incremental) analysis  

At the quiescent point let

 gm = ∂ID/∂VGS = β (Vin – Vout – Vth) = 2 ID / Vov.

Neglecting ro first:

KCL at the source node (output)

 Vout/RS = gm (Vin – Vout)

⇒ (1/RS + gm) Vout = gm Vin

Small-signal gain (output referred to source)

 Av = ∂Vout/∂Vin = gm RS / (1 + gm RS)   (2)

Properties  
• 0 < Av < 1; for gm RS ≫ 1, Av → 1 and the stage behaves like an almost ideal voltage follower.  
• The deviation from unity gain, ε = Vin – Vout, is ε ≈ Vov = 1/gm when gm RS ≫ 1.

Including channel-length modulation (finite ro) simply puts another resistor ro from the source node to ac ground (VDD).  Replace RS with RS || ro in eqn. (2):

 Av ≈ gm (RS || ro) / [1 + gm (RS || ro)].

4. Input and output impedances  

Input resistance Rin ≃ ∞ (only the MOS gate is seen).  

Output resistance with the gate ac-grounded:

 Rout,open = RS / (1 – gm RS).  
For gm RS > 1 the open-circuit Rout is negative; once a load RL is attached the closed-loop output resistance becomes

 Rout = (RS || RL) / (1 + gm RS) ≈ 1/gm   when gm RS ≫ 1,

demonstrating the low-impedance property of a source follower.

5. Design / bias example  

Suppose VDD = 3.3 V, Vth = 0.5 V, β = 200 µA/V², choose ID = 1 mA.  
Pick RS = Vout / ID.  Iterate with (1):

 Initial guess Vout ≈ 1 V → RS ≈ 1 kΩ  
 Then Vov = √(2 ID / β) ≈ 100 mV.  
 Vin = Vout + Vth + Vov ≈ 1.6 V.  
 gm = 2 ID / Vov ≈ 20 mS,  gm RS = 20 > 1.  
 Av ≈ 20/21 ≈ 0.95.

Thus with a 1 kΩ source resistor the stage produces roughly 0.95 V/V small-signal gain, input at 1.6 V biases 1 mA, and the output follows the input within about 100 mV.

Summary  
The circuit is a self-biased source follower.  Negative feedback through RS fixes the drain current and forces the output to track the input with a gain slightly smaller than unity, a very high input impedance, and a low output impedance.  Equations (1) and (2) fully describe its dc and small-signal behavior; operation remains in saturation provided Vin < VDD + Vth.

Circuit identification  
The transistor M1 is an n-channel MOSFET whose drain is tied to the positive supply VDD, the source is returned to ground through a resistor RS, and the output is taken at the source node.  
This is therefore a common-drain stage, usually called a source follower or voltage buffer.

1. DC (large–signal) analysis  

   1.1 Regions of operation  
   • OFF (cut–off):  
     Vin < VTH  ⇒ ID ≈ 0 ⇒ Vout ≈ 0 V  
   • ON (normally in saturation):  
     ID = ½ kn (W/L) (Vin – VTH – Vout)^2 = Vout / RS  
     where kn = µnCox.  
     M1 remains in saturation as long as  
        VDS ≥ VGS – VTH → VDD – Vout ≥ (Vin – Vout) – VTH  
        → Vin ≤ VDD + VTH        (always true in normal operation).  
     Hence as soon as the device turns on it stays in saturation for all practical Vin < VDD.  

   1.2 DC transfer characteristic  
     Solve the quadratic for Vout:  

       (Vin – VTH – Vout) = √( 2 Vout / (kn (W/L) RS) )  

     An approximate closed-form expression that engineers use is obtained by noting that once ID is a few hundred µA or more, the over-drive VOV = Vin – VTH – Vout is almost constant.  Therefore, to first order

       Vout ≈ Vin – VGS(on)      (with VGS(on) ≈ VTH + VOV ≈ 0.7 … 1 V)

     i.e. the source “follows” the gate about one VGS below it.

   1.3 Input-/output swing limits  
     • Minimum Vin that produces non-zero output:    Vin(min) ≈ VTH  
     • Maximum useful Vin: limited by headroom across RS or by the next stage; practically Vin(max) ≈ VDD (a little larger is possible but rarely used).  
     • Consequently the output swing is roughly

          0 V   ≤ Vout ≤   VDD – VGS(on)

2. Small-signal analysis (ac)  

   Small-signal model (body effect neglected for clarity):  

     gm (vin – vout)  =  vout / RS

     ⇒   Av = vout / vin = gm RS / (1 + gm RS)

     Special cases  
        RS → ∞   (current-source tail)   → Av → 1          (ideal voltage buffer)  
        gm RS ≫ 1                       → Av ≈ 1 – 1/(gm RS)

   Output resistance seen looking into the source:

        Rout ≈ 1 / (gm + gmb)  ||  RS      (gmb = body-transconductance)  
        For a discrete MOSFET with source tied to its body, gmb ≈ 0 and ro ≫ RS ⇒ Rout ≈ RS || 1/gm.

3. Input and output impedances  

   • Rin ≈ ∞ (MOS gate).  
   • Rout (as above) is low (a few tens of ohms if gm ≈ 5 mS and RS is not huge), which is why the stage is used as a buffer/level-shifter.

4. Power dissipation  

      ID,quiescent = Vout / RS   
      P ≈ ID,quiescent (VDD – ½ Vout)

   By choosing RS the designer fixes both the quiescent current and the source bias voltage.

5. Typical applications  

   • Voltage buffer between a high-impedance source and a low-impedance load.  
   • Level shifter that produces an output one VGS below the input.  
   • Part of bias networks (self-biased current sources, mirrors, etc.).

Summary  
The circuit is an NMOS source follower biased by a source resistor.  
• It turns on when Vin exceeds VTH.  
• Once on, M1 almost always stays in saturation.  
• The output tracks the input with a loss of roughly one VGS, giving Av just below unity.  
• The stage presents an extremely high input impedance and a comparatively low output impedance, hence it is well suited as a voltage buffer or level shifter.

The network is nothing more than a common-source NMOS stage whose drain current is converted to a voltage by a load-resistor RD.  
Because it can be looked at either as an analog amplifier or as a digital inverter, the analysis is usually split into

• large-signal (static transfer characteristic)  
• small-signal (incremental gain and input/output resistances).

Assumptions used below  
 - Enhancement NMOS, threshold VT (≈ Vth)  
 - Square-law model with conduction factor k n = ½ µnCox W/L  
 - Channel-length–modulation neglected unless stated  
 - Source at 0 V; supply VDD.

-------------------------------------------------
1.  Large-signal (dc) behaviour  
-------------------------------------------------
Let ID be the drain current and Vout the drain voltage.

Load line:                           ID  = (VDD – Vout)/RD             (1)

The transistor can be in three regions:

A. Cut-off (Vin ≤ VT)  
   M1 OFF → ID ≃ 0 → from (1) Vout = VDD.  
   (This is the ‘logic-high’ output.)

B. Saturation (Vin > VT  and  VDS ≥ VGS – VT → Vout ≥ Vin – VT)  
   ID  =  (kn/2)(Vin – VT)²                           (2)  
   Insert (2) in (1):  
      Vout = VDD – (kn RD/2)(Vin – VT)²               (3)  
   Valid as long as Vout from (3) fulfils the saturation inequality.

C. Triode (linear) (Vin sufficiently large so that Vout < Vin – VT)  
   ID  =  kn[(Vin – VT)Vout – ½ Vout²]                (4)  
   Equate (1) and (4) and solve for Vout(Vin).

‘Knee’ between B and C (called Vi1, Vo1) is found by combining  
Vout = Vin – VT  with (1) and (2):  

      (kn RD/2)Vi1² + Vi1 – VDD + VT = 0,   where Vi1 = Vin – VT  (5)

The complete dc transfer curve consists of

  • A flat segment at VDD (region A)  
  • A parabolic segment given by (3) (region B)  
  • A third‐order segment from (4) (region C) that rapidly drives Vout toward 0.

Typical logic levels  
   VOH  =  VDD  
   VOL  ≈  VDD /[1 + kn RD (VIH – VT)]  ≈ 0   if kn RD is large.

Because a finite dc current ID = (VDD – VOL)/RD flows whenever the input is high, the inverter dissipates static power; this is the well-known drawback of the resistive-load NMOS gate compared with CMOS.

-------------------------------------------------
2.  Small-signal (analog) operation  
-------------------------------------------------
Bias the input somewhere inside region B so that M1 is in saturation; call the quiescent point  
VinQ ,  IDQ ,  VoutQ (= VDSQ).

Small-signal parameters  

   gm = ∂ID/∂VGS = kn (VinQ – VT) = 2√(kn IDQ)  
   ro ≈ 1/(λ IDQ)   (include λ if long-channel accuracy is needed)

Incremental gain (mid-band)  

   Av = –gm (RD || ro)  ≈ –gm RD   if  ro ≫ RD.

Example  
   VDD = 5 V, RD = 10 kΩ, VT = 1 V, kn = 200 µA/V², VinQ = 2 V  

   IDQ = (VDD – VoutQ)/RD  =  (from (3)) ≈ 100 µA  
   gm  ≈ 0.9 mA/V  
   |Av| ≈ gm RD ≈ 9.

The input resistance is essentially infinite (MOS gate); the output resistance is RD || ro.

-------------------------------------------------
3.  Summary of what the circuit does  
-------------------------------------------------
1. Acts as a digital inverter:  
  Vin low  → NMOS OFF → Vout ≈ VDD (logic “1”)  
  Vin high → NMOS ON  → Vout pulled toward 0 (logic “0”).

2. Acts as a common-source voltage amplifier if the input is biased so that the transistor stays in saturation; small-signal gain ≈ –gm RD.

3. Three operating regions can be located precisely with the conditions derived above; the load line (1) intersects the device I-V curves and fixes Vout for any Vin.

4. Consumes static power when the input is high: Pstat = VDD · ID(on).  
   This is why modern logic uses CMOS rather than the resistive-load NMOS of the figure.

That completes the analysis of the circuit shown.

The single-ended stage you see is nothing more than a common–source n-MOSFET (M1) whose
drain is pulled-up to the positive supply VDD through a resistor RD.  
Because the output node is taken at the drain, the circuit is often called

• a “resistive-load n-MOS inverter” in digital design, or  
• a “common-source amplifier with a resistive load” in analog design.

The analysis below is therefore given in two parts: large–signal (DC transfer) and small-signal
(analog gain).  Throughout the discussion

β ≜ μn Cox (W/L)  (the familiar k′(W/L) of the transistor)  
VTH = threshold voltage of the MOSFET  
ID = drain current of M1

1. Large-signal (DC) behaviour

For any input VIN the drain current that flows through the MOS device must be the same
current that flows through the load resistor:

ID(VIN , VOUT) = (VDD – VOUT) ⁄ RD   (1)

The MOSFET can be in one of three regions depending on VIN and VOUT:

a. Cut-off   (VIN ≤ VTH)

 ID ≃ 0 → (1) gives VOUT ≃ VDD  
 Therefore the gate-to-drain voltage is small, M1 is off and the output is a logic ‘1’.

b. Saturation   (VIN > VTH    and    VDS ≥ VGS – VTH  →  VOUT ≥ VIN – VTH)

 ID = ½ β (VIN – VTH)²   (channel length modulation neglected)

 Put this in (1):

   ½ β (VIN – VTH)² = (VDD – VOUT) ⁄ RD  
   ⇒ VOUT = VDD – ½ β RD (VIN – VTH)²           (2)

   The expression is valid only if the result obeys the saturation condition
   VOUT ≥ VIN – VTH.  If it does, the device is indeed saturated.

c. Triode (linear) region   (VIN > VTH   but   VOUT < VIN – VTH)

 ID = β[(VIN – VTH) VOUT – ½ VOUT²]

 KCL again:

   β[(VIN – VTH) VOUT – ½ VOUT²] = (VDD – VOUT) ⁄ RD     (3)

 (3) is a quadratic in VOUT whose physically meaningful root (0 ≤ VOUT ≤ VDD)
 is taken when the saturation expression (2) no longer satisfies the
 inequality VOUT ≥ VIN – VTH.

Plotting (2) and (3) piece-wise against VIN gives the complete DC transfer characteristic
VOUT(VIN).  Two obvious logic points are

• VIN = 0 → M1 off → VOUT ≃ VDD (logic 1)  
• VIN ≥ (VTH + a safety margin) → M1 strongly on, a large drop appears across RD and
  VOUT falls toward 0 V (logic 0)

Because current flows whenever VIN is high, the gate consumes static (quiescent)
power PDC = ID(VIN_HIGH) · VDD, a key disadvantage compared with complementary
CMOS logic.

Switching threshold (VM)

A convenient reference point is the value VM at which the input equals the output
(VIN = VOUT = VM).  For most practical designs the MOSFET is still in
saturation at this point, so substitute VIN = VOUT = VM in (2):

½ β (VM – VTH)² = (VDD – VM) ⁄ RD

Re-arranging,

(VM – VTH)² = 2(VDD – VM) ⁄ (β RD)     (4)

(4) is a quadratic that yields the unique solution 0 < VM < VDD.  Noise-margin
quantities (VIL, VIH, NML, NMH) can be extracted by differentiating (2)/(3)
around VM.

2. Small-signal (analog) analysis

Choose a bias point (VIN0 , VOUT0) somewhere on the curve (usually within the
saturation region for largest gain).  Around that point define small excursions
vin, vout:

VIN = VIN0 + vin  
VOUT = VOUT0 + vout

Ignoring channel-length modulation (λ ≃ 0) the incremental drain current is

id = gm vin – (vout ⁄ ro) ≈ gm vin    because ro ≫ RD

where gm = ∂ID/∂VGS |bias = β (VIN0 – VTH).

KCL at the output gives

vout / RD = id = gm vin  
⇒ vout = –gm RD vin

Therefore

Input resistance: Rin ≃ ∞ (gate is insulated)  
Output resistance: Rout ≃ RD ││ ro ≈ RD  
Small-signal voltage gain: AV = vout ⁄ vin = –gm RD = –β RD (VIN0 – VTH)

Key observations

1. The stage inverts (negative gain), just as any common-source amplifier.  
2. The magnitude of the gain is proportional to the product gm RD; larger W/L
   and/or a larger load resistance increase the gain.  
3. Band-width is mainly set by the node capacitance at the drain and the
   resistance RD; f–3 dB ≈ 1 ⁄ (2π RD Cout).  
4. Static current = (VDD – VOUT0) ⁄ RD gives a continuous dc power loss when the
   transistor is conducting.

3. Summary

• VIN low (≤ VTH): transistor off, ID ≈ 0, VOUT ≈ VDD (logic ‘1’).  
• VIN high (≫ VTH): transistor on, ID flows through RD, VOUT pulled toward 0 V
  (logic ‘0’).  
• In the transition region VOUT follows the equations above, passing through the
  switching point VM determined by (4).  
• Small-signal gain around any chosen bias is –gm RD, with infinite input
  resistance and output resistance essentially equal to RD.  
• Although simple, the topology dissipates static power and exhibits limited
  noise margins compared with a complementary CMOS inverter, which is why CMOS
  logic has replaced the resistive-load n-MOS inverter in modern digital
  circuits.

The drawing is the textbook “resistively-loaded common-source stage’’:

• M1 is an enhancement NMOS transistor  
• RD is a passive load that ties the drain to the positive supply VDD  
• the source is connected to ground (that connection is made on the right-hand supply rail),  
• Vin is applied to the gate and the output is taken at the drain node Vout.

Because the MOSFET works against an ohmic load, the dc operating point is found by
equating

 ID(MOSFET)  =  IL(DRAIN ­RESISTOR)  =  (VDD – Vout) / RD           (1)

to the appropriate MOSFET i-v law.

Notation  
 kn = μnCoxW/L   (thus βn = kn/2)  
 Vth = threshold voltage (positive for an n–channel device)  
 λ  = channel-length modulation coefficient (set to 0 first, then added if needed).

1. DC transfer characteristic Vout(Vin)

Region 1 – cut-off (Vin ≤ Vth)  
 ID ≃ 0 ⇒ Vout = VDD.   
 (The stage outputs a logic “1’’.)

Region 2 – saturation (Vin > Vth and Vout ≥ Vin – Vth )  

 ID = βn (Vin – Vth)^2                                       (2)  
 Insert (2) in (1):

 Vout = VDD – RD βn (Vin – Vth)^2                           (3)

The quadratic fall given by (3) is valid as long as (saturation condition)

 Vout ≥ Vin – Vth.                                          (4)

Inserting (3) into (4) yields the largest Vin for which M1 can remain in
saturation:

 Vin,max(sat) – Vth = xS = [ –1 + √(1 + 2knRD VDD) ] / (kn RD).       (5)

Region 3 – triode (Vin > Vin,max(sat))  
 ID = kn[ (Vin – Vth) Vout – Vout^2/2 ]                     (6)

Combining (6) with (1) gives a quadratic equation in Vout,
which can be solved in the usual way.  
As Vin → large, M1’s on–resistance rDS(on) ≈ 1 / [kn (Vin – Vth)] limits the
current and the lowest attainable output voltage is

 Vout,min ≈ VDD · rDS(on) / (RD + rDS(on)).                 (7)

Thus the complete VTC starts at VDD, bends parabolically while the device
is in saturation, and finally flattens in triode at a value a few hundred
millivolts above ground (it never reaches an ideal 0 V because of the load
resistor).

The switching point (trip point) VM, often used in digital work, is
obtained by letting Vin = Vout = VM in the saturation expression:

 (VDD – VM)/RD = βn (VM – Vth)^2                            (8)

which one solves for VM.

2. Small-signal behaviour around a chosen bias point (IDQ , VoutQ)

 gm = 2IDQ / (VinQ – Vth) = √(2 kn IDQ)  
 ro ≃ 1 / (λ IDQ) (include it if λ ≠ 0)  
 Rout ≃ RD ∥ ro  

Voltage gain (low frequency)

 Av = –gm (RD ∥ ro).                                        (9)

Because gm grows with bias current while rd is fixed,
|Av| can range from a few units to several tens.

Input resistance: practically ∞ (gate is insulated).  
Output resistance: ≃ RD at low frequency.  
If the drain node drives a capacitance CL, the dominant pole is

 ωp ≈ 1 / [ (RD ∥ ro) CL ].    Time constant τ ≈ (RD ∥ ro) CL.

3. Digital view (inverter):

High input (Vin < Vth) → MOSFET off → Vout ≈ VDD (“1”).  
Low input (Vin sufficiently above Vth) → MOSFET on → Vout pulled toward
ground through M1 (“0’’), the exact low level given by (7).  
Noise–margin limits are obtained from the points where |dVout/dVin| = 1,
using the derivative of (3) in saturation and of the triode expression
in region 3.

Summary

• Below threshold the stage is open-circuit and the output sits at VDD.  
• Above threshold the drain current is set by the intersection of
   the MOSFET i-v curve with the load line (VDD – Vout)/RD.  
• With increasing Vin the device moves from saturation into triode,
   Vout falls from VDD to a few hundred millivolts, and the small-signal
   gain around the steep part of the curve is roughly –gm RD.  
• The circuit may be used either as a linear amplifier (proper bias chosen)
   or, when Vin is driven rail-to-rail, as a resistively-loaded NMOS logic
   inverter.

The circuit is a common–gate (CG) NMOS amplifier that is dc-biased through the gate and excited through the source with an a-c signal that is coupled in by C1.  
(At a-c, C1 is a short, the gate is an a-c ground because Vb is a low-impedance bias node, and VDD is a-c ground.)

1. DC (large-signal) bias  
   Gate voltage VG = Vb  
   Source voltage VS = 0 V (ground)  
   VGS0 = Vb – 0  
   For VGS0 > VTH the device operates in saturation if  

     VDS0 = VOUT0 = VDD – ID0 RD   >   VGS0 – VTH

   Drain current  
     ID0 = ½ k′(W/L)(Vb – VTH)^2(1 + λVDS0) (k′ = μnCox)  

   The quiescent output voltage is VOUT0 = VDD – ID0 RD.

2. Small-signal model  

   gm = ∂ID/∂VGS |Q, ro = 1/λID0 , gds = 1/ro  
   Body is tied to ground → vbs = 0, but body-effect trans-conductance gmb can be included if desired.

   Because C1 is a short at signal frequencies, vin appears at the source node: vs = vin.  
   With the gate at a-c ground, vgs = –vin.

   Drain current increment  
     id = gm vgs + gds vds = –gm vin + gds vout.

   KCL at the drain (vDD = 0 for a-c):  
     (–gm vin + gds vout) + vout / RD = 0

   Small-signal gain  
     Av = vout / vin = gm /(gds + 1/RD) = gm (RD || ro)

   • If RD ≪ ro → Av ≃ gm RD (positive, i.e. non-inverting).  
   • ro can be kept in the formula for more accuracy.

3. Input, output resistances

   Input resistance (looking into the source)  
     Rin = 1 / (gm + gmb)  ≈ 1/gm   (typically a few 100 Ω – a key property of the CG stage).

   Output resistance  
     Rout = RD || ro.  
     If the next stage is capacitive, CL simply adds to the drain capacitances in the high-frequency pole.

4. Frequency response  

   Low-frequency pole: set by C1 and Rin.  
     fL ≈ 1 / (2π Rin C1)   (C1 is usually chosen so large that this pole is far below the band of interest.)

   High-frequency pole: no Miller multiplication because the gate is a-c ground; bandwidth is therefore large.  
     fH ≈ 1 / [2π (CL + Cdb + Cgd) (RD || ro)]

5. Salient features of the stage  

  • Non-inverting voltage gain ≈ gm RD with low input impedance.  
  • No Miller effect → wide bandwidth; often used as RF/LNA input stage or as a cascode device.  
  • Bias point set solely by Vb; signal is a-c coupled, so the dc level of Vin does not disturb the operating point.

In summary, the circuit is a common-gate amplifier whose small-signal transfer is

     vout/vin = gm (RD || ro)   (≈ gm RD when ro ≫ RD)  

with Rin ≈ 1/gm and Rout ≈ RD || ro.

1. Topology and qualitative behaviour  
• M1 is an n-channel MOSFET.  
• Its gate is tied to a fixed dc voltage Vb, therefore the signal source must enter through the source
  – the transistor is used in the common-gate (CG) configuration for small-signal work.  
• RD converts the drain-current variations into a voltage at the output node.  
• C1 is only a coupling capacitor; it is open-circuit for dc (so it does not disturb the bias) and a short-circuit for the wanted signal band.  

Because the gate is an ac ground, a positive increment at Vin raises the source node, reduces VGS, decreases IDS, and therefore makes Vout rise.  The stage is non-inverting and can give a large positive gain.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. DC (large–signal) bias analysis  

With C1 open for dc, the source is at 0 V.  
Assuming M1 is kept in saturation,

    ID  = ½ k′ (W/L) (Vb – Vth)² ( 1 + λVDS )         (1)

    Vout,DC = VDD – ID · RD                           (2)

Saturation requires     Vout,DC ≥ (Vb – Vth).  
Choose Vb so that the desired drain current ID,Bias is obtained while (2) satisfies the above inequality.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Small–signal equivalent circuit  

Gate node: ac ground (vg = 0).  
Source node: input node vs (= vin, the right plate of C1).  
Drain node: output node vd (= vout).  

Small–signal elements:  
• gm  : transconductance of M1 at the chosen bias point.  
• ro  : drain–source small-signal resistance (= 1/λID).  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Small–signal voltage gain  

Writing KCL at the drain node (currents leaving the node taken positive)

    vd/RD + (vd – vs)/ro – gm vs = 0

Solve for Av = vd/vs:

    Av = (gm + 1/ro) / (1/RD + 1/ro)                    (3)

or, more compact,

    Av = (gm ro + 1) / (1 + ro/RD)                      (3a)

Limiting cases  
• ro » RD  →  Av ≈ gm RD     (the familiar ideal CG gain)  
• ro « RD  →  Av ≈ +1        (voltage follower).

Note that the gain is positive (non-inverting).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Input and output resistances  

Looking into the source with the gate ac-grounded:

    Rin ≈ 1/gm   ( ro appears in parallel but gm dominates )

Hence the input resistance is low (tens of ohms in RF MOSFETs, a few hundred ohms in low-frequency parts).

Output resistance:

    Rout ≈ RD || ro ≈ RD        (because ro is normally much larger than RD).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Effect of the coupling capacitor C1  

C1 forms a high-pass network with Rin.

    fL = 1 / (2π Rin C1) ≈ gm / (2π C1)               (4)

Since Rin is small, fL is usually high; C1 is chosen so that fL lies below the lowest frequency of interest.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Summary  

• The circuit is a common-gate NMOS amplifier.  
• DC bias is set by Vb; C1 isolates the bias from the signal source.  
• Small-signal gain (exact) is given by (3); for the usual case ro » RD the stage gain is gm RD, positive.  
• The input resistance is approximately 1/gm, the output resistance about RD, and the lower cut-off frequency is set by C1 and Rin.  

These relations allow you to pick Vb, RD, gm (via device sizing and bias current), and C1 to meet a required gain, bandwidth, and input/output impedance.

What you have is a common-gate (CG) NMOS voltage-amplifier stage.  
The gate of M1 is fixed at a dc bias voltage Vb, the small-signal input is injected
into the source through the coupling capacitor C1, and the output is taken at the
drain through the load resistor RD.

────────────────────────────────
1. DC (bias-point) analysis
────────────────────────────────
For dc the capacitor is open-circuited, so VS = 0 and

    VGS(Q) = Vb
    ID ≃ ½ kn (Vb – VTH)²(1 + λVDS)               (saturation model)

The quiescent output voltage is

    VOUT(Q) = VDD – ID RD.

To keep M1 in saturation

    VDS(Q) = VOUT(Q) > VGS(Q) – VTH = Vb – VTH.

Hence Vb is chosen so that the required ID is obtained while the above inequality
is satisfied and VOUT(Q) stays comfortably inside the rails (often ≈ VDD/2).

────────────────────────────────
2. Small-signal (ac) model
────────────────────────────────
At signal frequencies C1 is a short, so the small-signal source node voltage is

    vS = vIN.           (gate is ac-ground because Vb is dc)

Small-signal drain current

    iD = gm(vG – vS) + gds(vD – vS)
       = –gm vIN + gds(vOUT – vIN)                    (vg = 0).

The same current must flow through RD (top of RD is ac ground):

    iD = –vOUT / RD.

Solve for the voltage gain Av = vOUT / vIN:

      –vOUT / RD = –gm vIN + gds(vOUT – vIN)

⇒  vOUT(1/ro + 1/RD) – vIN(gm + 1/ro) = 0

⇒  Av  =  vOUT / vIN  =  (gm + 1/ro) / (1/ro + 1/RD)
        = (gm ro + 1) / (1 + ro / RD).

Useful limiting case (ro ≫ RD, gm ro ≫ 1):

      Av ≈ gm RD        (positive, i.e. no phase inversion).

────────────────────────────────
3. Input and output impedances
────────────────────────────────
Input current (into the source):

    iIN = gm vIN + gds(vIN – vOUT)
         = vIN[gm + gds(1 – Av)].

With Av given above and gm ro ≫ 1 the second term is negligible, so

    RIN = |vIN / iIN| ≃ 1 / gm      (very low – typical of CG stages).

Output resistance looking into the drain:

    ROUT ≃ RD || ro.

────────────────────────────────
4. Frequency response (role of C1)
────────────────────────────────
C1 merely removes the dc path from the signal source to the transistor.
Together with the Thevenin resistance of the source (RSIG) and RIN it forms a
high-pass network whose lower –3 dB pole is

    fL ≈ 1 / [2π C1 (RSIG + RIN)].

The upper bandwidth of the stage is set by the transistor’s parasitic Cgd, Cdb,
the load, and any circuitry that follows.

────────────────────────────────
5. Salient features of the stage
────────────────────────────────
• Configuration: common gate, non-inverting.  
• Voltage gain: ≈ gm RD (tens of V/V easily).  
• Input impedance: low (≈ 1/gm), useful for current-source or RF matching.  
• Output impedance: high (≈ RD), good for driving high-impedance loads or
  for use as the first device in a cascode stack.  
• C1 allows the input node to sit at ground while the gate is biased at the
  optimum Vb; at signal frequencies it is effectively a short.

Hence the circuit is a single-transistor common-gate amplifier that provides
a substantial, non-inverting voltage gain with low input and high output
resistance, widely used in RF front ends and as the “cascode” device in many
analog integrated-circuit blocks.

Only two circuit nodes are able to accumulate charge and therefore store energy dynamically:

1. Gate node (the node between RS and the MOS gate).  
   • Capacitances connected to it: CGS to ground, and CGD to the drain node.

2. Drain/output node.  
   • Capacitances connected to it: CDB to ground, and the other plate of CGD to the gate node.  
   • RD returns the node to AC ground (VDD is an AC short).

The source and body are tied to ground, so CSB does not create an independent energy-storage node, and VDD is AC ground as well.

Because there are only two independent energy-storage nodes, the small-signal transfer function Vin → Vout is second-order; i.e., the amplifier exhibits

2 poles.

In small-signal (ac) analysis every pole is produced by an independent node whose voltage has to change the charge on at least one capacitor.  

1. Source, bulk and the supply node VDD are ac grounds, so any capacitor that is tied only to those nodes (e.g. CSB, part of CGS, part of CDB) does not introduce an independent state variable.  
2. The remaining high-impedance nodes are  
   • the gate node (behind RS) – it sees CGS to ground and C GD to the drain,  
   • the drain/output node – it sees RD (to ac ground), CDB to ground and C GD to the gate.  

Thus there are exactly two independent energy-storage nodes → the transfer function is second-order and the stage exhibits two poles (plus whatever zeros the C GD feed-forward path creates).

Look at how many independent signal nodes can store energy.

1. Gate node (Ng) – it is not fixed; it is reached through the source resistance RS.  
   • Capacitances connected to it: CGS (to ground) and CGD (to the drain node).

2. Drain / output node (Nd) – its voltage is set by RD, ro, etc., not by an ideal voltage source.  
   • Capacitances connected to it: CDB (to ground) and CGD (to the gate node).

The source and body are hard-wired to ground, so CSB is strapped across ground and does not create a state variable.  
Because only two independent node voltages (vg and vd) can vary, the small-signal model yields two first-order differential equations. Hence the transfer function denominator is second-order:

Number of poles = number of independent energy-storage nodes = 2.

(If the driving source had zero impedance, i.e. RS = 0, the gate node would be forced, leaving only one pole at the output.)

1.  What the circuit is  
   • M1 is an n-channel MOS transistor used in common–source mode (gate = Vin , drain = Vout , source = VF).  
   • RD is the load in the drain.  
   • R1–R2 form a resistive feedback network that ties the source node (VF) to the output node (Vout).  
   • Because the feedback is taken from the output and returned to the source, the device operates the way an op-amp with “series–shunt” (voltage-series) feedback would: the MOSFET contributes a large open-loop gain, while the divider forces a precise closed-loop gain that is almost independent of gm once the loop gain is high.

2.  Large-signal (dc) bias equations  
   Id  = (1/2)k′(W/L)(Vin – VF – VTH)²        (M1 in saturation)        (1)  
   Vout = VDD – Id RD                                                       (2)  
   KCL at VF :      Id  = (Vout – VF)/R1 + VF/R2                           (3)  

   Solving (1)-(3) simultaneously gives the dc operating point {Id , Vout , VF }.  
   To keep the device in saturation we must also have                             
        Vout – VF  ≥  Vin – VF – VTH.

3.  Small-signal model  
   Substitute the small-signal quantities (lower-case) into the MOS π-model (ro may be added but is neglected here for clarity).

   id  =  gm (vin – vs)                               (4)  
   vout = – id RD                                    (5)  
   KCL at the source node vs :  
        id  = vs/R2  + (vs – vout)/R1                (6)

   Solve (4)-(6) for the closed-loop gain Av  =  vout / vin :

        Av  =  – gm RD (R1 + R2) 
               ───────────────────────────────                           (7)
              (R1 + R2) – gm R2 (RD – R1)

4.  Behaviour for high loop-gain ( gm RD  »  (R1 + R2) )  
   When RD ≫ R1,  the term gm R2 (RD – R1) dominates the denominator.  
   Equation (7) then collapses to

        Av  ≃  (R1 + R2) / R2  =  1 + R1/R2       (8,  non-inverting gain)

   Thus the closed-loop gain is set almost completely by the two resistors and is positive (the circuit has become a non-inverting amplifier).  The parameter gm has virtually disappeared, giving good gain accuracy and temperature stability—exactly the purpose of the feedback.

5.  Other small-signal quantities  
   • Input resistance:  Rin ≈ ∞ (MOS gate).  
   • Output resistance (with feedback):  Rout ≈ RD ∥ R1 /(1+|Aβ|) ≈ RD /(1+gm R2 (RD – R1)/(R1+R2)), i.e. much lower than RD when the loop-gain is large.  
   • Bandwidth is extended by the same feedback factor 1 + R1/R2.

6.  Design guidelines / operating conditions  
   • Choose RD ≫ R1 to guarantee negative feedback and to obtain the closed-loop gain of (1+R1/R2).  
   • Verify that for the worst-case Vin the inequality for saturation is satisfied.  
   • Check that the current through R1-R2 (≈ Vout / (R1+R2)) is at least 5-10 × smaller than Id so that the divider does not load the transistor excessively (if this is not true, include that current in the bias equations above).  
   • The usable Vin range is limited on the upper end by the saturation condition and on the lower end by VTH.

7.  What to remember  
   • Open-loop the network is an ordinary common-source stage with gain −gmRD.  
   • Closing the loop with the R1–R2 network converts it into a precision non-inverting amplifier whose gain is (1+R1/R2) provided the loop-gain gmRD is large.  
   • The circuit offers the high input resistance of a MOS gate, a closed-loop gain set by passive components, and an output resistance much smaller than RD.

The drawing is nothing more than a single n-MOSFET (M1) used as an amplifier, but its source is not returned directly to ground; instead it is tied to ground through the series pair R1 – R2 while the junction of the two resistors is fed back to the drain through R1.  
Because a fraction of the drain voltage is injected into the source, the stage behaves like a common-source amplifier that contains a resistive, voltage-sampling feedback loop.  
Below the circuit is analysed step by step.

1. DC (bias) relations  
   Let   β ≜ R2 /(R1 + R2)        (0 < β < 1)  

   Voltage divider:                   VF = β · Vout                (1)  

   Drain current through the MOSFET (assume strong inversion, saturation, body effect neglected)

            ID = ½ kn (Vin – VF – VTH )²                          (2)

            kn = μn Cox W/L  

   Drain current through RD

            ID = ( VDD – Vout ) / RD                              (3)

   (1)–(3) give the static transfer characteristic

         ½ kn ( Vin – VTH – β Vout )² = ( VDD – Vout ) / RD       (4)

   Equation (4) can be solved for Vout for any applied Vin; it also shows
   that by choosing R1 and R2 the bias point can be shifted without having to
   change Vin or RD.

   Saturation condition  
           VDS = Vout – VF = (1 – β) Vout ≥ VGS – VTH   
           ⇒   Vout ≥ (Vin – VTH)/(1 – β)                         (5)

2. Small–signal model  
   Introduce the conductances

      gD = 1 / RD ,       g1 = 1 / R1 ,      g2 = 1 / R2 ,  
      gm = kn (Vin – VF – VTH)  (evaluated at the bias point)

   Ignoring ro (it can easily be appended) the nodal equations around drain (vo) and source (vs) are

      (gD + g1) vo – (g1 + gm) vs + gm vi = 0                     (6)
      – g1 vo + (g1 + g2 + gm) vs – gm vi = 0                     (7)

   Solving (6)–(7) gives the small-signal gain

      Av ≜ vo / vi =  –  gm ( RD || R1 ) / [ 1 + gm ( R1 || R2 ) ] (8)

   A useful way of reading (8)  

   • Numerator  gm (RD || R1)  is exactly what an ordinary
     common-source stage would produce if its drain load were the
     parallel-combination RD || R1.  

   • The feedback network appears only in the denominator
     1 + gm (R1 || R2).  For gm (R1 || R2)  » 1 the magnitude of the
     gain is reduced roughly by the factor gm (R1 || R2).  
     Hence the loop provides a controllable degeneration that improves
     linearity at the expense of gain.

   Limiting cases  
   a) R1 → ∞ :  β → 0,  the feedback vanishes, the circuit degenerates to a
      normal common-source with a single source resistor R2.  
      Av →  – gm RD / (1 + gm R2).  

   b) R2 → ∞ :  β → 1,  the source is almost at the drain potential, so the
      stage turns into a source follower (gain ≈ +1).  

   c) R2 → 0  (β → 0) :  complete source degeneration, gain tends to –RD/R1.

3. Input, output and noise considerations  
   • Rin (at the gate) ≈ ∞ (MOS gate).  
   • Rout (looking into the drain) ≈ RD || R1 (≃ RD if RD ≪ R1).  
   • The feedback lowers distortion in the same way a source resistor does,
     but without consuming large headroom because the feedback signal is
     taken from the drain rather than from ground.

4. Practical design hints  
   • Choose R1, R2 so that  gm (R1 || R2) ≳ 3 … 5  for worthwhile linearity
     improvement.  
   • Verify (5) to ensure M1 remains in saturation over the intended signal
     swing.  
   • If large gain is required, make R1 ≫ RD; if wide swing and good
     linearity are preferred, make R1 comparable to RD.

In short, the circuit is a self-biased common-source amplifier in which a resistive voltage divider (R1-R2) feeds a portion of the output voltage back to the source.  
This negative feedback fixes the operating point and at the same time introduces controlled source degeneration, giving a tunable compromise between gain, head-room and linearity.

The network is nothing more than a common-source NMOS stage (M1 + RD) that is closed around a shunt-series negative-feedback loop made with the divider R1–R2.  
A rise of Vout is coupled through R1 to the source node VF; VF rises, VGS = Vin–VF falls, the drain current decreases and Vout is pulled back – therefore the feedback is negative.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. DC (large-signal) bias
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Let βF ≜ R2 /(R1 + R2)           (feedback factor)  
VF   = βF Vout                   (by the divider)             (1)

For M1 in saturation (λ≈0 for the moment)

ID = ½ k´(W/L)(Vin – VF – VTH)²                         (2)

while in the drain branch

ID = (VDD – Vout)/RD                                   (3)

Combining (1), (2) and (3) gives the bias equation

(VDD – Vout)/RD = ½ k´(W/L) [Vin – βF Vout – VTH]²     (4)

together with the saturation condition

Vout – VF ≥ VGS – VTH  →  Vout(1–βF) ≥ Vin – VF – VTH. (5)

(4) can be solved graphically or numerically for Vout; once Vout is known, VF and ID follow directly from (1) and (3).  
Because of the feedback, the quiescent current depends only weakly on the MOS parameters: a percentage change in k´ or VTH produces a much smaller percentage change in the operating point.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Small-signal model
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Adopt the usual small-signal symbols  
gD = 1/RD ,  g1 = 1/R1 ,  g2 = 1/R2 ,  go = 1/ro .

Writing KCL at the drain node (vo) and at the source node (vs)

(gD + g1 + go) vo – (g1 + go + gm) vs + gm vi = 0       (6)
–(g1 + go) vo + (g1 + g2 + go + gm) vs – gm vi = 0      (7)

Solving (6)–(7) for the gain Av = vo / vi gives the exact
closed-loop expression

Av = – gm g2
     ────────────────────────────────────────────────          (8)
     gD (g1 + g2 + gm + go) + (g1 + go) g2

With ro ≫ R1 (go ≈ 0) (8) reduces to

Av = – gm g2
     ────────────────────────────────                           (9)
     gD (g1 + g2 + gm) + g1 g2

Multiplying top and bottom of (9) by RD R1 R2 gives a handier
resistance form

Av = – gm RD R1
     ──────────────────────────────────                           (10)
     RD + R1 + R2 + gm R1 R2

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Behaviour of the gain
--------------------------------------------------------------------
• Weak loop-gain (gm R1 R2 ≪ RD + R1 + R2)   
  Av ≈ – gm RD R1 /(RD + R1 + R2)  → proportional to gm.  

• Strong loop-gain (gm R1 R2 ≫ RD + R1 + R2)   
  Av ≈ – RD / R2                                  (11)

Thus, once gm is high enough the gain is fixed almost completely by the
passive resistors RD and R2; MOS-parameter spread or temperature
variations hardly move it – the principal advantage of the topology.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Input and output resistances
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Input: the gate is insulated, so  
Rin ≅ very large (≈ the gate leakage resistance).

Output: looking into the drain

Rout ≅ RD ∥ (ro + (1 + gm R2⁄(R1+R2)) R1) ;  
for gm R1,R2 » 1 this approaches RD.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Open-loop / feedback viewpoint
--------------------------------------------------------------------
If the feedback network is “opened” (R1, R2 disconnected from
the source) the transconductance amplifier alone provides

A0 = –gm RD  (Vout / (Vin–VS)).

With the feedback factor βF = R2/(R1+R2)

Closed-loop:   Av = A0 / (1 + βF A0)  
and substituting A0 reproduces (9).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Summary of key points
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. VF is a fractional copy of Vout; that turns the circuit into a
   single-transistor op-amp closed by a resistive divider.
2. The DC bias is set by the intersection of the MOS I–V characteristic
   with the line (VDD–Vout)/RD; feedback makes it almost insensitive to
   device spread.
3. Exact small-signal gain is given by (8) or (10).  
   For the usual case gm R1 R2 ≫ RD + R1 + R2,

        Av ≈ – RD / R2                                  (design rule)

4. Very high input resistance, moderate output resistance (≈ RD).  
5. The circuit is a convenient way to obtain a precise, programmable
   negative gain with only one active device; choosing RD and R2 fixes
   the gain, while R1 can be used to help satisfy the saturation
   condition or to trim bias current.

What you have is a single-ended NMOS “source follower’’ (common-drain stage) that is biased with an NMOS current-sink load.

1.  How the circuit works  

    •  M2 is given a fixed gate–bias Vb.  
       Provided    Vout ≥ Vb – Vtn2,   M2 is in saturation and sinks an (almost) constant current  

                 ID2 ≈ (β2 / 2)·(Vb – Vtn2)²        (β = μCoxW/L)                (1)

    •  The same current must flow through M1.  
       With its drain at VDD, its source at Vout and its gate driven by Vin, M1 is an NMOS
       operated as a source follower and (for the usual Vin range) is also in saturation
       because   

                 VDS1 = VDD – Vout  ≥  VGS1 – Vtn1 = (Vin – Vout) – Vtn1          (2)
                 →  VDD ≥ Vin – Vtn1  (always true if Vin ≤ VDD).  

       Therefore  

                 ID1 = (β1 / 2)·(Vin – Vout – Vtn1)²                            (3)

    •  At dc ID1 = ID2, so from (1) and (3)

                 Vin – Vout – Vtn1 = √[ (β2 / β1) ] · (Vb – Vtn2)               (4)

       and finally

                 Vout = Vin – Vtn1 – √(β2/β1)·(Vb – Vtn2).                      (5)

       If the two transistors are laid out identically (β1 = β2):

                 Vout = Vin – ( Vb – Vtn )                                      (6)

       i.e. the output follows the input with unit slope, merely shifted downward by a
       constant voltage ≃ (Vb – Vtn).  This is the hallmark of a source-follower buffer.

2.  Large-signal limits  

    •  Turn-off of M1:  the pair conducts only while Vin > Vtn1.  
    •  M2 leaves saturation when Vout < Vb – Vtn2; below that point the simple square-law
      relation no longer holds and the node is pulled close to ground.  
    •  The highest output obtainable while keeping M1 in saturation is
                  Vout,max ≈ VDD – (Vin – Vtn1)  (≃ VDD – a few hundred mV).

3.  Small-signal behaviour  

    Using the hybrid-π model (gds1 = 1/ro1, gds2 = 1/ro2):

          gm1·(vin – vout) + gds1·vout + gds2·vout = 0

          ⇒   Av ≡ vout / vin = gm1 / (gm1 + gds1 + gds2).                    (7)

    When gm1 ≫ (gds1 + gds2) the gain approaches unity.  
    The small-signal output resistance seen at Vout is

          Rout = 1 / (gm1 + gds1 + gds2)  ≈ 1 / gm1   (for gm1 ≫ gds).         (8)

4.  Power  

          PDC ≈ VDD · ID   with ID set by (1).

5.  Summary  

    •  M2 fixes a bias current;  
    •  M1, connected as a source follower, transfers the input to the output with almost
      unity gain and a constant level shift;  
    •  The stage provides a low-impedance output node whose voltage swing is roughly
      Vin minus one threshold, limited at the bottom by M1 turn-off and at the top by the
      saturation condition of M2.

The schematic is nothing more than a very small-signal “one-transistor” inverter that uses a constant-current sink instead of the usual n-device that is driven by the input.  
If we adopt the conventional CMOS orientation  

• M1 is a p–MOS device (source at VDD, drain at the output node)  
• M2 is an n–MOS device (source at ground, drain at the output node)  

the circuit can be viewed as a common-source amplifier whose load is the p-device and whose bias current is furnished by the n-device.  
(If you choose to draw both transistors as n-devices the algebra is the same, only the sign of the threshold voltage of the upper device changes.)

1. Large-signal (dc) operating point  

Let  

β1 = μp Cox (W/L)1            (transconductance parameter of M1, p-MOS)  
β2 = μn Cox (W/L)2            (parameter of M2, n-MOS)  
|VTP|, VTN                    (threshold voltages)  
λp , λn                       (channel-length modulation factors)

We bias M2 with a fixed gate voltage Vb, so in saturation its drain current is  

ID = ½ β2 (Vb – VTN)^2 (1 + λn VDS2)         (1)  

(as long as VDS2 ≥ VGS2 – VTN, i.e. Vout ≥ Vb – VTN).

Exactly the same current must flow through M1.  
If M1 is kept in saturation (VSD1 ≥ |VSG1| – |VTP|, i.e. Vout ≤ Vin – |VTP|),  

ID = ½ β1 (VDD – Vin – |VTP|)^2 (1 + λp VDS1)         (2)  

with VDS1 = VDD – Vout.

Equating (1) and (2) gives the dc transfer law of the stage:

½ β1 (VDD – Vin – |VTP|)^2 (1 + λp (VDD – Vout))  
            = ½ β2 (Vb – VTN)^2 (1 + λn Vout)             (3)

If channel-length modulation is ignored (λp = λn = 0) the relation is simple:

β1 (VDD – Vin – |VTP|)^2 = β2 (Vb – VTN)^2              (4)

so that the gate voltage that centres the output is

Vin(mid-point) = VDD – |VTP| – √(β2/β1) (Vb – VTN).      (5)

Whenever Vin is lower than the value given by (5) M1 conducts more than the
constant current pulled by M2, so the only way to match currents is to raise
Vout toward the supply; the output therefore sits at a high level.  
If Vin is raised above (5) M1 delivers too little current,
M2 pulls the node down, and Vout drops toward ground.  
Thus, in the large-signal sense, the stage works like an
inverting switch:

• Vin low  ⟶  Vout ≈ VDD (logic “1”)  
• Vin high ⟶  Vout ≈ 0 V (logic “0”)  

but the exact switching point is set by device sizes (β-ratio) and by the bias
voltage Vb that fixes the tail current.

Boundary conditions for validity of (4):

Vb – VTN  ≤ Vout ≤ Vin – |VTP|                 (both devices in sat.)  (6)

If either inequality is violated the transistor concerned moves into triode
and Vout is clamped close to a rail.

2. Small-signal (incremental) behaviour  

Bias the stage at some quiescent current ID (found from (3)).  
In saturation the small-signal parameters are

gm1 = ∂ID/∂VSG1 = √(2 β1 ID)           (p-device)  
ro1 = 1/(λp ID)  

gm2 = ∂ID/∂VGS2 = √(2 β2 ID)           (tail n-device)  
ro2 = 1/(λn ID)

Because the gate of M2 is fixed, its transconductance does not influence the
gain; only its output resistance does.  
With the usual small-signal half-circuit one obtains

AV = vout / vin = – gm1 (ro1 ∥ ro2)                (7)

Replacing gm1 and ro with the expressions above,

AV = – √(2 β1 ID) · 1 / [ ID (λp + λn) ]  
   ≈ – √(2 β1 / ID) / (λp + λn)                    (8)

Important observations:

• AV is negative – the node inverts the input.  
• |AV| rises if the bias current ID is reduced (1/√ID dependence) and if long
  channels are used (λ → 0).  
• With the intrinsic output resistance of both
  devices in parallel, ro sets the upper bound on gain.

3. What the circuit is good for

a) Digital point of view  
If Vb is chosen so that M2 sinks only a weak current, the inverter is
“pseudo-CMOS”: it consumes static current but can be used, for instance, as a
ratioed pull-up/pull-down element in low-performance logic.

b) Analog point of view  
With Vb selected to give a few tens of micro-amps, the stage is a very
compact voltage amplifier (common-source with active current mirror load).
It is the core of many op-amp input stages, one-stage OTAs and sense
amplifiers.

4. Summary of operating regions

1. Vin < VDD – |VTP| – √(β2/β1)(Vb – VTN)  
   – M1 strongly ON, M2 sets current  
   – Vout rises until VSD1 ≈ (VSG1 – |VTP|)sat → Vout ≈ VDD – VDS(sat)  
   – Output “high”.

2. Vin ≈ switching point  
   – Both devices in saturation  
   – Equation (3) determines exact Vout  
   – Highest small-signal gain.

3. Vin > VDD – |VTP| − √(β2/β1)(Vb – VTN)  
   – M1 nearly OFF, current forced through sub-threshold only  
   – M2 discharges node to ground  
   – Output “low”.

Because the tail device is always on, the stage exhibits static power
dissipation equal to VDD·ID.

That set of results—dc transfer law, small-signal gain expression, qualitative
logic function and range of validity—completely characterises the circuit
shown in the figure.

What the circuit is  
• Both transistors are n-channel MOSFETs.  
• M1 is connected with its drain at the supply, therefore the signal is taken from its source; this is a common-drain (source-follower) stage.  
• M2 has a constant gate-voltage Vb and works as an n-MOS current source that pulls the follower node toward ground.  

Hence the block is nothing more than an n-MOS source follower whose tail-current is furnished by another n-MOS device.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Large-signal (DC) analysis  

Notation  
β1 = μn Cox (W/L)1  β2 = μn Cox (W/L)2  
Vov2 = Vb – Vth2  (over-drive of M2)  
Assume both devices operate in saturation, i.e.  

 M1 (VDD – Vout) ≥ (Vin – Vout – Vth1)  (always true if Vin ≤ VDD)  
 M2 Vout ≥ (Vb – Vth2)

Step 1 – current of the bias transistor  

     ID2 = ½ β2 (Vb – Vth2)² = ½ β2 Vov2²        (1)

Step 2 – the same current must flow through M1  

     ID1 = ½ β1 (Vin – Vout – Vth1)²              (2)

Equating (1) and (2) gives the DC transfer characteristic

     Vin – Vout = Vth1 + √(β2/β1) (Vb – Vth2)     (3)

or, solving for the output

     Vout = Vin – Vth1 – √(β2/β1) (Vb – Vth2)     (4)

Observations  
• If M1 is made much wider than M2 (β1 ≫ β2) the second term is small and we get the familiar follower relation

     Vout ≈ Vin – Vth1

 i.e. the stage shifts the input down by one threshold voltage.  
• The lowest value the output can reach while M2 is still in saturation is

     Vout,min = Vb – Vth2                         (5)

• With Vin driven as high as VDD the highest obtainable output is

     Vout,max ≈ VDD – Vth1                        (6)

 (the follower can never rise all the way to the rail).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Small-signal (incremental) behaviour  

Small-signal parameters (at the bias current I)  

     gm1 = 2I / Vov1 , gm2 = 2I / Vov2  
     ro1 , ro2 = 1/λI (channel-length modulation)

Because Vb is a DC quantity, vgs2 = 0 in the small-signal model, so M2 contributes only its output resistance ro2.  
Writing KCL at the output node:

     gm1( vin – vout ) + vout/ro1 + vout/ro2 = 0

Hence the voltage gain is

     Av = vout / vin = gm1 / ( gm1 + 1/ro1 + 1/ro2 )     (7)

If both ro’s are large, Av → 1, which is the hallmark of a source follower.  
The output (small-signal) resistance is therefore

     Rout ≈ 1 / ( gm1 + 1/ro1 + 1/ro2 )   ≈ 1/gm1      (8)

and the input resistance is practically infinite (MOS gate).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Design guidelines / useful numbers  

1. Pick Vb so that Vov2 ≈ 0.15–0.25 V.  
   → This sets the bias current with (1) and fixes Vout,min via (5).  
2. Make M1 wide enough so that β1 ≫ β2; then the follower drop is almost one Vth and the small extra term in (4) can be neglected.  
3. Check that (5) ≤ the lowest signal level you ever need and that (6) ≥ the highest one.  
4. Verify that both transistors remain in saturation over the whole signal swing.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
What the circuit is useful for  

• Level-shifting a signal down by approximately one threshold voltage.  
• Buffering a high-impedance node while keeping the voltage loss (droop) small.  
• Source-degeneration or cascode bias networks in analog CMOS blocks.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Key results to remember  

DC:   Vout ≈ Vin – Vth1               (if β1 ≫ β2)  
Gain: Av ≈ 1                          (follower)  
Swing: Vb – Vth2  ≤  Vout ≤ VDD – Vth1

The drawing is the elementary CMOS inverter – a complementary pair consisting of  

• M₂ : a p-channel MOSFET whose source is tied to the positive supply VDD  
• M₁ : an n-channel MOSFET whose source is tied to ground  

The two drains are shorted to form the output node Vout, and the two gates are shorted to the input node Vin.  
Only one device conducts in the static states, so the quiescent (dc) power loss is ideally zero.

1. Logic (qualitative) operation  
   a) Vin ≈ 0 V → M₁ off (VGSₙ < VTN), M₂ on (VSGₚ > |VTP|) → Vout pulled to VDD (logic 1).  
   b) Vin ≈ VDD → M₂ off (VSGₚ < |VTP|), M₁ on (VGSₙ > VTN) → Vout pulled to 0 V (logic 0).  
   Thus the stage performs the NOT function.

2. D-C transfer characteristic  
   Let βn = μnCox(W/L)n and βp = μpCox(W/L)p.  
   In the transition region (VTN < Vin < VDD – |VTP|) the two devices conduct simultaneously and, to first order, both are in saturation. Equating their drain currents

          βn/2 · (Vin – Vout – VTN)²  =  βp/2 · (VDD – Vin – |VTP|)²        (1)

   gives Vout(Vin).  For the special case βn = βp and |VTP| = VTN the locus is

          Vout = 2Vin – VDD

   and the switching (mid-point) voltage, obtained by also requiring dVout/dVin = –1, is very close to VDD/2.  With unequal β–values the switching point is

          VM ≈ (VDD + |VTP| + √(βp/βn)·VTN) / (1 + √(βp/βn))

   which is centred by choosing (W/L)p ≈ (μn/μp)(W/L)n so that βp ≈ βn.

3. Noise margins  
   VIL and VIH are obtained from |dVout/dVin| = 1 in (1); the noise margins follow

          NML = VIL – VOL     ,     NMH = VOH – VIH
          VOL ≈ 0 , VOH ≈ VDD

   Because the gain |dVout/dVin| in the transition region can exceed 40–50, good noise margins (typically > 0.4 VDD) are obtained.

4. Dynamic behaviour  
   • Low-to-high delay (n-device releases load):

          tPLH ≈ Rp · CL ≈ CL / [βp (VDD – |VTP|)]                        

   • High-to-low delay (n-device pulls down):

          tPHL ≈ Rn · CL ≈ CL / [βn (VDD – VTN)]

   Matching βp to βn equalises the two delays.  
   Dynamic power: Pdyn = CL VDD² fCLK ; short-circuit power exists only for the brief time both devices conduct.

5. Key features that make the CMOS inverter the basic building block of modern digital ICs  
   • Rail-to-rail output swing (0 – VDD)  
   • Large noise margins determined mainly by device sizing, not by resistor ratios  
   • Essentially zero static power (only leakage)  
   • Symmetric transfer when βp ≈ βn, giving equal rise/fall delays  
   • Very high input resistance; fan-out determined by capacitive loading only

Hence the circuit in the figure is a standard complementary MOS inverter and its behaviour is completely described by the relations above.

The drawing is the standard complementary MOS (CMOS) inverter, built with one p-channel transistor (M2) and one n-channel transistor (M1).

1. Node connections  
   • M2 (pMOS): source → VDD, drain → Vout, gate → Vin  
   • M1 (nMOS): drain → Vout, source → GND, gate → Vin  
   • The two gates are shorted together, so both devices see the same input voltage.

2. Static (DC) behaviour  
   a. Vin = 0 V (logic 0)  
      – pMOS: VSG = VDD  ⇒ ON  
      – nMOS: VGS = 0     ⇒ OFF  
      ⇒ Vout is pulled up to VDD  (logic 1).

   b. Vin = VDD (logic 1)  
      – pMOS: VSG ≈ 0     ⇒ OFF  
      – nMOS: VGS = VDD   ⇒ ON  
      ⇒ Vout is pulled down to 0 V  (logic 0).

   c. Intermediate Vin  
      Both transistors conduct simultaneously; the exact switching point VM is obtained from
            βn (Vin – Vtn)² = βp (VDD – Vin – |Vtp|)²
      (βn = kn Wn/Ln, βp = kp Wp/Lp).  
      If βn ≈ βp, VM ≈ VDD/2, giving nearly equal noise margins.

3. Voltage-transfer characteristic (VTC)  
   • VOL ≈ 0 V, VOH ≈ VDD (rail-to-rail).  
   • High small-signal gain (–dVout/dVin) around VM.  
   • Noise margins:  NML = VIL – VOL,  NMH = VOH – VIH; with symmetric sizing both approach VDD/2.

4. Dynamic operation  
   – Only one device conducts strongly while the other is OFF, so static power ≈ 0.  
   – During transitions both devices momentarily conduct, creating a short-circuit current but only for nanoseconds.  
   – Dynamic (switching) power:  Pdyn = CL VDD² fsw.  
   – Propagation delays (first-order):  
         tPHL ≈ 0.69 RN CL,  tPLH ≈ 0.69 RP CL,  
     where RN and RP are the equivalent on-resistances of the n- and p-devices.  
     Because μn ≈ 2–3 μp, designers make Wp ≈ 2–3 Wn to equalise tPHL and tPLH.

5. Summary of merits and drawbacks  
   + Rail-to-rail output swing  
   + Large noise margin  
   + Essentially zero static power  
   + Simple to cascade (output of one can directly drive the input of the next)  
   – Requires both n- and p-type devices (larger area than a single-device pull-up inverter).

Hence the circuit is a CMOS inverter that produces the logical complement of the input while delivering high switching speed, low static dissipation, and robust noise immunity.

The drawing is the textbook “static-CMOS inverter”, made with one p-channel MOSFET (M2) in series with one n-channel MOSFET (M1).  
• The two gates are shorted together and driven by the input node Vin.  
• The two drains are shorted together and form the output node Vout.  
• M2’s source is tied to the positive supply VDD; M1’s source is tied to ground.

1. Logical behaviour  
   – Vin = 0 (logic “0”):  
     • NMOS: VGS-N = 0 < Vthn  → OFF.  
     • PMOS: VSG-P = VDD > |Vthp| → ON, pulls Vout → VDD.  
     Result: Vout ≈ VDD (logic “1”).  
   – Vin = VDD (logic “1”):  
     • PMOS: VSG-P = 0 < |Vthp| → OFF.  
     • NMOS: VGS-N = VDD > Vthn → ON, pulls Vout → 0.  
     Result: Vout ≈ 0 (logic “0”).  

   Hence the circuit inverts the input.

2. Regions of operation  
   • For Vin ≤ Vthn  → NMOS off, PMOS on (usually linear once Vout reaches VDD).  
   • For Vin ≥ VDD – |Vthp|  → PMOS off, NMOS on.  
   • For intermediate Vin both transistors conduct simultaneously; this is the only time a d.c. path exists between VDD and ground.

3. Static transfer characteristic  
   Ignoring channel-length modulation and using the square-law model,

     Idn = (βn/2)(Vin – Vthn)²  (saturation, since Vout ≈ Vin)  
     Idp = (βp/2)(VDD – Vin – |Vthp|)²

   At the switching point VM (Vin = Vout, Idn = Idp):

     (VM – Vthn)² / (VDD – VM – |Vthp|)² = βp / βn

     ⇒ VM = ( VDD + |Vthp| + √(βn/βp)·Vthn ) / (1 + √(βn/βp))

   With matched devices (βn ≈ βp, |Vthp| ≈ Vthn) the trip point is close to VDD/2, giving a symmetrical VTC and large noise margins.

4. Noise margins and logic levels  
   VOH ≈ VDD,  VOL ≈ 0  
   VIL and VIH are found where |dVout/dVin| = –1 on the VTC.  
   NMH = VOH – VIH,  NML = VIL – VOL  
   Because the gain around VM is large, NMH and NML are typically close to VDD/2.

5. Power  
   • Static power: essentially zero, because in either stable state one transistor is OFF, so no direct path exists from VDD to ground (leakage excepted).  
   • Dynamic power: Pd ≈ α·CL·VDD²·fclk + Pshort, where Pshort is the brief shoot-through current that flows while Vin is crossing the transition region.

6. Propagation delay (with load capacitance CL)  
   tpHL ≈ CL·(VDD – VM) / Idsn(Vin = VDD)  
   tpLH ≈ CL·VM / Idsp(Vin = 0)  
   With equal β’s the high-to-low and low-to-high delays are comparable.

Summary  
The circuit is the fundamental CMOS inverter:  
• Rail-to-rail output swing (0 → VDD).  
• Very small static power.  
• Large noise margins and steep transfer characteristic.  
• Propagation delays and switching threshold that can be tailored through the βn/βp ratio.

The network is the basic CMOS (complementary-MOS) inverter.

1. Which device is which  
   • M1, the transistor tied to VDD, must be a p–channel MOSFET.  
     – Source at VDD, drain at the output node.  
   • M2, the transistor tied to ground, is an n-channel MOSFET.  
     – Drain at the output node, source at ground.  
   (If the upper device were n-channel its body diode would conduct whenever
   VDD > ground, so the circuit could not work.)

2. Logic (static) operation  
   a) Vin ≈ 0 V (logic 0)  
      – M1 : VSG = VDD > |VTP|  → ON  
      – M2 : VGS = 0            → OFF  
      → Output node pulled to VDD → VOH ≈ VDD (logic 1).  
      – No steady dc current because only the p-device conducts.

   b) Vin ≈ VDD (logic 1)  
      – M1 : VSG = 0            → OFF  
      – M2 : VGS = VDD > VTN    → ON  
      → Output node pulled to 0 V → VOL ≈ 0 (logic 0).  
      – Again no dc current; only the n-device conducts.

   c) Vin in the middle (around the switching point VM)  
      – Both devices partially ON; for a brief time there is a
        current path VDD → M1 → M2 → ground (the “shoot-through” or
        “crowbar” current).  This happens only while the input is
        switching, so the static power of the gate is essentially zero.

   Hence the gate produces the logical NOT of its input with rail-to-rail
   swing and almost zero static power-dissipation, which is why it is the
   work-horse of modern digital ICs.

3. Transfer characteristic and trip point VM  
   Using the long-channel square-law model in saturation and equating the
   drain currents of the two devices at the transition point:

        βn (VM – VTN)^2 = βp (VDD – VM – |VTP|)^2
        β ≜ μ Cox (W/L)

   Solving,

        VM = (βp (VDD + |VTP|) + βn VTN) / (βn + βp)

   • If |VTP| = VTN and the devices are sized so that βn = βp,
     VM = VDD / 2 (symmetrical inverter).

4. Noise margins (ideal abrupt transition)  

        NML ≈ VM – VOL       (≈ VM, because VOL ≈ 0)
        NMH ≈ VOH – VM       (≈ VDD – VM)

   For the symmetric case, NML ≈ NMH ≈ VDD/2 – VT, giving large
   tolerance to noise on both logic levels.

5. Dynamic behaviour with a load capacitance CL  

        tPHL ≈ (CL VDD) / (βn (VDD – VTN))   (high-to-low delay)  
        tPLH ≈ (CL VDD) / (βp (VDD – |VTP|)) (low-to-high delay)

   Delays are adjusted in practice by the W/L ratio (i.e. β) of the two
   transistors; typically the p-device is made wider to compensate for its
   lower mobility (µp ≈ 0.4 µn).

6. Power dissipation  

        Pstatic   ≈ 0                       (only leakage paths)  
        Pdynamic  = CL VDD² fSW             (plus the brief shoot-through
                                             component while Vin ≈ VM)

Summary  
The circuit is a complementary push-pull stage that inverts the input,
switches all the way between 0 V and VDD, exhibits large noise margins,
draws essentially no dc power, and forms the fundamental building block
for all CMOS digital logic.

The drawing is nothing more than the basic CMOS inverter.

•  M1 is a p-channel MOSFET whose drain is tied to VDD and whose source is the output node.  
•  M2 is an n-channel MOSFET whose source is tied to ground and whose drain is the same output node.  
•  The two gates are shorted together and driven by Vin.

1. Qualitative operation (logic level description)

   Vin = 0 (LOW)  
  Vgp = 0 − VDD = –VDD < Vthp ⟶ M1 ON  
  Vgn = 0           ⟶ M2 OFF  
  Output is pulled up to VDD  →  logic “1”

   Vin = VDD (HIGH)  
  Vgp = VDD − VDD = 0     ⟶ M1 OFF  
  Vgn = VDD > Vthn      ⟶ M2 ON  
  Output is pulled down to 0 V  →  logic “0”

   For Vin in the transition region both devices conduct simultaneously; a short-lived “crowbar” current flows from VDD to ground, giving the inverter its characteristic steep transfer curve.

2. DC transfer characteristic

   Treat both transistors as long-channel devices and assume they enter saturation around the switching point.  
   Idn = (βn/2)(Vin − Vthn)^2  
   Idp = (βp/2)(VDD − Vin − |Vthp|)^2  

   The switching threshold V­M is found from Idn = Idp :

        Vin − Vthn
   ----------------------  =  √(βp/βn)
    VDD − Vin − |Vthp|

   If βn ≈ βp and |Vthp| ≈ Vthn, VM ≈ VDD/2, which gives the inverter its large, almost symmetric noise margins.

3. Static power

   •  In either logic state one transistor is OFF, so the DC current is essentially zero (ideal CMOS draws no static power).  
   •  Only during switching do both devices conduct simultaneously, producing a short dynamic current spike.

4. Logic truth table

        Vin   Vout
        0  →  1
        1  →  0

   Hence the circuit implements the NOT function.

5. Key properties

   •  Rail-to-rail output swing (0 V and VDD).  
   •  Large noise margins ≈ ⅔ VDD (for symmetrical devices).  
   •  Very low static power dissipation.  
   •  High input impedance.

In summary, the two-transistor stack with a common gate connection is the fundamental CMOS inverter: it produces the logical complement of the input while dissipating power only during switching.

The two transistors form the elementary CMOS inverter (NOT gate).

1. Circuit topology  
   • M1: p-channel MOSFET (source tied to VDD).  
   • M2: n-channel MOSFET (source tied to ground).  
   • Drains of M1 and M2 are shorted; that node is Vout.  
   • Gates are shorted and driven by Vin.

2. Static (DC) operation  
   a) Vin ≈ 0 V  
      – NMOS: VGS = 0  ⇒ OFF  
      – PMOS: VSG = VDD > |VTp| ⇒ ON  
      – Vout is pulled up to VDD (logic ‘1’).  
      – No DC path from VDD to GND → zero static current.  

   b) Vin ≈ VDD  
      – NMOS: VGS = VDD > VTn ⇒ ON  
      – PMOS: VSG = 0  ⇒ OFF  
      – Vout is pulled to ground (logic ‘0’).  
      – Again no DC through-current.

   Result: the gate inverts the input, giving rail-to-rail logic levels  
        VOH ≈ VDD ,  VOL ≈ 0.

3. Switching point (VM)  
   Around the mid-range both devices conduct simultaneously.  
   Assuming both are in saturation and equating their drain currents

        IDn = βn/2 (Vin – VTn)²  
        IDp = βp/2 (VDD – Vin – |VTp|)²

        βn(Vin – VTn)² = βp(VDD – Vin – |VTp|)²

        VM = [VTn + k(VDD – |VTp|)] / (1 + k) ,
        k = √(βp/βn)  ,  β = μCox(W/L).

   Choosing W/L so that k ≈ 1 places VM near VDD/2 and yields large, nearly symmetrical noise
   margins
        NMH ≈ VDD – VM ,  NML ≈ VM.

4. Dynamic behaviour  
   • Only a short-lived current flows from VDD to GND while Vin crosses VM, so static power is
     essentially zero.  
   • With a load capacitance C_L,

        tpHL ≈ Rn C_L ,  tpLH ≈ Rp C_L ,
        tp ≈ (tpHL + tpLH)/2.

     Rn and Rp are the on-resistances evaluated at the appropriate overdrive voltages.  
   • Average dynamic power: Pdyn = α C_L VDD² f (α = switching activity factor).

5. Key advantages  
   – Full-swing outputs (0 → VDD).  
   – Large noise margins.  
   – Very low quiescent power.  
   – Basis of all static CMOS logic.

Hence the figure is the canonical CMOS inverter, and its behaviour is completely described by the transfer point VM derived above, the rail-to-rail output levels, the large noise margins, and the very low static power dissipation.

The little two-transistor cell is nothing more than

• an n-channel MOSFET (M1) used as a common-source transistor whose gate is the input, and  
• a p-channel MOSFET (M2) whose gate is shorted to its drain, i.e. a “diode–connected” PMOS that behaves like a non-linear load tied to VDD.

Because the load is an active device rather than a passive resistor this structure is usually called a
“CMOS active-load inverter” or “common-source stage with PMOS load”.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.   Useful notation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Vtn  = threshold of the NMOS  ( >0 )  
|Vtp|= absolute value of the PMOS threshold ( >0 )  
βn   = kn(W/L)n = μnCox(W/L)n      ( A/V² )  
βp   = kp(W/L)p = μpCox(W/L)p      ( A/V² )  
α    = √(βp/βn)                    (mobility- and size-weighted ratio)

We neglect channel-length modulation (λ≈0) to keep the algebra short; it does not change the
qualitative conclusions.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.   DC operating regions and the transfer characteristic Vout(Vin)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
REGION 1 :  Vin < Vtn
   • M1 is OFF (Id1≈0).
